C0161.d: The ABS or traction control module has detected an implausible signal from the brake light switch. The switch tells the module whether the driver is braking and is used to inhibit traction control during braking.

c: Outlet solenoid valve failed
Internal hydraulic unit fault
C0163.d: Electrical fault in the outlet solenoid for the left rear wheel. ABS pressure release for this wheel is no longer possible.
C0163.t: Left Rear ABS Outlet Solenoid Circuit Malfunction

c: Inlet solenoid valve failed
Internal hydraulic unit fault
C0168.d: Electrical fault in the inlet solenoid for the right rear wheel. ABS is disabled while the fault is active.
C0168.t: Right Rear ABS Inlet Solenoid Circuit Malfunction

c: Outlet solenoid valve failed
Internal hydraulic unit fault
C0173.d: Electrical fault in the outlet solenoid for the right rear wheel. ABS pressure release for this wheel is no longer possible.
C0173.t: Right Rear ABS Outlet Solenoid Circuit Malfunction

c: Lateral acceleration sensor failed or drifted
Sensor mounting loose or misaligned after body repair
Calibration after replacement not performed
C0185.d: The stability control module has detected that the lateral acceleration sensor signal is out of the expected range or does not match other inertial sensors. ESP and roll-stability functions may be disabled.

c: Lateral acceleration sensor failed
Sensor cluster loose or mounted incorrectly
Wiring or connector fault
C0186.d: The stability control module has detected an implausible signal from the lateral acceleration sensor. ESP uses lateral g-force together with yaw rate and steering angle to detect skid conditions — without it, ESP is disabled.

c: Yaw rate sensor failed
Sensor not calibrated after replacement or alignment
Wiring or connector fault
C0196.d: The stability control module has detected an implausible signal from the yaw rate sensor. The yaw sensor measures rotation around the vertical axis and is essential for ESP — a fault disables stability control.

c: Solenoid coil open
Internal short to ground in valve block
C0200.d: The ABS control module detects a fault in the inlet/outlet solenoid for the front left brake circuit. The valve is integrated in the hydraulic block; replacement is generally a workshop task.
C0200.t: ABS Solenoid Valve Front Left Circuit

c: Brake fluid level low (worn pads or hydraulic leak)
Float switch in reservoir failed
Wiring or connector fault
C0201.d: The ABS or brake control module has detected a fault in the brake fluid level switch circuit. A low fluid level indicates a potential leak in the hydraulic system and disables ABS while a separate brake warning lamp is illuminated.

c: Pedal position sensor failed
Sensor not calibrated after replacement
Wiring or connector fault
C0202.d: The chassis or brake control module has detected an implausible signal from the brake pedal position sensor. Modern brake systems use this sensor for brake assist, regenerative braking and adaptive cruise control functions.

c: Solenoid coil open
Internal short to ground
C0203.d: Fault in the front right ABS solenoid (mirror of C0200).
C0203.t: ABS Solenoid Valve Front Right Circuit

c: Stop lamp switch failed or misadjusted
Wiring or connector fault
Blown stop lamp fuse
C0205.d: The ABS or stability control module has detected a fault in the stop lamp switch circuit. The brake light switch tells the module whether the driver is braking and is used to coordinate ABS, traction control and cruise control.

c: Solenoid coil open
Internal short to ground
C0206.d: Fault in the rear left ABS solenoid valve.
C0206.t: ABS Solenoid Valve Rear Left Circuit

c: Solenoid coil open
Internal short to ground
C0209.d: Fault in the rear right ABS solenoid valve.
C0209.t: ABS Solenoid Valve Rear Right Circuit

c: Battery undervoltage
Ground point corroded
C0220.d: Supply voltage to the ABS valve block is out of range, disabling all valve control.

c: Valve relay failed
Relay control circuit open
C0225.d: The valve relay supplying the ABS solenoids does not respond as commanded.

c: Sensor failed
Pedal linkage loose, biasing sensor
C0230.d: The brake pedal position sensor reports an implausible signal. Required for brake-by-wire and stability control.

c: Tone ring damaged, missing teeth, or contaminated
Sensor air gap incorrect (loose mounting)
Wheel speed sensor degraded
C0234.d: The ABS control module has detected that one of the wheel speed sensor signals has a frequency outside the plausible range, e.g. unrealistically high pulses or signal dropouts at speed. Stability control may be limited.

c: Tone ring damaged or contaminated with metal debris
Wheel speed sensor loose in housing
Excessive hub bearing play
C0235.d: The ABS control module has detected an erratic wheel speed sensor signal — sudden jumps or dropouts compared to the other wheels. Typical causes are a damaged tone ring or a loose sensor.

c: Wheel speed sensor failed
Wiring break at wheel arch
Tone ring damaged
C0237.d: The ABS control module has lost the wheel speed signal from the front left wheel during driving. ABS and stability control are disabled because wheel-individual speed information is required for slip detection.
C0237.t: Loss of Speed Sensor Signal Front Left

c: Tyre sizes or wear levels do not match across axles
Tone ring missing teeth on one wheel
Wheel speed sensor degraded
C0238.d: The ABS control module has detected an implausible speed difference between wheels that cannot be explained by cornering. This typically points to one suspect sensor, mismatched tyre sizes or a damaged tone ring.

c: Brake pressure sensor failed
Wiring or connector fault
Air in brake system
C0240.d: The ABS or stability control module has detected a fault in a brake pressure sensor. Pressure information is used by ESP and brake assist to determine driver intent and modulation pressure during regulation.

c: Lamp bulb/LED failed
Control wiring shorted
C0241.d: The ABS warning lamp control circuit is shorted or open. The driver may see a permanently lit or non-functional ABS warning lamp.

c: Traction control torque request fault
Bus communication loss
C0242.d: The powertrain control module reports a fault that the ABS module must consider (e.g. traction control engine torque request fault).

c: Module PWM output stage fault
C0244.d: The PWM control of the brake pressure modulation valves is faulty.

c: Tone ring damaged or contaminated
Wheel speed sensor degraded
Tyre size mismatch
C0245.d: The ABS control module has detected that the frequency of one wheel speed sensor signal does not match the others under stable driving conditions. This often indicates a tone ring with extra or missing teeth or a sensor with degraded signal quality.

c: Module internal fault
C0246.d: Internal plausibility check of the combined ABS/TCS control module fails.

c: Power steering fluid low or contaminated
Power steering pump worn
Pressure sensor failed
C0250.d: The power steering control module has detected an implausible pressure or load signal from the steering pump. On hydraulic systems this may indicate low fluid or a worn pump; on electric systems it may indicate excessive motor load.

c: Ground strap corroded
Ground wire broken
Pin pushed back out of connector body
C0252.d: The pump motor ground return is open. The motor cannot run, and the system disables ABS and stability control.

c: Vacuum hose leak
Sensor failed
C0258.d: The brake booster vacuum sensor reports an implausible signal; brake assist functions are reduced. The vacuum sensor tells the brake control module how much vacuum is stored in the booster; with too little vacuum the assist drops, so the module uses the signal to request more vacuum (electric pump or engine intervention) or to add hydraulic brake assist. If power assist is lost, the brakes still work through the master cylinder, but a much higher pedal force is needed.
s: Brake system warning lamp or message
Firmer brake pedal, longer pedal travel or higher pedal force
Driver-assistance functions such as automatic emergency braking or adaptive cruise control may be disabled

c: EBCM relay failed
Internal EBCM fault (relay integrated)
Power supply wiring or fuse fault
C0265.d: The Electronic Brake Control Module has detected a fault in its main supply relay circuit. Without proper relay supply the EBCM cannot operate the hydraulic unit and ABS as well as stability control are disabled.

c: Active booster motor or solenoid failed
Vacuum supply weak (vacuum pump or hose fault)
Wiring or connector fault
C0266.d: The brake control module has detected a fault in the active (electric or vacuum-controlled) brake booster. Active boosters are used by emergency brake assist and adaptive cruise control to autonomously build brake pressure.

c: Brake pump motor failed
Pump motor relay failed
Power supply wiring fault
C0267.d: The ABS or brake control module has detected an electrical fault in the brake pump motor circuit. The pump is used to build brake pressure during ABS, ESP and brake-by-wire operations and a fault disables these functions.

c: Hydraulic leak in brake system
Air in brake system
Brake pump worn or weak
C0268.d: The brake control module has detected that the brake pump has run longer than the allowed maximum time. This typically indicates the pump cannot reach target pressure due to a hydraulic leak, air in the system or a worn pump.

c: Vacuum sensor failed
Leak in vacuum supply line
Vacuum pump weak
C0269.d: The brake control module has detected an implausible signal from the vacuum sensor on the brake booster. Modern systems monitor booster vacuum to ensure brake assist is available, especially with stop-start engines and electric vacuum pumps.

c: Booster pressure sensor failed
Wiring or connector fault to sensor
C0273.d: The brake control module has detected an out-of-range or implausible signal from the brake booster pressure sensor. Brake assist and electronic boost functions may be limited.
C0273.t: Brake Booster Pressure Sensor Circuit Malfunction

c: Vacuum sensor failed
Vacuum leak in booster or hose
C0277.d: The brake control module has detected an implausible signal from the booster vacuum sensor. Loss of vacuum signal can cause hard pedal and reduced power assist.
C0277.t: Brake Booster Vacuum Sensor Circuit Malfunction

c: Boost sensor failed
Sensor wiring or connector fault
C0279.d: The brake control module has detected an electrical fault in the booster boost (assist pressure) sensor circuit. Power-assist regulation may default to a backup strategy.
C0279.t: Brake Booster Boost Sensor Circuit Malfunction

c: Sensor calibration required after repair
Sensor cluster loose or mounted incorrectly
Secondary fault on individual sensor
C0287.d: The stability control module has detected that overall ESP performance is degraded — typically a plausibility check between yaw rate, lateral acceleration, steering angle and wheel speeds has failed. ESP is deactivated until the root cause is resolved.

c: Sensor not calibrated
Yaw rate sensor failed
Sensor cluster mounted incorrectly
C0288.d: The stability control module has detected that the yaw rate sensor signal is outside the plausible range during stable driving. This typically indicates a sensor offset, an incorrect mounting or a degraded sensor element.

c: Pedal stroke sensor failed
Sensor mounting or pedal linkage misadjusted
C0290.d: The brake control module has detected an out-of-range signal from the brake pedal stroke sensor. Pedal travel information is required for brake assist and electronically boosted braking.
C0290.t: Brake Pedal Stroke Sensor Circuit Malfunction

c: Pedal apply sensor failed
Wiring or connector fault
C0291.d: Electrical fault in the brake pedal apply sensor circuit. The module cannot reliably detect whether the brake pedal is pressed, which affects ABS, ESP and brake assist functions.
C0291.t: Brake Pedal Apply Sensor Circuit Malfunction

c: Steering angle sensor calibration required
Wheel alignment incorrect
Steering angle sensor failed
C0295.d: The stability control module has detected that the steering wheel position sensor reports a non-zero angle when the vehicle is driving straight. This bias makes ESP intervene incorrectly and the system requires recalibration.

c: Valve stuck due to brake fluid debris
Coil resistance drift
C0300.d: The front left inlet solenoid valve does not respond hydraulically as expected during ABS self-test.

c: Compressor relay failed
Relay wiring or fuse fault
Internal module fault
C0301.d: The air suspension control module has detected a fault in the compressor relay circuit. The compressor cannot be energized which prevents the system from refilling the air struts and ride height drops over time.

c: Valve stuck
Coil resistance drift
C0302.d: The front left outlet solenoid valve does not respond hydraulically as expected.

c: Valve stuck
Coil resistance drift
C0303.d: The front right inlet solenoid valve does not respond hydraulically as expected.

c: Valve stuck
Coil resistance drift
C0304.d: The front right outlet solenoid valve does not respond hydraulically as expected.

c: Valve stuck
Coil resistance drift
C0305.d: The rear left inlet solenoid valve does not respond hydraulically as expected.

c: Ride height sensor failed
Sensor linkage broken or detached
Wiring or connector fault
C0306.d: Ride Height Sensor Front Left: the control module has detected this fault condition. Without this signal the suspension control module cannot self-level the vehicle.

c: Valve stuck
Coil resistance drift
C0307.d: The rear right inlet solenoid valve does not respond hydraulically as expected.

c: Ride height sensor failed
Sensor linkage broken or detached
Wiring or connector fault
C0308.d: Ride Height Sensor Front Right: the control module has detected this fault condition. Without this signal the suspension control module cannot self-level the vehicle.

c: Valve stuck
Coil resistance drift
C0309.d: The rear right outlet solenoid valve does not respond hydraulically as expected.

c: Ride height sensor failed
Sensor linkage broken or detached
Wiring or connector fault
C0310.d: Ride Height Sensor Rear Left: the control module has detected this fault condition. Without this signal the suspension control module cannot self-level the vehicle.

c: Ride height sensor failed
Sensor linkage broken or detached
Wiring or connector fault
C0312.d: Ride Height Sensor Rear Right: the control module has detected this fault condition. Without this signal the suspension control module cannot self-level the vehicle.

c: Compressor relay failed (stuck or open)
Compressor motor shorted, dragging supply down
Relay wiring or connector fault
C0317.d: The air suspension control module has detected a circuit fault on the compressor relay output — typically open circuit, short to ground or short to power. Self-levelling is disabled and the vehicle may sit lower than normal.

c: Encoder motor failed (worn brushes or seized)
Wiring or connector fault
Internal control module fault
C0327.d: The transfer case control module has detected a fault in the encoder motor used to shift between 2WD and 4WD ranges. A fault prevents range changes and may leave the transfer case in an undefined position.

c: Coupling actuator failed
Coupling oil overheated
Wiring or connector fault
C0374.d: The 4WD or AWD control module has detected a fault on the electronic drive coupling that distributes torque between axles. Reduced torque transfer or a complete loss of all-wheel drive function may result.

c: Disconnect actuator failed (motor or solenoid)
Wiring or connector fault
Axle position switch failed
C0376.d: The 4WD control module has detected a fault on the front axle disconnect actuator. On part-time AWD vehicles this actuator decouples the front axle for fuel saving, and a fault prevents engagement or disengagement of front-wheel drive.

c: Transfer case position sensor failed
Wiring or connector fault
Encoder motor stuck between positions
C0387.d: The transfer case control module has detected an implausible signal from the position sensor that reports the current shift position (2HI, 4HI, 4LO, neutral). Without a valid position the system cannot complete a range change.

c: High range position switch failed
Shift actuator out of position
C0388.d: The transfer case control module has detected an implausible state from the high range (4H) position switch. Range selection in 4WD mode may be limited.
C0388.t: Transfer Case High Range Switch Circuit Malfunction

c: Low range position switch failed
Shift actuator out of position
C0389.d: The transfer case control module has detected an implausible state from the low range (4L) position switch. Engagement of low range may be inhibited.
C0389.t: Transfer Case Low Range Switch Circuit Malfunction

c: Mode selector switch failed
Wiring or connector fault
C0399.d: The transfer case or 4WD control module has detected an invalid signal from the driver-operated 4WD mode selector. Mode requests from the dashboard may be ignored.

c: Solenoid coil open
Short to ground
C0400.d: The dedicated traction control isolation valve in the hydraulic block reports an electrical fault.

c: Switch failed
Wiring shorted
C0401.d: The TCS on/off switch reports an implausible state.

c: Indicator bulb/LED failed
Wiring shorted
C0402.d: The TCS indicator lamp control circuit is shorted or open.

c: Persistent low-friction surface
Wheel speed sensor drift
C0405.d: TCS regulation has been continuously active longer than allowed, suggesting persistent low-friction conditions or a sensor fault.

c: Radar sensor blocked by snow, ice or dirt
Sensor misaligned after front-end impact
Radar/lidar sensor failed
C0410.d: The adaptive cruise control module has detected a fault in its forward-looking radar or lidar sensor circuit. ACC and forward collision warning are unavailable while the fault is active.
C0410.t: Adaptive Cruise Control Sensor Circuit Malfunction

c: ACC module internal fault
Supply voltage out of range
Module configuration invalid after part exchange
C0420.d: The adaptive cruise control module has reported an internal performance fault — for example self-test failure, supply voltage out of range or invalid configuration. ACC is disabled.
C0420.t: Adaptive Cruise Control Module Internal Performance

c: Steering angle sensor failed
Clock spring damaged
C0440.d: The steering angle sensor reports an electrical fault. ESC and lane keeping assistance functions are typically disabled.

c: Calibration not performed after alignment/repair
C0445.d: The steering angle sensor has not been calibrated after a service operation, or the calibration value is implausible.

c: Sensor failed
Actuator harness chafe
C0450.d: On vehicles with active rear wheel steering, the rear position sensor reports an electrical fault. The system disables rear steering.
C0450.t: Rear Wheel Steering Position Sensor Circuit

c: Steering angle sensor failed
Sensor not calibrated after alignment
Wiring or connector fault
C0455.d: The chassis or stability control module has detected a fault in the steering wheel position sensor circuit. ESP and lane assist systems require an accurate steering angle and may be deactivated.

c: Wheel alignment off after impact
Sensor drift
C0460.d: Steering angle signal is implausible compared with yaw rate, lateral acceleration and wheel speeds.

c: Yaw rate sensor failed
Wiring shorted
C0496.d: The yaw rate sensor reports an electrical fault. ESC is disabled while the fault is active.

c: Sensor drift with age
Sensor mounting loose
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
C0497.d: The yaw rate sensor signal is implausible relative to steering angle and lateral acceleration.

c: Sensor failed
Wiring open
C0498.d: The lateral acceleration sensor reports an electrical fault.

c: Sensor drift
Sensor mounting loose
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
C0499.d: The lateral acceleration sensor signal is outside the plausibility range.

c: Underlying ABS fault disables function
Communication bus fault to ABS module
C0500.d: A general status code indicating that ABS function has been disabled by the brake control module. It is set in addition to the underlying root-cause code that disabled ABS.
C0500.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor A Circuit/Open

c: Brake pads heavily worn
Hydraulic block internal wear
C0501.d: ESC interventions occur but do not produce the expected vehicle response. May indicate hydraulic or mechanical limitation.
C0501.t: Left Front Wheel Speed Sensor A Range/Performance

c: Signal wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
C0502.d: Left-front wheel speed sensor A signal voltage below expected range. Wheel-speed signals feed ABS, ESC, traction control, transmission and odometer — a single dropped signal disables all of these safety functions until repaired.

In an electromechanical booster an electric motor drives a gear stage that pushes on the master cylinder piston; some designs split the motor into two windings or channels, A and B, so that one can keep working if the other fails. If power assist is lost, the brakes still work through the master cylinder, but a much higher pedal force is needed.

P0001.d: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. P0001 is set when the control module detects that the control circuit of this valve is open, i.e. no plausible current flows when the valve is driven. Rail pressure can then no longer be controlled as intended. Whether the valve is open or closed without current depends on the design, so the same fault can cause excess pressure in one system and no pressure in another.
s: Engine cranks but does not start, or stalls (normally closed valve)

P0002.d: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. With P0002 the circuit is electrically intact, but command and effect do not match: the measured current does not fit the duty cycle, or rail pressure does not follow the regulator position plausibly. P000A.d: This monitor does not judge the end position of the intake camshaft on bank 1 but how fast it follows a change of the commanded angle. The code is set when the actual angle lags behind the target for too long during several adjustments. P000E.d: The fuel volume regulator (also called metering unit or suction control valve) is a solenoid valve on the inlet side of the high-pressure pump, used mainly on common-rail diesel engines. The engine control module pulses it to set how much fuel the pump draws in and delivers to the rail, and in this way controls rail pressure. To compensate for tolerances and wear, the control module learns a long-term correction of the regulator control. P000E is set when this correction leaves its calibrated range. The regulator is electrically fine, but the system needs an unusually large correction all the time, which points to wear or contamination of regulator or pump, a weak low-pressure supply, or a missing calibration after a pump replacement.

P000F.d: On common-rail diesel and some gasoline direct-injection systems a spring-loaded pressure relief valve protects the rail and injectors: if pressure rises too far, it opens and returns fuel to the tank, often holding a reduced pressure for limp-home operation. The control module recognises the opening from the rail pressure signal and stores P000F. The code reports an event, not a defect of the relief valve itself; the actual cause usually lies in pressure control, for example a regulator that delivers too much fuel.

P003A.d: The electric boost actuator A positions the variable turbine vanes or the wastegate and reports its position through a sensor. In a learning run, for example with the engine warm at idle or after switching off, the control module drives the actuator to its mechanical end stops and stores the sensor values as reference. P003A is set when a learned end position or the total travel lies outside the permitted limits. Typical reasons are worn or sticking vanes or linkage, a faulty actuator, a broken actuator lever, or a replacement actuator that has not been learned in. P003C.d: The camshaft profile actuator A switches the intake camshaft (camshaft A) on bank 1 between fixed cam profiles, usually a low-lift base profile and a high-lift profile. In most designs the unactuated state ("off") is the base profile; which profile counts as "on" is defined by the manufacturer. The control module does not need a position sensor to check the switchover: it detects the actual profile indirectly, for example from oil pressure in the switching gallery, intake pressure per cylinder or crankshaft speed fluctuations. This code is set when the switchover is commanded but the camshaft stays on the base profile, or switches too slowly or incompletely. The engine then lacks power at higher engine speed.

P0040.d: On engines with two exhaust banks, the control module checks whether the upstream oxygen sensors are assigned to the right bank. It changes the mixture on one bank only, actively or as part of normal bank-wise control, and watches which sensor responds. If the sensor that should sit on the other bank reacts, the signals are swapped. This logic is documented for the manufacturer-specific predecessor codes; the usual cause is connectors plugged in crosswise after a repair. If the swap remains, each bank is controlled by the other bank's signal, so fuel trims drift towards their limits.
s: Fuel trim and mixture codes possible
Unstable idle or higher consumption possible

P0045.d: "Boost control A" is the electrically driven actuator the engine control module uses to set boost pressure: depending on the engine a pulse-width modulated solenoid or vacuum converter at the wastegate, the control valve of variable turbine vanes, or an electric actuator with position feedback. The letters A and B denote two separate actuators, for example on the low- and high-pressure turbocharger of a two-stage system, not the cylinder banks. This code is set when the control circuit is open: with the driver switched off no load can be measured, or the measured state does not match the command. P005A.d: The camshaft profile actuator A switches the exhaust camshaft (camshaft B) on bank 1 between fixed cam profiles, usually a low-lift base profile and a high-lift profile. In most designs the unactuated state ("off") is the base profile; which profile counts as "on" is defined by the manufacturer. The control module does not need a position sensor to check the switchover: it detects the actual profile indirectly, for example from oil pressure in the switching gallery, intake pressure per cylinder or crankshaft speed fluctuations. This code is set when the switchover is commanded but the camshaft stays on the base profile, or switches too slowly or incompletely. The engine then lacks power at higher engine speed.

P005E.d: "Boost control B" is the electrically driven actuator the engine control module uses to set boost pressure: depending on the engine a pulse-width modulated solenoid or vacuum converter at the wastegate, the control valve of variable turbine vanes, or an electric actuator with position feedback. This code concerns the supply voltage that the control module switches to the actuator (high side): it is too low, for example because of a short to ground or an open circuit. P0065.d: Air-assisted injectors have an air sleeve around the nozzle tip: air flowing past at high speed breaks the fuel spray into finer droplets, which improves combustion and cold starts and lowers hydrocarbon emissions. On port-injected engines this air is taken upstream of the throttle and dosed by a pulse-width modulated bypass solenoid; because it bypasses the throttle, it is part of the idle air. The system is rare and mainly found on older engines. P0065 means the control is electrically in order, but the effect is implausible. One documented method compares the idle speed controller correction with the air assistance switched on and off during stable idle; if the difference is too large, the code is set.

P0068.d: The engine control module compares the air quantity measured by the manifold pressure and/or mass air flow sensor with the quantity the throttle position leads it to expect. P0068 is set when they do not match, typically because more air arrives than the nearly closed throttle allows, i.e. an air leak behind the throttle, or because the throttle body is dirty or a sensor reads wrong. On engines with electronic throttle this check protects throttle control, so the engine often goes into reduced power. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.

c: Manifold pressure sensor drifting
MAP sensor hose blocked, kinked or leaking
Barometric pressure sensor (often inside the control module) faulty
5 V reference or connector faulty
P0069.d: With the ignition on and the engine stopped, the intake manifold is at ambient pressure, so the manifold pressure sensor and the barometric pressure sensor (often inside the control module) must read almost the same. P0069 is set when they differ by more than a threshold. Some systems also compare the barometric reading with a value estimated from manifold pressure at wide-open throttle while driving. Altitude and weather shift both values equally and do not cause the code. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.
P0069.t: Manifold Absolute Pressure - Barometric Pressure Correlation

c: EGR valve dirty or sticking open
Air leak or crankcase ventilation hose leaking
Mass air flow sensor dirty or manifold pressure sensor faulty
Air filter or intake restricted
P006A.d: The engine control module compares the air quantity measured by the mass air flow sensor with the quantity it calculates from manifold pressure, engine speed and temperature. P006A is set when the two deviate too far. A typical cause is an exhaust gas recirculation valve that does not close: recirculated exhaust raises manifold pressure without passing the air flow sensor. Air leaks, a leaking crankcase ventilation hose or a dirty sensor have the same effect. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.
P006A.t: MAP - Mass or Volume Air Flow Correlation Bank 1

P006B.d: On engines with an exhaust pressure sensor, mostly turbocharged diesels, the control module checks whether manifold pressure and exhaust back pressure fit each other, for example with the engine stopped, when both should be at ambient pressure. P006B is set when they do not. No manufacturer description of this code was found; the explanation follows the general rule for plausibility checks of input sensors. Suspects are the exhaust pressure sensor or its sooted hose, and the manifold pressure sensor. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.

Throttle body fault
P006C.d: On turbocharged or supercharged engines the control module compares manifold pressure with the pressure measured upstream of the throttle, for example at idle or with the throttle wide open, where the two must lie close together. P006C is set when the difference exceeds a threshold. Manufacturers interpret "inlet pressure" differently: some mean boost pressure upstream of the throttle, others the pressure at the compressor inlet. Typical causes are a leak in the charge-air path or a faulty pressure sensor. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.

P006D.d: Without boost, for example with the engine stopped or at low load, the pressure sensor ahead of the turbocharger or supercharger must read about the same as the barometric pressure sensor. P006D is set when the difference is too large; some manufacturers compare against an estimated barometric value instead and run the check once per ignition cycle. Typical causes are a faulty inlet pressure sensor, a faulty barometric sensor (often inside the control module) or a wiring or reference-voltage fault. Each sensor can be electrically fine on its own; regulations require such plausibility checks for input sensors with a code of their own.

P006E.d: "Boost control A" is the electrically driven actuator the engine control module uses to set boost pressure, for example a wastegate solenoid, the control valve of variable turbine vanes or an electric actuator. Some engines supply it through two driver stages in the control module: a high side that switches the supply voltage and a low side that switches ground. The low side is covered by P0045 to P0048; this code concerns the high side. P006E is set when the switched supply voltage is too low, typically because the supply wire is shorted to ground or interrupted. Without supply the actuator stays in its rest position, which on most engines means low boost and reduced power.

P0070.d: The ambient air temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor whose resistance falls as temperature rises. Its value is used by the climate control, the outside temperature display and the engine control module, which needs it to enable other diagnostics and to correct its maps. Depending on the vehicle the engine control module reads the sensor directly, or the instrument cluster or another module sends the value over the data bus; some vehicles have no sensor and estimate ambient temperature from intake air temperature. P0070 is the general circuit fault or an invalid signal, for example when the instrument cluster reports the value as invalid or the reading is implausibly low.
s: Wrong or missing outside temperature display

Depending on the vehicle the engine control module reads the sensor directly, or the instrument cluster or another module sends the value over the data bus; some vehicles have no sensor and estimate ambient temperature from intake air temperature. P0071 is a plausibility check: after a long standstill (several hours) ambient, intake air and coolant temperatures should be close together. If the ambient reading deviates by more than a threshold at the next start, the code is set; an engine block heater or strong sunshine are excluded where the system can detect them.

P0087.d: On common-rail diesel and gasoline direct-injection engines, a high-pressure pump feeds the fuel rail, a sensor measures rail pressure, and the engine control module regulates it towards a target from its maps. P0087 is set when the actual pressure stays below the target by more than a threshold for some time. It is a system code: it does not say which component is at fault. Typical causes are a weak low-pressure supply, a worn high-pressure pump, a sticking control valve, a leak or a drifting pressure sensor; the engine usually goes into reduced power.
s: Loss of power or reduced power mode

P0088.d: On common-rail diesel and gasoline direct-injection engines, a high-pressure pump feeds the fuel rail, a sensor measures rail pressure, and the engine control module regulates it towards a target from its maps. P0088 is set when the actual pressure stays above the target by more than a threshold for some time. On many gasoline systems the pump can only raise pressure, which is then reduced only by injecting. Typical causes are a sticking pressure control or metering valve, a drifting pressure sensor or, on diesels with a pressure control valve, a blocked return. Real overpressure can cause harsh combustion noise and smoke.
s: Loss of power or reduced power mode

P0089.d: On common-rail diesel and gasoline direct-injection engines, a high-pressure pump feeds the fuel rail, a sensor measures rail pressure, and the engine control module regulates it towards a target from its maps. The fuel pressure regulator A is the actuator the manufacturer designates for this: depending on the system a pressure control valve that releases fuel from the rail, or the control valve on the high-pressure pump. Some manufacturers report the pump valve under the "fuel volume regulator" codes instead. P0089 is a function check: pressure may still be plausible, but the regulator works at its limit, needs too much correction, or pressure does not follow its control signal. P009A.d: After a long standstill with the engine cold, intake air temperature and ambient air temperature should be about the same. P009B.d: The fuel pressure relief control is an electrically controlled valve on the fuel rail that the engine control module opens to reduce rail pressure deliberately, for example on overrun, on load drops or when the engine is switched off. It differs from the purely mechanical pressure relief valve, which opens passively at overpressure, and from the pressure regulator, which controls pressure continuously. Manufacturer documents show this code mainly on heavy-duty diesel engines. P009B reports an open control circuit of this valve. Rail pressure can then not be reduced as intended, and the engine may be derated.

P00AF.d: Boost control A here is an electronic actuator with its own electronics (a "smart" actuator), usually on the variable turbine geometry, with its own position sensor and controlled over a data bus or a pulsed signal. It checks itself and reports internal faults to the engine control module; documented examples are pattern errors, overcurrent and checksum errors. The control module cannot narrow down a fault inside the actuator further. P00AF is set when actuator A reports such an internal fault. Manufacturer bulletins recommend checking the vane mechanism for free movement and, if it moves freely, replacing only the actuator rather than the whole turbocharger.
s: Loss of power or limp mode with reduced boost
Often stored with actuator position or boost codes

P00B7.d: When the engine is hot, the thermostat should be open and coolant should flow through the radiator. P00B7 is set when the engine coolant temperature is very high (above about 117 to 119 °C in documented cases) while the radiator side stays much colder, so too little coolant flows through the radiator. The usual cause is a thermostat stuck closed; low coolant, air in the system, a pump that delivers too little or a blocked radiator have the same effect. If the temperature keeps rising, stop driving to avoid engine damage.

P00BA.d: "Forced limited power" is a term for a protective strategy in which the engine control module deliberately limits engine power. Regulations require the check engine light to come on within seconds when such an emissions-relevant limp-home mode is active. These codes report the reason for the limitation; usually further codes point to the actual cause. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found. P00BA: power has been limited because fuel pressure is too low, which protects the engine and the pump against running lean or losing rail pressure.

P00BC.d: The control module compares the air mass measured by the air flow meter with the air mass it expects from a model, for example from manifold pressure, boost pressure and throttle position. These codes report the deviation with its direction: "too low" means the meter measures less air than expected, "too high" more. Regulations allow manufacturers to use one code for both directions or separate codes, as here. P00BC concerns air flow meter A. Typical causes are air entering behind the meter, a charge-air leak, a dirty meter or a restricted intake. No manufacturer description naming this exact code was found; the explanation follows its documented counterpart.

P00D1.d: This code concerns the heated oxygen sensor upstream of the catalytic converter (sensor 1) on bank 1. Unlike the heater circuit codes, which report an open or short circuit, this code means the heater is driven but does not bring the oxygen sensor to the expected temperature. One documented method, used where no current-measuring shunt is fitted, measures the internal impedance of the sensor element: a hot element has a low impedance. If the impedance stays above a limit that depends on the calculated element temperature and the voltage at the sensor connector, the heating is judged insufficient. The test runs once per trip. Typical causes are an aged heating element or added resistance from corrosion in the heater circuit. For this sensor position no manufacturer description of the test was found; the code appears in a manufacturer's code list, and the explanation follows the documented counterpart for sensor 2.
s: Oxygen sensor heater readiness stays incomplete

P00D5.d: During fuel cut-off on overrun the exhaust gas is pure air, so the oxygen sensors before and behind the catalytic converter must both report the same lean value. P00E3.d: Some engines, mainly hybrids and fuel-saving designs, have an exhaust heat exchanger behind the catalytic converter that transfers exhaust heat into the coolant for faster warm-up of engine and cabin. A bypass valve sends the exhaust either through the heat exchanger or around it. Documented diagnostics compare the coolant temperature rise at the heat exchanger with the commanded mode: if it behaves like bypass while recovery is commanded, or the other way round, the valve is considered stuck. P00E3 reports the valve stuck open. How "open" and "closed" map to bypass and recovery is not publicly documented, so both possible effects should be considered: slow warm-up and weak heating, or excessive coolant heat. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.
s: Slow warm-up and weak heating in winter
Or high coolant temperature and long fan run-on

P00F7.d: This is the bank 2 counterpart of the comparison between barometric pressure and the pressure ahead of the turbocharger or supercharger. At low air flow the inlet pressure sensor reads close to ambient pressure, minus the small loss across the air filter, so it must match the barometric reading. The code is set when the difference is too large; a clogged air filter or a leaking intake hose on bank 2 can cause it as well as a drifting sensor. None of the published manufacturer documents searched uses this code; the explanation follows regulations and comparable manufacturer monitors.
s: Reduced power or boost limitation possible

P00FB.d: The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly after the compressor, usually ahead of the charge air cooler; FCA fits it as a combined temperature and pressure sensor. Boost control and compressor protection use the value. P00FB means the signal voltage is above its valid range: typically a signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage, an open ground, or a failed sensor. It does not mean the boost really is too high – that would be P0234. The circuit is monitored continuously from key-on; comparable GM pressure sensors fail above 86–97 % of the reference for about 4 s. The engine then works with a substitute value and may limit boost. GM and Ford do not use this code family in their published summaries – they rely on the boost sensor ahead of the throttle (P0235–P0238) – so no manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found.
s: Loss of power or limp mode with boost limit

P00FC.d: The turbocharger outlet pressure sensor A measures the pressure directly after the compressor, usually ahead of the charge air cooler; FCA fits it as a combined temperature and pressure sensor. Boost control and compressor protection use the value. P00FC covers short dropouts or jumps in the signal that are each too brief for the low or high code, or changes faster than real pressure can move. P00FD.d: 'Battery B' here is not a hybrid high-voltage battery (those have codes from P0B27) but, in the only documented use by FCA/Stellantis, the 12 V auxiliary battery of the start-stop system. When the engine restarts automatically, a relay separates main and auxiliary battery so that the auxiliary one keeps the control units stable while the main battery cranks. The engine module sets P00FD if the auxiliary battery is disconnected on the first start, drops below about 8 V during an auto-start, or repeatedly falls below 10.3 V (counter reaches ten). Start-stop is then disabled; often it follows a jump start or many short trips. Whether the MIL comes on is not stated in the sources.
s: Start-stop out of service, 'Service Start/Stop' message
'Service Shifter' message with electronic gear selector

P00FE.d: The evaporative emission system stores fuel vapour from the tank in a charcoal canister and later purges it into the engine. P00FE means the vapour path between tank and canister is restricted or blocked. That matters because a blocked line can hide the tank side from the leak test and disturb tank venting and refuelling. Ford, where P00FE replaces its own code P144A, checks this once per drive cycle during the cruise leak test, while purging with the vent valve closed, and confirms suspicious pressure responses with an intrusive test. VW used the same code on the 2013–2019 Golf, where the diagnosis covers the purge valve and the leak detection module. Typical causes are kinked or pinched lines and charcoal grains from a broken canister.
s: Fuel nozzle clicks off early when refuelling
Hiss or vacuum when opening the fuel cap

P00FF.d: P00FF is an information code in the engine control module: the body control module has detected an emissions-relevant fault of its own and asks over the data bus for the check engine light. The engine module stores P00FF so that a generic OBD scanner can see why the MIL is on; the actual fault is stored in the body control module as B or U codes and must be read there. GM documents two cases – a 2020 Cadillac CT5 with climate flap actuator codes and 2025 full-size SUVs with U1962 – both cured by reprogramming the body control module, not by replacing parts. The mechanism matches other 'module requested MIL' codes such as P069E. P00FF itself causes no limp mode.
s: Check engine light on without an engine fault

P0100.d: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0100 means the control module gets no usable signal at all. Ford uses it for a broken sensing element on digital sensors (period longer than 1.3 ms, i.e. below about 0.78 kHz, for half a second); on GM's 3.0 V6 in the Saab 9-4X it is set at 0 Hz. Many systems with voltage sensors skip P0100 and report low or high directly. The engine then runs on air mass calculated from manifold pressure, throttle angle and speed; Ford also disables start-stop.
s: Rough idle, hesitation, lack of power (substitute value)

P0101.d: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0101 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically fine but does not match the engine's state. GM petrol engines model the expected air flow from manifold pressure, throttle, speed and boost and blame the MAF if it is off by more than 20 g/s; GM diesels check the measured-to-estimated ratio (0.8–1.2) with EGR closed; Bosch ME9 compares it with the throttle angle. Common causes are air leaks after the sensor, a soiled element (oiled sport filters) or a disconnected crankcase vent; GM also documents a bad crimp in the fuse box. Ford uses P0068 instead. Two trips are needed.
s: Check engine light on, often without driveability problems
Hesitation, flat spot, poor throttle response

P0102.d: The mass air flow sensor (MAF) sits between the air filter and the throttle or compressor and measures how much air the engine draws in; fuel quantity, load and ignition are calculated from it. Most are hot-film or hot-wire sensors that output either a voltage or, on GM, Saab and newer Ford systems, a frequency. P0102 means the signal is below its electrical lower limit – a frequency that is too low or a voltage that is too low. Documented limits: GM petrol 450 Hz or less, GM diesel below 276 Hz, Ford digital below 1.5 kHz for 5 s, Ford analogue below 0.244 V. 'Low' describes the signal: typically an open or grounded signal wire, missing supply voltage or failed electronics. Saab notes that a large leak between sensor and throttle can also cause it. GM and Saab need two trips; the engine runs on a calculated substitute value.

P0105.d: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. P0105 is the general circuit fault and is rarely used today: most petrol engines report low, high and intermittent separately (P0107–P0109). It appears mainly where the fault cannot be broken down further – Ford's 2023 diesels set it when the digital SENT sensor reports a bad status or an out-of-limit value for 5 s (lost communication is a separate U code), and Bosch EDC16 diesels use it with a fault type byte, for example signal below 0.2 V. Saab then substitutes 101.3 kPa, limits torque and switches off EGR and boost control.
s: Loss of power, limp mode with torque limit (diesel)
Rough idle, hard starting, higher consumption (petrol)

P0106.d: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. P0106 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but implausible – stuck, offset or drifting. Two tests are common. With the engine stopped, all pressures equalise, so MAP must match ambient (and boost) pressure; Ford allows 1.5–3 inHg. While running, MAP is compared with a value modelled from air mass, throttle and speed – GM blames the MAP sensor above about 23–30 kPa error, with two trips on petrol and one on diesel. Turbo engines with three sensors find the odd one out by majority. Besides the sensor, intake or boost leaks often cause it.
s: Higher consumption, black smoke possible on diesels

P0107.d: The manifold absolute pressure (MAP) sensor measures the pressure behind the throttle; on vehicles without a separate barometric sensor it also supplies the ambient pressure, read at key-on or wide-open throttle – hence 'MAP/BARO'. It is a three-wire sensor with 5 V reference, ground and signal. P0107 means the signal voltage is below its lower limit. 'Low' refers to the voltage, not to a real low pressure: typically the signal wire is grounded, the signal or 5 V reference is open, or the sensor has failed. A short on another sensor sharing the same reference can pull it down too, so GM often sees several codes at once. Documented limits: GM below 3.3 % of 5 V (about 0.17 V), GM/Saab 2.0T below 0.19 V for 4 s, Ford petrol below 0.19 V for 5 s, Ford diesel below 0.1 V. GM petrol needs two trips, GM diesel one. P010A is the general circuit fault of sensor B: no usable signal at all, just like P0100 for sensor A. Ford's 2020–2023 petrol summary lists it for a broken element of digital sensor B, with the same limit as sensor A (period above 1.3 ms for half a second); which engines carry sensor B is not stated. P0115.d: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. Its value drives cold-start enrichment, idle speed, ignition timing, the radiator fan and the release of closed-loop mixture control. Some Ford engines measure cylinder head temperature instead and calculate a coolant value from it. P0115 is the general circuit fault without telling low from high. Today it has largely been replaced by P0117, P0118 and P0119; GM and Ford do not set it in the tables checked. Older or individual systems still use it as a collective code, for example Saab Trionic T5 (1998). The circuit is monitored continuously; when it fails, the module uses a substitute value and many systems run the radiator fan permanently.

Some Ford engines measure cylinder head temperature instead and calculate a coolant value from it. P0116 is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but not believable. Most often it checks for a sensor stuck too warm. After a long soak (GM 8 h, Ford 6 h) coolant must be close to intake air temperature; GM fails it above about 19 °C difference without a detected block heater, Ford if it reads over 110 °C or sits at 79–110 °C. P0119.d: The engine coolant temperature sensor 1 is an NTC thermistor: the control module feeds 5 V through a resistor, and as the coolant warms the resistance and signal voltage fall. CARB requires that this happens within set times – from 2006 two minutes if the engine starts up to 8 °C below the release temperature, five minutes if 8–19 °C below. P0125 means it took too long. Ford checks once per cold start and fails if coolant is still below 10 °C while its model already expects over 27 °C; Mitsubishi expects about 7 °C within 90–300 s and also fails if coolant drops back below 40 °C. The only implementation documented in a manufacturer source is Subaru's (via the Saab 9-2X service information): there P0126 is a stuck-sensor check – if the coolant signal changes by less than 5 mV during 20 s of driving or idling after start, the sensor counts as frozen. It runs once per drive cycle, lights the MIL after two consecutive cycles and has no fail-safe mode. The logic is documented for a Bosch EDC16 diesel (Saab 9-3): if the intake air exceeds 130 °C and does not fall below it within 45 s after the exhaust gas recirculation valve is closed, hot exhaust gas is evidently still entering or the sensor is wrong. The engine then disables EGR and runs in limp mode with reduced torque. P0128.d: After a cold start the thermostat stays closed so the engine warms up quickly. CARB requires the coolant to reach a temperature at most 11 °C below the thermostat's rated value within a set time. GM models the heat put in (fuel energy minus losses to ambient, cabin heater and coasting) and fails if enough energy has gone in without coolant reaching about 65 °C (55 °C in cold weather). Ford compares the measured value with a modelled one, typically failing below 78 °C with an 89 °C thermostat. The test runs once per drive cycle, pauses with much idling or below about −7 °C, and needs two trips. Usually the thermostat is stuck open; a sensor reading too low is the other suspect.
s: Temperature gauge stays low or drops while driving
Heater does not get properly warm
P0128.t: Coolant Thermostat (Coolant Temperature Below Thermostat Regulating Temperature)

P0129.d: The engine control module needs the ambient air pressure for mixture, altitude correction and boost limits. It comes either from a dedicated barometric sensor or from the MAP sensor, read at key-on with the engine stopped and updated at wide-open throttle. P0129 means this value is lower than physically possible – even on the highest drivable passes air pressure stays around 50 kPa, and GM and Ford use 50 kPa as their lower plausibility limit. Usual causes are a MAP or baro sensor reading too low, a blocked sensor port or high resistance in the wiring. No manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found: GM and Ford file the same finding under P2227.
s: Rich mixture, higher consumption, rough idle

P012A.d: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits between the air filter and the compressor. The engine uses it for the compressor pressure ratio, to judge air filter restriction (ambient minus inlet pressure) and to cross-check the other pressure sensors. P012A is the general circuit fault. Ford's 2023 diesels use a digital SENT sensor here and set P012A when its error flag is raised or the value exceeds a limit for 5 s; lost communication is reported separately (U068B). FCA's 2019 Jeep Wrangler 2.0 turbo could set P012A, P012C and P012D falsely and was fixed with new engine software, so the software level is worth checking before replacing parts. GM's supercharged V8 uses only P012B–P012D. A substitute value, usually ambient pressure, is used.

P012B.d: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits between the air filter and the compressor. The engine uses it for the compressor pressure ratio, to judge air filter restriction (ambient minus inlet pressure) and to cross-check the other pressure sensors. P012B is a plausibility fault: the signal is electrically valid but stuck or offset. On GM's supercharged 6.2 V8 the sensor must read 50–115 kPa and agree within 10 kPa with MAP and ambient pressure after the engine has been off for more than 8 s; while running, it is compared with modelled values (fault above about 25–30 kPa). GM normally needs two trips, one in some 2019 applications. In operation inlet pressure is slightly below ambient because of filter losses, so a clogged filter or blocked intake lowers it further.

P012C.d: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits between the air filter and the compressor. The engine uses it for the compressor pressure ratio, to judge air filter restriction (ambient minus inlet pressure) and to cross-check the other pressure sensors. P012C means the signal voltage is below its lower limit – typically a signal wire shorted to ground, an open signal or 5 V reference wire, or a failed sensor. GM's supercharged V8 sets it below 3 % of the 5 V reference (about 0.15 V), with 320 of 400 samples failing, continuously monitored; two trips are normal, one in some 2019 applications. FCA documented false settings on the 2019 Jeep Wrangler 2.0 turbo that were cured by a software update. A substitute value is used and power may be limited.

P012D.d: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits ahead of the compressor – between air filter and turbocharger, or on GM's supercharged V8 between throttle and supercharger. It is an analogue 5 V pressure sensor used for the compressor pressure ratio, filter restriction and cross-checks with the other pressure sensors. P012D means the signal voltage is above its upper limit – typically the signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage, or an open sensor ground that lets the signal rise to the reference. GM's supercharged LT4/LT5 sets it above 97 % of the reference (about 124 kPa) with 320 of 400 samples failing, monitored continuously; two trips on the LT4, one on the 2019 LT5. FCA documented false settings on the 2019 Jeep Wrangler 2.0 turbo, fixed by new engine software. The control module substitutes a modelled or ambient value and may limit boost.

P012E.d: The turbocharger/supercharger inlet pressure sensor A sits ahead of the compressor – between air filter and turbocharger, or on GM's supercharged V8 between throttle and supercharger. It is an analogue 5 V pressure sensor used for the compressor pressure ratio, filter restriction and cross-checks with the other pressure sensors. P012E covers a signal that jumps or drops out briefly without staying below or above the circuit limits – typically a loose contact. Such intermittent monitors usually count short limit violations or changes faster than real pressure can move. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found: GM handles jumps of this sensor through its range check P012B and the counting windows of P012C/P012D, and Ford's 2023 diesels report their digital sensor under P012A. The description therefore rests on CARB's circuit monitoring requirement and component information. A substitute value is used while the fault is present.
s: Occasional power reduction or boost fluctuation

P012F.d: P012F compares the coolant temperature sensor with the engine oil temperature sensor. The documented user is Ford's Power Stroke diesel. After a calibration update for the 6.0 litre engine, Ford uses it to monitor oil cooler efficiency: if the oil gets much hotter than the coolant at certain speed and load, the oil-to-coolant heat exchanger is probably clogged, and P012F sets together with the wrench lamp. On the 6.7 litre (2015–2018) several bulletins treat P012F as a false setting – partly below 5 °C ambient – cured by reprogramming the engine module. Ford's 2023 diesels run the cold-start comparison of coolant against oil temperature (35 °C limit after 6 h) under P0196 instead. GM does not use the code, and the code does not say which sensor or which system is at fault.
s: Check engine light and/or wrench lamp (Ford)
Raised oil temperature with a clogged oil cooler
Often no driving symptoms when software is the cause

P0130.d: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. P0130 is the general circuit code, and manufacturers fill it very differently. Ford used it up to 2010 as the collective code for all wiring faults reported by the wide-band interface chip and has split it into specific codes since 2011. Subaru sets it when the interface voltages leave their range for 5 s, with immediate MIL. GM calls it 'closed loop performance': cross-talk from the heater (signal rises above 2 V with the heater off) or disagreement with the downstream sensor, two trips. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring.
s: Higher consumption, possibly rough running (no mixture control)
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure

P0131.d: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. On switching sensors it means the signal stays below about 40–60 mV (GM, two trips; some GM engines also require the downstream sensor to read rich at the same time, since a genuinely lean mixture would show there too). On wide-band sensors (Ford from 2011, GM) it has nothing to do with the mixture: the interface chip reports one of the sensor wires shorted to ground. A really lean mixture leads to P0171/P2195 rather than this code. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring.
s: Higher consumption, possibly rough running (no mixture control)

P0132.d: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. On switching sensors the signal is above what the sensor can physically produce (about 1 V): Ford above 1.1 V for 10 s, GM above 1050 mV, Saab Trionic above 1.5 V for 5 s. The cause is almost always electrical – the heater supply or battery voltage on the signal wire, or a heater-to-signal short inside the sensor; some GM modules also read an open wire this way. On wide-band sensors the interface chip reports a sensor wire shorted to voltage. If P0132 and P0138 appear together, a shared short in the harness is likely. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring.
s: Higher consumption, possibly soot or fuel smell

P0133.d: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. P0133 means the sensor does not react fast enough to mixture changes. Methods differ fundamentally: GM measures passively how long the signal takes to cross 400–600 mV in each direction, averaged over 60 s; Ford forces the mixture to swing at 1.5 Hz and fails a switching sensor whose amplitude stays below 0.5 V, or evaluates response times of a wide-band sensor against a no-fault area; Subaru compares controller activity with measured lambda over 210 s. The test runs once per drive at warm part load; two trips. Mixture control usually stays active, but worse.
s: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure

P0134.d: The oxygen sensor before the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 1) is the main control sensor for the mixture. It is either a switching sensor (about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich) or a wide-band sensor that works with a pump current evaluated by an interface chip. P0134 means the sensor delivers no moving signal, typically because the circuit is open or the cell is cold or dead. The control module feeds a bias voltage, and that is all it sees: GM fails a signal stuck at 350–550 mV (or above 1700 mV with a 1.9 V bias) after warm-up, within about 15 s, or a cell resistance above 20 kΩ in hot exhaust; two trips. Subaru's wide-band sensor fails above 500 Ω cell impedance with immediate MIL. Ford's Bosch wide-band systems have used P2237 for this since 2011. A stored code usually switches mixture control to open loop and suspends adaptation and converter monitoring.
s: No mixture control (open loop), higher consumption
Higher emissions, possible emissions test failure

P0135.d: The upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 (sensor 1) has an electric heater so that it reaches its working temperature of about 300 °C soon after a cold start. The control module switches the heater on the ground side and checks driver voltage and heater current: GM fails it outside 0.3–2.5 A (or 3.1 A) and calls it 'heater performance', Ford outside roughly 0.22–0.465 A minimum to 3 A, Saab Trionic outside 0.5–2.3 A for 5 s. Manufacturers split heater faults differently between P0030–P0032, P0053 and P0135. With the heater dead, closed-loop control starts late after a cold start. If P0135 and P0141 appear together, check the shared fuse.
s: Longer cold-start phase without mixture control, more fuel and emissions

P0136.d: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. P0136 is the general circuit code, and its exact meaning varies by manufacturer. Ford sets it as 'no activity' in a functional check: if the sensor never swings beyond about 0.42/0.48 V despite rich and lean phases – if needed after forced enrichment and leaning – once per drive cycle. Opel/GM Europe set it if the average voltage stays outside 400–500 mV after 10 min of closed loop; older Bosch Motronic if it stays at 0 V for 200 s despite heating. GM North America does not use P0136. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode.
s: Check engine light on (usually after two drive cycles)
Slightly higher consumption possible without downstream trim

P0137.d: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. P0137 means the signal stays below the lower limit. Documented limits: GM below 40–60 mV (two trips); Ford switches in a pull-up and reads open above 1 MΩ (20 kΩ from 2020) or short to ground below 10 Ω, within 10 s. Subaru uses the code as a functional test instead: the sensor never reaches 550 mV within 200 s after fuel cut-off, i.e. it behaves as if permanently lean – so a real exhaust leak can also trigger it there. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode.

P0138.d: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. P0138 means the signal stays above the upper limit. A zirconia sensor can hardly produce more than about 1 V, so readings above 1.05–1.15 V point to an outside voltage such as the heater supply on the signal wire; GM also sees an open circuit here because of its bias voltage. Ford: above 1.1 V for 10 s; GM: above 1050 mV. Subaru again uses a functional test: the minimum voltage never falls below 250 mV within 200 s after fuel cut-off, so the sensor looks permanently rich. Monitored continuously, two trips. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode.

P0139.d: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. P0139 means the sensor reacts too slowly to mixture changes. Subaru measures it around fuel cut-off: rich to lean from 500 to 300 mV must take no more than 0.51 s, lean to rich from 300 to 500 mV no more than 2 s; two drive cycles set the MIL. CARB requires such a test because a sluggish downstream sensor could let a worn converter pass. Since about 2009–2011 GM and Ford report this as direction-specific codes P013A–P013F instead; P0139 remains in use on older, Asian and Jaguar Land Rover systems. When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode.

P013A.d: The downstream oxygen sensor (sensor 2, after the catalytic converter) is used for fine mixture trim and to monitor the converter. 'Slow response' means the signal transition itself is too sluggish – it takes too long to pass between two voltage levels. This code covers the rich-to-lean direction, usually tested during deceleration fuel cut-off. GM forces the test itself and measures how quickly the signal passes from 450 to 150 mV relative to air flow; a filtered value above its limit sets the code after one trip (fallback: target not reached before about 60 g of air). Ford measures the slew rate during fuel cut-off, normalised to the converter's stored oxygen. Lexus traced one case to a leaking manifold gasket ahead of the sensor; on Ram diesels it is soot-related. CARB requires separate detection of slow and delayed faults in each direction (phased in from 2009 for downstream and 2011 for upstream sensors).
s: Usually no noticeable change in driving
Catalyst monitor may stay incomplete (inspection readiness missing)
With a converter cause, P0420/P0430 may follow

P0140.d: The oxygen sensor after the catalytic converter on bank 1 (sensor 2) is a switching sensor (about 0.1–0.9 V) used for converter monitoring and fine mixture trim. P0140 means the sensor produces no voltage of its own and the control module only sees its own reference (bias) voltage. P0141.d: The downstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 (sensor 2) has an electric heater so it reaches its working temperature quickly. The control module switches the heater on the ground side and checks both the driver voltage against the commanded state and the heater current. GM fails it outside 0.3–2.5 A (two trips; pure circuit faults are P0036–P0038 there); Ford uses P0141 as its general heater circuit code with a current window of roughly 0.22–0.465 A minimum to 3 A maximum depending on sensor supplier. Without heat the sensor signal is useless, so converter monitoring and trim are suspended.

P0142.d: Sensor 3 is a third oxygen sensor on bank 1, behind a second converter or converter brick. It only exists on some vehicles – documented for Jaguar Land Rover's 3.0 V6 supercharged (2013–2016, where sensor 2 is 'mid-cat' and sensor 3 'post-cat') and Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. P0142 is the general circuit code of this sensor. Jaguar Land Rover lists it with P0143, P0144 and P0147 for the post-cat sensor and names software (fixed by reconfiguring the engine module) and water-induced thermal shock as causes. No published thresholds exist for sensor 3; the logic follows the sensor 2 checks (P0136). When it fails, the control module stops the downstream trim and cannot evaluate the converter; there is no limp mode.

P015E.d: Diesel fuel systems correct injection timing and quantity in closed loop, often with learning routines that run during suitable overrun phases. CARB requires a fault when such feedback control does not start within a manufacturer-defined time. P015E is the code of this kind for injection timing control: the closed-loop correction does not become active in time, or does not learn. It belongs to a family of similar codes – Ford's 2023 diesels, for example, set the sister code P016D when rail pressure adaptation has learned nothing after 300 s. No manufacturer document describing P015E itself, or its threshold, was found; the description rests on CARB and the sister code. Frequent causes are learning conditions that occur too rarely, software, or injectors outside tolerance.
s: Possibly louder combustion noise or uneven running with unlearned injectors

P016A.d: With closed-loop control the engine module corrects the injected fuel using the oxygen sensor: short-term fuel trim reacts within fractions of a second, long-term trim stores a learned base correction per load and speed range. Positive values mean fuel is being added because the mixture was lean, negative values mean fuel is being removed; around ±10 % is normal. Closed loop needs a heated, working oxygen sensor and plausible engine data. P016A means the mixture control did not switch to closed loop within the calibrated time after starting; the engine then runs on map values with higher emissions but no actual limp mode. CARB requires this check, and since 2019 also after every automatic restart in start-stop systems. Bentley and other VW group petrol engines set it together with oxygen sensor heater codes when the heater fuse holder was damaged; Ram's 3.0 EcoDiesel listed it in bulletins fixed with new software and sensors. Time limits are not public.

P016D.d: Common-rail diesels regulate rail pressure in closed loop: the control module compares the rail pressure sensor with the target and adjusts a volume or pressure control valve, learning correction factors as it goes. CARB requires faults to be flagged when this feedback control does not start in time or runs out of authority. P016D means the pressure control has not settled into closed loop, or has not learned, in the time allowed. Ford's 2023 diesels (6.7 and 3.0 litre) set it when, within the learning conditions – target rail pressure 600–1300 bar, fuel at most 40 °C – no new adaptation factor has been learned after 300 s; the check only runs while the rail pressure sensor and its supply are fault-free. P0176.d: The fuel composition sensor is fitted only to flex-fuel vehicles that can run on petrol or ethanol up to E85. GM uses a capacitive sensor in the fuel line whose square-wave output frequency gives the ethanol content – 50 Hz for E0 up to 150 Hz for E100 – while the pulse width carries the fuel temperature. Ford has calculated the ethanol content from the oxygen sensor feedback after refuelling since model year 2000 and has no such sensor. P0176 is the general circuit fault of this sensor without telling low from high. GM's current documents use P0178/P0179 instead, so P0176 is mainly to be expected on older flex-fuel vehicles or other makes. GM issued a special coverage for 2013–2014 flex-fuel models (10 years/150,000 miles) because road salt could make the sensor fail electrically, turning on the MIL and disabling remote start. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found; the description rests on CARB's circuit monitoring requirement and component information.

Some Ford engines use it instead of a coolant temperature sensor and calculate a coolant value from it; VW group V8 petrol engines use it as sender G407. P017F.d: Leak detection pump modules in the evaporative emission system (for example Bosch's DM-TL, used by VW, BMW, Porsche, Volvo, Mini, Land Rover and Kia/Hyundai) draw fresh air through their own filter, often mounted separately via a hose; at rest the charcoal canister is also vented through it. A GM patent describes detection via the pressure difference across the filter during purge (above about 8 inH2O for 10–20 s). P018A.d: Fuel pressure sensor B is a second fuel pressure sensor; which one is up to the manufacturer. On GM it is the low-pressure sensor in the supply line of direct-injection engines (0–743 kPa), read by the engine module or the fuel pump control module; on Ford engines with dual injection it is the sensor on the port-injection rail (0.5–4.5 V for about 0–70 psi). GM checks actively whether the sensor responds: if the pump duty sits at its limit for 5 s or the pressure error varies too little, the module changes pump output and fails the sensor if pressure moves 30 kPa or less – a 'frozen' sensor; two trips. P018F.d: Common-rail diesels have a pressure relief valve in the rail – usually a spring-loaded valve, on some truck engines electronically controlled. It opens on overpressure and then holds a low limp-home pressure; every opening wears the seat, and after many openings it may no longer close tightly. P018F means the valve has opened too often: the control module recognises openings from the rail pressure trace (overshoot, then a steep drop to the limp-home level) and counts them. The code therefore usually points to an underlying problem – the pressure control repeatedly lets overpressure build up. No manufacturer document describing P018F was found; the function and counting logic come from patents on large engines (example: opening at about 1950 bar, then about 800 bar).
s: Sudden loss of power (limp mode with low rail pressure)
Starting problems once the valve no longer seals
Smoke or harsh combustion noise beforehand

P0191.d: The rail pressure sensor A measures the pressure in the high-pressure fuel rail of common-rail diesels and petrol direct-injection engines; it is either a three-wire sensor (5 V reference, ground, signal rising with pressure, about 0.5 V at 0 bar) or a digital SENT sensor with two measuring channels. The engine module uses it as the feedback signal for rail pressure control. P0191 means the signal is electrically valid but not believable – stuck, offset or drifting. Manufacturers check it differently: Ford's 2023 diesels and GM's diesels test the offset with the system depressurised (Ford before starting after 10 min and 12 s after switch-off, window about 0.25–0.38 V; GM 6.5–14 % of supply); GM petrol direct injection compares the two SENT channels (limit 1.0 MPa); Saab's V6 diesel flags a large target deviation while the signal barely moves.
