P0195.d: The engine oil temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. The engine module uses the oil temperature for variable cam timing (Ford disables it with cold oil or a sensor fault), engine protection and the oil life monitor; many engines have no such sensor and use a calculated oil temperature instead. P0195 is the general circuit fault without telling low from high. With analogue sensors most manufacturers use P0197/P0198 instead. The documented use is Ford's 2023 diesels with a digital SENT oil temperature sensor: P0195 is set when the sensor reports a status or data fault for 5 s, while a complete loss of communication is U0667. The module then uses a substitute value (Saab: 100 °C), and functions relying on oil temperature are restricted.

P0197.d: The engine oil temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. The engine module uses the oil temperature for variable cam timing (Ford disables it with cold oil or a sensor fault), engine protection and the oil life monitor; many engines have no such sensor and use a calculated oil temperature instead. P0197 means the signal voltage is below its lower limit, so the module would read implausibly hot oil (around 145–150 °C) – practically always a signal wire shorted to ground or an internally shorted sensor. Ford sets it below 0.16–0.20 V for 5 s; GM below 25 Ω in 20 of 50 samples – without a warning light on the 2018 LT4, with two trips on the 2019 version, so MIL behaviour depends on the manufacturer and model year. A substitute value is used.

P0198.d: The engine oil temperature sensor A is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. The engine module uses the oil temperature for variable cam timing (Ford disables it with cold oil or a sensor fault), engine protection and the oil life monitor; many engines have no such sensor and use a calculated oil temperature instead. P0198 means the signal sits near the 5 V reference, so the module sees extremely cold oil (below −40 °C) – typically an unplugged connector, a broken wire, an open sensor element or a short to voltage. P019A.d: Sensor 3 on bank 1 is a switching oxygen sensor behind a second converter or converter brick; it exists on Jaguar Land Rover's supercharged V6 and V8 (on both banks) and on Ford systems that monitor part of the converter volume. 'Delayed response' means the sensor starts reacting too late after a mixture change – unlike 'slow response' (P0145/P0165), where the transition itself is too flat. This code covers the rich-to-lean direction, tested during forced fuel cut-off. For sensor 2, GM checks whether the signal falls below 450 mV before a calibrated air mass has passed; behind two converters their oxygen storage buffers the change, so limits are wide. No manufacturer document using exactly this code was found – the Jaguar Land Rover bulletins list only P0142ff/P0162ff for sensor 3 – so the description rests on CARB's response requirement and the sensor 2 logic. There is no limp mode; the converter monitor cannot complete.

P019E.d: These codes only apply to vehicles that run on a gaseous alternative fuel – compressed natural gas (CNG) or LPG – either as bi-fuel models alongside petrol (for example GM's 2015–2016 Impala Bi-Fuel or 2013–2016 Silverado/Sierra 2500HD) or as dedicated gas engines. CNG is stored at up to about 250 bar (3600 psi); a regulator reduces it to a few bar for the gas rail and injectors. The tank pressure sensor A sits at or in the regulator; together with the tank temperature it gives the gas level, and it decides whether gas operation is possible. P019E is the general circuit fault of this sensor without telling low from high. Ford's earlier bi-fuel CNG system showed the gauge as empty on a tank pressure sensor fault. Typical reaction: gas operation is blocked and a bi-fuel vehicle switches to petrol. No manufacturer document naming exactly this code was found; GM's bulletins only state that faults are reported like on petrol models. The description rests on CARB, which treats such vehicles like petrol engines for model years 2004–2018, and on the documented system design.
s: Gas level gauge wrong, jumping or showing empty
Gas operation blocked or automatic switch to petrol
Dedicated gas engines: limp mode or starting problems possible

P01B9.d: The engine oil temperature sensor B is an NTC thermistor fed with 5 V through a resistor: the hotter the oil, the lower the signal voltage. P01CB.d: Diesel engines must detect when fuel can no longer be injected at the correct crank angle – CARB requires this for every injector individually, hence one code per cylinder. The start of injection is not measured directly: during overrun with fuel cut-off the control module fires a tiny test injection into one cylinder (GM: about 1.5 mm³) and evaluates the resulting speed change at the crankshaft sensor. From this it learns how much extra energizing time the injector needs (Bosch calls this zero fuel calibration). This code means injector 1 needs clearly more energizing time than intended, i.e. it opens too late – GM sets it above 80 µs of extra time, after two trips. Documented users are GM's 6.6 litre Duramax (LML, L5P) and FCA's 3.0 litre EcoDiesel; Ford reports the same function under P2B11ff. Bulletins often point away from the injector: GM fixed false settings on 2020–2021 L5P trucks with new software and warns that vibration, for example from off-road tyres, disturbs the evaluation; FCA lists wrong injector correction codes, boost leaks and loose injector clamps.
s: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)

P01F0.d: Since model years 2019–2021 CARB requires petrol engines to detect a thermostat fault not only during warm-up but also when the coolant, after reaching operating temperature, drops back below the temperature needed for other diagnostics. P01F0 is this check. GM sets it when coolant falls below 64 °C with a conventional thermostat or 70.5 °C with an electrically heated one (2019 Corvette: 65/78.5 °C) after having been above it, with at least 0.8 km driven, ambient above −7 °C, enough heat input and no long overrun downhill; two trips. GM also uses it on the 6.6 litre Duramax diesel as a 'stuck open thermostat' check. Ford does not use the code in the documents checked. Usual cause is a thermostat stuck open.
s: Check engine light on (after two drive cycles)

P01F1.d: Sensor 4 on bank 1 is a fourth oxygen sensor, behind a third converter or converter brick. The OBD standard provides for up to four sensors per bank, and the code standard defines sensor 4 for bank 1 only. No manufacturer or vehicle using these codes could be identified; the description rests on CARB's requirements for downstream oxygen sensors and the logic of sensors 2 and 3. A switching sensor delivers about 0.1–0.9 V. P01F1 is the general circuit code of this sensor, the counterpart of P0136/P0142 for sensors 2 and 3. Typical causes are an aged sensor, open or high-resistance wiring and a failed heater.

P01F8.d: The engine module switches an electric coolant heater A through a power stage (driver). This code means the driver itself has reported excessive current or overheating and has shut down to protect itself – it concerns the control circuit, not the coolant temperature. Such heaters warm the coolant around a cold start, shortening warm-up and providing cabin heat sooner; a GM patent describes how the module recognises a pre-heated engine so other temperature diagnostics do not misfire. No manufacturer using this code family was found in GM, Ford or FCA documents; the description rests on CARB's requirements for output components. Siblings for heater A are P01E8–P01EB.

P0200.d: P0200 is the injector circuit fault without a cylinder assignment. The large US manufacturers do not use it – GM and Ford report injector faults per cylinder (P0201 ff) or as faults of the shared injector supply (P062D/P062E, P2146 ff). Saab documents it on the 3.0 V6 diesel of the 9-5, whose injectors are driven by a separate power stage behind the glovebox: there P0200 means an electrical fault in that power stage or its wiring, and the engine is shut down. Generally the cause lies in something all injectors share – supply, fuse, relay, ground or driver stage – so several cylinders are affected at once. CARB does not require separate codes for each kind of circuit fault.
s: Engine does not start or shuts down

P0201.d: P0201 reports an electrical fault, mainly an open circuit, in the injector circuit of cylinder 1. The engine module watches each injector output: GM flags an open circuit at an impedance of 200 kΩ or more – on direct injection and diesel engines in 10 of 20 or 5 of 10 samples and with the warning light in the first trip, on some port-injected engines only after two trips. Ford's port injection reads a fault bit from the driver chip that covers open, short to ground and short to voltage alike; Ford diesels report only the open circuit here and shorts as P0261/P0262. On direct injection the affected injector is switched off; the cylinder misfires.
s: Misfire and rough running, misfire code P0301
Limp mode possible on diesel and direct injection

P0202.d: P0202 reports an electrical fault, mainly an open circuit, in the injector circuit of cylinder 2. The engine module watches each injector output: GM flags an open circuit at an impedance of 200 kΩ or more – on direct injection and diesel engines in 10 of 20 or 5 of 10 samples and with the warning light in the first trip, on some port-injected engines only after two trips. P020A.d: P020A reports a fault in the injection timing of cylinder 1 on a diesel engine. Unlike P01CB/P01CC ('over retarded/advanced', the result of the injector learning routine in overrun), this code has no direction, and what it checks is up to the manufacturer. GM uses it as an electrical check on a four-cylinder diesel and on the 6.6 litre L5P Duramax V8: at every injection the engine module measures how long the injector current takes to reach its pull-in level of 13 A. If on the V8 that time is outside 60–150 µs in 10 of 20 samples, the code sets and the warning light comes on in the first trip. FCA lists it for the 3.0 litre EcoDiesel V6 together with the learning codes: check injector coding, charge air leaks and the injector clamp, reset the zero fuel calibration and repeat the learning drive; if the code returns, the injector is replaced.
s: Rough running or misfire, rough idle

P0213.d: A cold start injector is an additional injector in the intake manifold that sprays extra fuel for a few seconds while a cold engine is cranked. In classic Bosch systems a thermo-time switch on the block powers it directly, without the engine module – such systems cannot set a code at all. A code is only possible where the engine module drives the valve and monitors its circuit, as CARB requires for output components. From the 1990s the main injectors took over cold-start enrichment, so the code only fits early OBD II engines. P0213 concerns cold start injector 1. No manufacturer using it was found in GM, Ford or Saab documents.
s: Poor cold start, long cranking in cold weather
Leaking valve: hot-start problems, flooding, black smoke

c: Shutoff solenoid faulty (open coil, sticking plunger)
Relay or fuse in the supply circuit faulty
Broken wire, corrosion or ground fault at the pump connector
Pump control module faulty
Engine module driver faulty
P0215.d: The engine shutoff solenoid is the electric stop valve on older diesel injection pumps, mainly distributor pumps. It is energised with the ignition on and lets fuel into the pump; with no current a spring closes it, the pump runs dry and the engine stops – also as a safety backup if the governor fails. P0215 reports a fault in this solenoid or its supply, typically a broken coil, a sticking plunger, a blown fuse or relay, or a wiring fault. The result is either an engine that will not start or dies, or one that keeps running after switch-off. Newer diesels stop through the injectors or a fuel shutoff valve with its own codes P0005–P0007. No manufacturer document describing P0215 was found; the description rests on CARB's requirements for output components and a Bosch patent on the valve.
s: Engine does not start or stalls while driving
Engine keeps running after ignition off (solenoid stuck open)

c: Injector harness or connector (broken pin) – common rail
Engine module or injector power stage faulty internally
Distributor pump electronics or timing advance faulty
Low supply pressure on distributor pumps (lift pump, filter)
Pump installed incorrectly, drive gear misaligned
P0216.d: P0216 is a diesel code for the control of injection timing. On 1990s distributor pumps with an electronic timing advance it meant that actual injection timing missed its target; today manufacturers use it for the electronic injector control, with different meanings. GM's Duramax diesels compare, inside the engine module, the summed injection pulse widths from the hardware driver with those calculated by the software; a mismatch in 30 of 124 or 60 consecutive checks sets the code with the warning light in the first trip. On GM's 3.0 litre LM2 it appeared together with P0202 from a broken pin in the injector 2 connector. Saab's 3.0 V6 diesel uses it for a fault in the separate injector power stage. The result can be loss of power, rough running, smoke and limp mode.
s: Hard starting or stalling (distributor pump), smoke

c: Low coolant (leak, head gasket)
Thermostat stuck closed
Radiator fan, fan clutch or water pump faulty, radiator clogged
Coolant temperature sensor or harness faulty (false reading)
Extreme load (towing, gradient, heat) with an intact cooling system
P0217.d: P0217 is a condition code: the engine module reports that coolant temperature has passed a protection threshold. The limit and the reaction depend on the manufacturer – Saab's 2.2 diesel sets it at 120 °C for over 10 s, limits fuel quantity and suspends EGR and boost diagnostics until the temperature drops; heavy-duty diesels cut power sharply and may shut down; Ford petrol engines use their own code P1299 and cut fuel to individual cylinders. Whether the warning light comes on varies, because CARB exempts overheat protection that only engages once the gauge reads red. Usual causes are low coolant, a thermostat stuck closed, a failed fan or water pump – but Ford traced some cases to a faulty coolant sensor or harness.
s: Temperature gauge in the red, overheat warning
Loss of power, limp mode, cylinders possibly shut off
Steam or coolant smell, coolant loss

c: High load (towing, hills, sustained full throttle, stop-and-go in heat)
Transmission fluid low or aged
Fluid cooler, thermostat or lines clogged, weak cooling system

P0218.d: P0218 is a condition code: the transmission or engine module reports that transmission fluid temperature sensor A reads above an overheat limit. Saab's Aisin automatic sets it above 170 °C for more than 10 s, or above 140 °C for two minutes at high speed, shows a 'transmission overheating' warning and shifts less smoothly; afterwards a fluid change is advised because the additives are spent. Ford uses its own code on diesels and lists P0218 without the warning light on other models. Reactions include earlier torque converter lock-up, a modified shift pattern and sometimes reduced power. Causes are real overheating – towing, hills, low or old fluid, a clogged cooler – or a sensor reading wrongly.
s: Limp mode or reduced power possible
P0218.t: Transmission Fluid Temperature Sensor A Over Temperature Condition

P0219.d: P0219 is a condition code: engine speed has exceeded the overspeed limit even though the rev limiter already cuts fuel – so the engine was driven from outside, usually by downshifting at too high a road speed or descending in too low a gear, or the speed signal was wrong. Limits: Ford 6.7 litre diesel above 4,200 rpm, 3.0 litre above 4,800 rpm, after 0.1 s; GM/Saab 2.8 V6 petrol with manual gearbox above 7,000 rpm for 1 s; Saab 2.2 diesel above 6,200 rpm, although fuel is cut from 5,000 rpm. Many manufacturers store it without the warning light. Saab advises: together with a camshaft sensor code it was real overspeed, alone check the speed signal; after real overspeed inspect the engine for valve train damage.
s: Usually no lasting symptoms, only a stored code
Briefly very high revs, limiter intervening
After real overspeed: rattling, loss of power

Unlike P01E1/P01E2 ('over retarded/advanced', the result of the injector learning routine in overrun), this code has no direction, and what it checks is up to the manufacturer. A cylinder 12 code only applies to engines with 12 or more cylinders. No manufacturer or vehicle using it was found – GM's documents stop at cylinder 8 (P021B), FCA's at cylinder 6, and Ford uses other codes. The description therefore follows the documented siblings: GM checks the injector's current rise electrically, FCA ties the code to injector learning. CARB requires diesel engines to detect injection that is too early or too late.

P022A.d: The charge air cooler bypass is a flap or valve that routes compressed air around the charge air cooler, so the engine and exhaust warm up faster after a cold start; when warm it closes or opens partly to control intake air temperature. P0230.d: The fuel pump circuit has two sides: the primary circuit is the engine module's output to the fuel pump relay coil (or to a pump control module), the secondary circuit is the power circuit from relay contact or module to the pump itself. P0230 concerns the primary side. GM's output driver compares the commanded with the actual state of the relay control circuit and sets the code at 8 of 10 mismatches, after two trips; Ford checks for open or short circuits for 2–5 s. With a failed relay control the pump stays off and the engine will not start or dies; a short to voltage keeps the pump running and drains the battery. On Ford systems with a pump control module the code means its power relay circuit; on the Subaru-based Saab 9-2X it is the pump module's collective fault report.

P0231.d: The fuel pump circuit has two sides: the primary circuit is the engine module's output to the fuel pump relay coil (or to a pump control module), the secondary circuit is the power circuit from relay contact or module to the pump itself. P0231 means the secondary side reads low, and the meaning differs by system. Ford's relay systems read the voltage in the pump power circuit through a monitor wire: if it is missing with the pump commanded on – relay contact not closing, fuse missing, wire open or shorted to ground – the code sets after 2–5 s. GM pumps with their own power module report a short to ground as overcurrent at 18 A or more, setting the warning light in the first trip and switching the output off. The pump gets no voltage, so the engine will not start or stalls.

P0234.d: P0234 is a function code, not a sensor fault: the engine module compares target and actual boost, and actual boost stays above target although the control is already lowering it (wastegate opened, variable vanes opened). GM petrol engines set it at 20–35 kPa over target with the warning light in the first trip; GM diesels with variable vanes at 7–10 kPa, after two trips; Ford EcoBoost at about 28 kPa (4 psi) over 5 s while the wastegate is already commanded fully open. Ford diesels instead use P0234 for exhaust back pressure above 4.0–4.5 bar. The engine limits boost or enters limp mode. Typical causes are a wastegate stuck closed, sooted variable vanes or a faulty control valve; Audi traced cases on the Q7 TDI to cracked exhaust parts jamming the turbo vanes. Check the boost sensor against barometric pressure first.

P023F.d: The fuel pump circuit has two sides: the primary circuit is the engine module's output to the fuel pump relay coil (or to a pump control module), the secondary circuit is the power circuit from relay contact or module to the pump itself. P023F means the power circuit to the pump is open. GM pumps with their own power module, whose speed is controlled by rail pressure, measure the pump current: if it stays below 1 A (older modules 0.5 A) although the pump is commanded, the code sets with the warning light in the first trip, and fuel pressure diagnostics are suspended. The cause lies in the wire from module to pump or its return, the pump connector or the pump motor itself. The pump stops, so the engine will not start or dies – there is no limp mode.
s: Engine does not start, no pump noise

P0240.d: Boost sensor B is a second boost pressure sensor, for a second turbo or bank on parallel twin-turbo engines or a second stage on two-stage systems. No manufacturer using sensor B codes was found – GM, Ford and Saab, even on two-stage and twin-turbo engines, use a single boost sensor; the description follows CARB and the documented sensor A codes. P0243.d: The wastegate lets exhaust bypass the turbine to limit boost; actuator A is either a pulse-width-modulated solenoid on a pneumatic wastegate can or an electric actuator with a position sensor. P0243 is the general circuit fault of actuator A. GM uses it for an open circuit: with the driver off, more than 200 kΩ between output and ground in 10 of 20 samples sets it with the warning light in the first trip (older modules: two trips). Ford uses P0243 on its electric wastegates as the collective code for open and short circuits (0.4 s), together with P2ABD for driver overcurrent or overheating. Boost control is then switched off and only the spring-set base boost remains – less power, but no risk of overboost.
s: Clearly less power, boost only at base level

P0244.d: The wastegate lets exhaust bypass the turbine to limit boost; actuator A is either a pulse-width-modulated solenoid on a pneumatic wastegate can or an electric actuator with a position sensor. P0244 means the actuator does not respond as commanded although its circuit is electrically sound, and manufacturers implement it differently. Subaru engines (Saab 9-2X) set it when manifold pressure exceeds an altitude-dependent limit – about 220 kPa absolute at sea level – for over 2 s, with the warning light at once. Stellantis documented it with a wastegate rod that had come off for want of a retaining clip. Older GM modules (Saab LDK, LLU) however use P0244 for an open solenoid circuit; newer GM and Ford systems do not use it and monitor function under P0234/P0299 or P25B3/P25B4.

P024A.d: The charge air cooler bypass is a flap or valve that routes compressed air around the charge air cooler, so the engine and exhaust warm up faster after a cold start; when warm it closes or opens partly to control intake air temperature. It is driven by an electric motor with a built-in position sensor or by a solenoid and vacuum can. P024A is the functional fault: the bypass does not follow its command, judged from the position sensor or from the expected temperature effect – Bosch describes comparing the cooler's efficiency with the valve closed and open, using modelled air temperature before and measured temperature after the cooler. FCA documents P024A, together with P026E, on the 2017 Alfa Romeo Giulia and 2018 Stelvio with the 2.0 turbo and fixed it with an engine software update, so check the software level first.
s: Longer warm-up or higher charge air temperature
Possibly less power from boost limitation

P024B.d: The charge air cooler bypass is a flap or valve that routes compressed air around the charge air cooler, so the engine and exhaust warm up faster after a cold start; when warm it closes or opens partly to control intake air temperature. It is driven by an electric motor with a built-in position sensor or by a solenoid and vacuum can. P024B means the bypass flap does not move at all despite being commanded – the position signal stands still or the air temperature shows no reaction. Bosch's patent describes exactly the case of a valve stuck closed or a blocked bypass, which raises emissions during warm-up. Stuck open, the charge air gets hotter and power drops; stuck closed, warm-up takes longer. No manufacturer document using this code was found – GM and Ford do not use the bypass codes; the description rests on CARB's component monitoring requirement and a Bosch patent on the bypass valve.
s: Stuck open: higher charge air temperature, loss of power

P0251.d: These codes cover the electrically controlled fuel metering actuator on a diesel injection pump. On older distributor pumps it was a solenoid that set the injected quantity; on common rail it is usually an inlet metering valve on the high-pressure pump that lets only as much fuel into the pumping elements as the rail needs, instead of spilling the excess through a pressure valve. Manufacturers use different codes for this part: Ford P0001–P0004, GM Duramax P0090–P0092. P0251 is the general circuit fault of actuator A. Saab's 2011 9-5 diesel uses it for an open circuit of the pressure regulator on the high-pressure pump: if the control wire does not show the expected voltage with the driver off for more than 1 s, the code sets with the warning light at once. Depending on the system, rail pressure and power are then limited.

P0252.d: These codes cover the electrically controlled fuel metering actuator on a diesel injection pump. On older distributor pumps it was a solenoid that set the injected quantity; on common rail it is usually an inlet metering valve on the high-pressure pump that lets only as much fuel into the pumping elements as the rail needs, instead of spilling the excess through a pressure valve. Manufacturers use different codes for this part: Ford P0001–P0004, GM Duramax P0090–P0092. P0252 is the range or performance fault of actuator A, and the meaning depends on the maker. Saab's 2011 9-5 diesel sets it when the driver stage of the pump pressure regulator overheats – a sign of a shorted turn or excessive current – with the warning light at once; Ford checks the same under P0002 at a driver temperature above 170 °C. Generally the code can also mean the actuator does not achieve the expected effect.

GM's pump module compares the enable line with the request on the data bus and sets P025A after about 1 s, with the warning light in the first trip; on some Ford vehicles the code does not light it.

P026A.d: P026A means the charge air cooler is not cooling enough. The module compares the temperature drop across the cooler with the maximum possible (inlet minus ambient) or with a model: GM's 6.6 litre LML diesel sets it below 25 % efficiency, later GM diesels below 50 %, both after two trips; Ford's 6.7 and 3.0 diesels when the measured temperature is 18–35 °C (3.0: 35–65 °C) off the model over about 10 s. GM's 3.0 twin-turbo petrol with a coolant-cooled charge air cooler sets it in the first trip when manifold air exceeds 110 °C or boost has been limited for a long time. Hot intake air costs power and raises NOx and soot.

P026B.d: P026B is the engine-wide injection timing monitor: CARB requires diesels from 2010 to detect injection that is too early or too late overall, or a timing control at its limit. Unlike P020A ff (per cylinder) it concerns the engine as a whole. It is documented on the Ram 6.7 Cummins, together with the per-cylinder timing and balance codes; FCA describes it as set falsely by software and fixes it with an engine module update, without publishing thresholds. GM and Ford handle timing with per-cylinder codes instead (P01CB ff, P2B11 ff).

P026C.d: From 2010, CARB requires diesel engines to detect when the commanded injection quantity is not delivered. The module estimates the fuel actually burned from airflow and the measured lambda (from the NOx or oxygen sensor) and corrects the quantity; if that correction passes a limit, the code sets. P026C means the engine gets less fuel than commanded. GM's 6.6 litre LML diesel checks it at idle with the vehicle stationary and the engine warm, setting it at a correction of −20 to −35 mm³ per stroke for 12 s; later GM diesels use the learned correction value (10 of 20 samples); both need two trips. FCA lists it with an injector cleaning procedure for deposits. Ford diesels do not use it. Typical causes are coked injectors, wrong airflow or lambda measurement and weak fuel supply.

P026D.d: From 2010, CARB requires diesel engines to detect when the commanded injection quantity is not delivered. The module estimates the fuel actually burned from airflow and the measured lambda (from the NOx or oxygen sensor) and corrects the quantity; if that correction passes a limit, the code sets. P026F.d: P026F is a general functional code for the coolant thermostat. CARB requires that the coolant reaches the temperature needed for other diagnostics in the approved time and comes within 11 °C of the thermostat's regulating temperature; from model years 2019–2021 petrol engines must also detect it dropping back below that temperature, and electric pumps or valves controlling coolant flow are monitored like a thermostat. The module follows coolant temperature against a heat model. No manufacturer using P026F was found – GM and Ford report thermostat faults as P0128, P01F0 or P2181 – so the description rests on CARB and the thermostat's function.

P027A.d: On demand-controlled fuel systems the engine module does not drive the pump itself but sends a pump control module the desired pump output on a separate control line, usually as a duty cycle; the module reports back on a monitor line or via CAN. Module B is a second pump module, for example on dual-tank commercial vehicles. P027A is the counterpart of P025A: the control line from the engine module to pump module B is open or faulty. No manufacturer using P027A was found – Ford reports line faults of both modules together under P025A, GM only uses P025A; the description follows CARB's circuit monitoring requirement and Ford's module B check. If the second tank's pump gets no valid command, fuel may run short when running from that tank.
s: Fuel shortage when running from the second tank

P027B.d: On demand-controlled fuel systems the engine module does not drive the pump itself but sends a pump control module the desired pump output on a separate control line, usually as a duty cycle; the module reports back on a monitor line or via CAN. Module B is a second pump module, for example on dual-tank commercial vehicles. P027B means pump module B receives an invalid command or its feedback does not match. Ford's module signals this with a 20 % (±4 %) duty cycle on its monitor line, checked continuously at 11–16 V over 2–5 s; on Ford commercial vehicles the module B monitor line runs via the smart relay module and CAN to the engine module. Whether the warning light comes on depends on the vehicle.

c: Limiter speed genuinely exceeded (downhill, trailer)

P0297.d: P0297 is a condition code: the engine module detects that road speed – from the vehicle speed sensor or wheel and output shaft speed – exceeded the calibrated maximum. Electronic speed limiters cut fuel or throttle at that limit, and the event is stored. Ford uses the code on its petrol trucks and stores it without the warning light; no manufacturer publishes a threshold. Common triggers are descending with a trailer beyond the limiter speed, wheelspin on the driven axle, a wrongly programmed tyre size or axle ratio, or spikes in the speed signal. Unlike P0219 it concerns road speed, not engine speed.
s: Usually no warning light, code only stored
Vehicle limits speed at its maximum
With a disturbed signal: jumping speedometer, odd shifting

c: High load in heat (trailer, mountain pass, stop-and-go)

Low oil level or wrong oil
P0298.d: P0298 is a protection code: engine oil temperature – from its own sensor, often combined with the oil level sensor, or modelled – has exceeded the protection limit. Saab's 3.0 diesel limits injection quantity when the oil stays at 135 °C or more for over 10 s, until it cools down; a heavy-duty bus engine warns in two stages and then derates. Ford stores the code without the warning light, in line with CARB's exemption for overheat protection. Usual causes are high load in heat, cooling problems, a clogged oil cooler or stuck oil thermostat, and occasionally a sensor reading too high.

P0299.d: P0299 means actual boost stays below target for a period although the control already demands more. Thresholds: GM petrol 30–55 kPa below target with the warning light in the first trip; GM diesels 10–50 kPa, two trips; Ford EcoBoost more than 4 psi (about 28 kPa) for 5 s with the wastegate already commanded fully closed; Ford diesels 30–40 kPa for 10–15 s, with a further underboost code P2263. Typical causes from manufacturer bulletins: a charge air leak, a wastegate that lost its preload or whose rod came off, a leaking bypass valve, sticking turbo vanes on diesels, and ice in the charge air cooler in winter. A faulty boost sensor can also fake underboost. Many engines then limit power.
s: Whistling or hissing from the charge air path under load

c: Injector of cylinder 1 coked or partly clogged

P029A.d: These codes belong to an individual-cylinder fuel correction: a diesel's cylinder balance control measures each cylinder's crankshaft acceleration and adjusts its injection quantity; on petrol engines a cylinder-selective mixture control does the same. CARB requires the system to report when such a correction has used up its range or one cylinder causes an imbalance. P029A means the correction for cylinder 1 is at its upper limit: the module keeps giving this cylinder more fuel and still cannot even it out – a sign that the cylinder receives too little fuel or builds too little pressure. GM and Ford use other codes for this (P0263 ff, P219A ff); no manufacturer document describing this code with thresholds was found, so the description follows CARB and published patents.

P02BF means the correction for cylinder 10 is at its lower limit: the module keeps taking fuel away from this cylinder and still cannot even it out – a sign that it receives too much fuel, for example from a dripping injector. Cylinder 10 only exists on engines with ten or more cylinders. GM and Ford use other codes for this (P0263 ff, P219A ff); no manufacturer document describing this code with thresholds was found, so the description follows CARB and published patents.
s: Higher consumption, smoke or fuel smell
P02BF.t: Cylinder 10 - Fuel Trim at Min Limit

P02CA.d: Turbocharger B is a second, separately controlled turbo – on twin-turbo or two-stage systems, or one per bank. No manufacturer using the turbo B codes was found; twin-turbo engines such as GM's 3.0 V6 and Ford's 3.5 EcoBoost report boost faults under P0234/P0299 with a shared boost sensor, so the description follows CARB and the turbo A codes. P02CA means actual boost of turbo B stays above target although the control is already lowering it; for turbo A, GM petrol engines use 20–35 kPa, Ford EcoBoost more than 4 psi over 5 s. Boost is then limited.
s: Check engine light, reduced power, limp mode

c: Charge air leak (hose, cooler, clamp) on side B
Wastegate B stuck open or control valve faulty
Turbo B worn (bearing play, compressor wheel)
Exhaust leak ahead of turbine B
P02CB.d: Turbocharger B is a second, separately controlled turbo – on twin-turbo or two-stage systems, or one per bank. No manufacturer using the turbo B codes was found; twin-turbo engines such as GM's 3.0 V6 and Ford's 3.5 EcoBoost report boost faults under P0234/P0299 with a shared boost sensor, so the description follows CARB and the turbo A codes. P02CB means actual boost of turbo B stays below target although the control demands more; for turbo A, GM uses 30–55 kPa (petrol) or 10–50 kPa (diesel). Typical causes are a charge air leak on that side, a wastegate stuck open or a worn turbo. Power is then limited.
s: Whistling with a leak, limp mode

c: Injector of cylinder 1 leaking or over-delivering at small quantities
Engine software (update available for some models)
Injector correction code not or wrongly programmed after replacement
Disturbed crankshaft signal (worn drive belt, tone wheel, dual-mass flywheel)
P02CC.d: The engine module learns a small-quantity correction for each injector: on overrun it gives one injector a tiny test injection (GM about 1.5 mm³), measures the resulting crankshaft acceleration and corrects the injector's activation time per rail pressure step. P02CC means the learned correction for cylinder 1 has reached its lower limit at at least one pressure step: the injector needs much less activation time than nominal – it delivers too much at small quantities or opens early. GM diesels set it at limits of roughly ±66–182 µs after two trips. It is documented on GM's 6.6 litre L5P and 2.8 litre diesels – on the 2.8 a worn drive belt caused it to return after injector replacement – and on Land Rover's 5.0 V8 petrol, where a software update is the first step. It differs from P01CC (over advanced), which some systems derive from the same learning.
s: Often nothing noticeable; possibly rough idle or knocking

P02DB.d: The engine module learns a small-quantity correction for each injector: on overrun it gives one injector a tiny test injection (GM about 1.5 mm³), measures the resulting crankshaft acceleration and corrects the injector's activation time per rail pressure step. P02DB means the learned correction for cylinder 8 has reached its upper limit at at least one pressure step: the injector needs much more activation time than nominal – it delivers too little or opens late, for example from coking. GM diesels set it at limits of roughly ±66–182 µs after two trips. Older GM calibrations (LML) use only this code of the pair, for both directions. It is documented on GM's 6.6 litre L5P diesel and on Land Rover's 5.0 V8 petrol, where a software update is the first step. It differs from P01D9 (over retarded), which some systems derive from the same learning.
s: Often nothing noticeable; possibly rough idle or knocking
Possibly smoke or loss of power

P02E0.d: The diesel intake air flow valve A is the throttle flap ahead of the intake manifold of a diesel engine: it creates the vacuum needed for high EGR rates, lowers airflow to heat the particulate filter and catalyst during regeneration and closes at switch-off against run-on shaking. A spring holds it open when unpowered; an electric motor positions it, with a position sensor reporting back. P02E0 means the motor circuit is open – cable, connector or motor winding. GM diesels detect more than 200 kΩ with the driver off, after about 1.5 s (6.6 litre LML: 7 s), two trips. On a fault the valve is switched off and the spring opens it: driving is usually little affected, but EGR control is restricted and filter regeneration may be blocked.
s: Filter regeneration does not run, soot load rises

P02EC.d: Ford's 6.7 and 3.0 diesels control the air mass through the EGR valve and the intake throttle. P02EC means the measured air mass stays above target with the control at its limit – too little EGR, or the throttle cannot restrict enough – for 10 s (6.7) or 5 s (3.0). Typical causes are a stuck-closed EGR valve or clogged EGR cooler, a throttle stuck open or a mass airflow sensor reading too high. NOx rises; driving is usually unaffected. Other manufacturers using this code were not found.

P02EE.d: P02EE reports an electrically implausible response of the cylinder 1 injector – not an open or short circuit (those are P0201, P0261, P0262), but a current or voltage pattern outside the expected range. GM's 8-cylinder diesel checks the time the current takes to fall from hold to zero (outside 20–50 µs in 10 of 20 samples, two trips); GM's petrol direct injection evaluates the voltage feedback of the opening and closing; Ford's diesels flag the injector's voltage or charge regulator at its limit (90 s), Ford's petrol direct injection its controlled-valve-operation adaptation at its limit. The injector may be shut off, causing misfire.

P02FA.d: The diesel intake throttle learns the position sensor values of its end stops, as a Toyota patent describes for the closed stop at engine stop. P02FA means a learned end-stop value is implausible. Ford's 6.7 and 3.0 diesels check it once after each learning run and set the code when the learned minimum offset is outside ±10 (6.7) or ±6.7 (3.0) – Ford only evaluates the minimum stop. Typical causes are soot and oil deposits at the flap and stop, a worn or shifted sensor, mechanical damage or a replacement part that has not been learned. EGR control may be restricted.
s: EGR control restricted, filter regeneration hindered

P02FB.d: Cold start fuel injection is an extra injection system for cold starts – for example on flex-fuel engines running on high ethanol blends, where a Hyundai patent describes a small auxiliary tank, a cold-start injector and a heater. CARB lists such heated fuel preparation systems among the monitored output components. P02FB means the control circuit of the cold-start injection is open or has a general fault – a broken coil, a loose or corroded connector or a broken wire. The engine then starts poorly or not at all in the cold; once warm it runs normally. No manufacturer document using this code was found; unlike the older P0213/P0214, these codes separate the fault types.
s: Hard or no start in cold weather (especially with high ethanol)
Rough running right after a cold start

P02FC.d: Cold start fuel injection is an extra injection system for cold starts – for example on flex-fuel engines running on high ethanol blends, where a Hyundai patent describes a small auxiliary tank, a cold-start injector and a heater. CARB lists such heated fuel preparation systems among the monitored output components. P02FC means the control circuit reads low – typically the control wire shorted to ground or a shorted turn in the cold-start injector. Depending on the circuit the valve then does not work, or it stays open and over-fuels the engine, causing fuel smell and hot-start problems. No manufacturer document using this code was found; unlike the older P0213/P0214, these codes separate the fault types.

P02FD.d: Cold start fuel injection is an extra injection system for cold starts – for example on flex-fuel engines running on high ethanol blends, where a Hyundai patent describes a small auxiliary tank, a cold-start injector and a heater. P02FF.d: Many diagnostics need to know how long the engine – or, on hybrids, the whole propulsion system – has been off: thermostat and evaporative checks and the cold-start strategy, for which CARB requires at least 6 hours of standstill. A timer measures this time, and the engine module checks its plausibility, for example against coolant cooling – a GM patent describes such a check. P02FF means that timer is implausible. Mercedes documents it on M256, M260, M264 and M274 engines of around 2020: after an internal reset the instrument cluster clock ran wrong; the fix is a software update for engine, transmission and instrument cluster modules. P0300.d: The engine module detects misfire from crankshaft speed: a cylinder that does not fire gives no acceleration impulse. At a catalyst-damaging rate (CARB: at least 5 % per 200 revolutions) the warning light flashes; at an emissions-relevant rate (at least 1 % per 1,000 revolutions – GM about 2–5 %, Ford 0.9–1.5 %) it comes on after two trips. Ford and GM may shut off a misfiring cylinder's injector to protect the catalyst. P0300 sets when the misfire cannot be assigned to one cylinder: several cylinders each account for more than 10 %, the cylinder changes randomly, or – at Ford – the cylinder cannot be identified at high speed. It often appears together with cylinder codes. Causes are usually systemic: false air, worn plugs on several cylinders, fuel pressure or fuel quality, valve timing – and false detection from a damaged tone wheel, rough roads or vibration. Bulletins name coils, cracked plug insulators and wrong plug gaps.

P030A.d: Ignition A is one of the control signal lines from the engine module to an ignition module, ignition output stage or group of coils; which cylinders it serves is defined by the manufacturer, not by the code standard. The code concerns the logic-level control signal, not the coil's primary current (that has its own codes, P0351 ff and P2300 ff). P030A means the control line is open – the module sees a voltage with its driver off that indicates high resistance. No manufacturer using these codes was found; GM reports coil control faults as P0351 ff (open above 30 kΩ, first trip), so the description follows CARB and that analogy. The affected coils fire wrongly or not at all, causing misfire; many modules then shut off injection to those cylinders to protect the catalyst.
s: Loss of power, possibly cylinders shut off

c: Tank nearly empty – the fuel pump draws air (corners, gradients, braking)

P0313.d: When the tank is nearly empty the fuel pump can draw air in corners or on gradients, which causes misfires. CARB allows misfire detection to be switched off at 15 % fuel or less; some manufacturers instead report misfires detected in this state under P0313 rather than P030x. Ford's normal misfire monitor runs from 15 % fuel, Saab's ME9 from 12 %; Saab's T8 sets P0313 below 5 litres with the same tests as P0300 (3 % per 1,000 revolutions, flashing light at a catalyst-damaging rate). GM petrol engines simply suspend the monitor without their own code. After refuelling the symptoms usually disappear – if not, look for a real misfire cause.
s: Check engine light on (flashing at a catalyst-damaging rate)
Jerking or power loss with an almost empty tank, especially in corners or uphill

c: Injector of one cylinder clogged or leaking (diesel), or coil/plug (petrol)
Leaking high-pressure line, fuel bridge or injector washer
Air, water or petrol in the diesel, clogged filter, low supply pressure
Compression loss (valve, piston)
P0314.d: P0314 means the misfire is attributable to a single cylinder, but the module does not say which one. CARB generally requires cylinder-specific codes and allows a general code only with approval where the cylinder cannot be identified reliably; for diesels identification is required only where possible without extra hardware. GM and Ford do not use P0314. It is documented on Saab's 2.2 TiD diesel with a Bosch distributor pump, as a mechanical misfire fault in two speed and quantity windows with the warning light and limp mode limiting injection quantity; the cylinder can still be read out with a scan tool. Typical causes are a faulty injector, leaking high-pressure lines, air or water in the fuel, or low compression.
s: Loss of power, limp mode with quantity limit (Saab diesel)

c: Relearn not performed after replacing sensor, crankshaft, damper, engine or engine module
Learned values lost through voltage loss (battery disconnected)
Tone wheel damaged or shifted, crankshaft runout, dirt on the sensor
Interference in the crankshaft sensor circuit
Engine module memory faulty
P0315.d: Manufacturing tolerances of the crankshaft tone wheel distort the speed fluctuations misfire detection relies on, so the engine module learns a correction for each tooth or segment. P0315 means these values have not been learned or are invalid. GM checks that the learned tooth angles add up to 360° (deviation above 0.001° sets the code in the first trip) and learns them with a scan tool: brakes held, full throttle in park until fuel cut-off. Ford learns the profile during up to three overrun phases from 60 to 40 mph and sets P0315 when that fails. Until relearned, misfire detection is suspended – at GM above 1,000 rpm – and misfire readiness stays incomplete. The relearn is needed after replacing the engine, engine module, crankshaft, damper or crankshaft sensor.
s: Check engine light on (GM; Ford depending on application)
Misfire readiness not set – emissions test fails

c: Moisture or water in the plug wells, coils arcing when cold or damp

P0316.d: P0316 concerns misfire within the first 1,000 revolutions after start. CARB requires a pending code here after the first exceedance of the emissions-relevant rate (later in the drive only after the fourth) and the warning light if it recurs at the next start. Ford sets P0316 in addition to the cylinder code; GM evaluates the start within P0300–P0308 without its own code. Typical causes are water in the plug wells (Mazda Tribute bulletin: blocked drain in the valve cover channel), coils that arc when cold and damp, injectors that drip after switch-off and over-rich starting – Ford traced cases on the 2.7 EcoBoost to engine software or leaking direct injectors.

Delayed start, fuel smell at start

c: Module configuration does not match the equipment (after engine or ABS module replacement)
ABS/ESP module not responding (supply, CAN line)
Separate rough-road sensor missing or unplugged, where fitted
Engine module faulty
P0317.d: Misfire detection works from crankshaft speed fluctuations, which rough roads also cause. CARB therefore allows misfire detection to pause on rough roads; many engines take a rough-road signal from the wheel speeds of the ABS module, a Ford patent describes such a detector. P0317 means the engine module is calibrated for an external rough-road signal but does not find the hardware: the supplying module does not respond on the data bus, or the configuration does not match the equipment – for example after replacing the engine or ABS module. Without the signal misfire detection cannot separate road bumps from misfires. No manufacturer document using P0317 was found; the description follows CARB and GM's rough-road sources in its misfire monitor.
s: Possibly false misfire codes on rough roads

c: Wheel speed sensor or wiring faulty – the brake module passes on the fault
Communication between engine and brake module lost (CAN, connector, supply)
Brake control module faulty
Separate rough-road sensor faulty, where fitted
P0318.d: Misfire detection works from crankshaft speed fluctuations, which rough roads also cause. CARB therefore allows misfire detection to pause on rough roads; many engines take a rough-road signal from the wheel speeds of the ABS module, a Ford patent describes such a detector. P0318 means rough-road signal A is missing or invalid. On GM engines (documented in Saab service information for the 1.6 turbo) the brake control module sends wheel speed over the data bus; the code sets between 1,520 and 4,000 rpm when that module reports a wheel speed sensor fault or no signal arrives for more than 5 s. GM files it without the warning light. Misfire detection then runs without its rough-road filter. ABS or stability warnings and further codes often appear at the same time.
s: Often ABS or stability warning at the same time

P0319.d: Misfire detection works from crankshaft speed fluctuations, which rough roads also cause. CARB therefore allows misfire detection to pause on rough roads; many engines take a rough-road signal from the wheel speeds of the ABS module, a Ford patent describes such a detector. P0319 is like P0318, but for a second rough-road signal source B – depending on the manufacturer, for example an acceleration sensor or transmission output speed. The signal is missing or invalid, so misfire detection runs without its rough-road filter. No manufacturer using P0319 was found; following GM's handling of P0318, the warning light often stays off.

P031A.d: Ignition C is one of the control signal lines from the engine module to an ignition module, ignition output stage or group of coils; which cylinders it serves is defined by the manufacturer, not by the code standard. The code concerns the logic-level control signal, not the coil's primary current (that has its own codes, P0351 ff and P2300 ff). P031A means the control line is open – the module sees a voltage with its driver off that indicates high resistance. No manufacturer using these codes was found; GM reports coil control faults as P0351 ff (open above 30 kΩ, first trip), so the description follows CARB and that analogy. The affected coils fire wrongly or not at all, causing misfire; many modules then shut off injection to those cylinders to protect the catalyst.
s: Loss of power, possibly cylinders shut off

P0320.d: P0320 originally covered the engine speed signal from the distributor or ignition module to the engine module (early OBD II); today Ford's engine module evaluates the crankshaft sensor directly and uses this code for it. Ford checks continuously from 200–500 rpm and sets it within 5 s when the number of teeth after the gap is wrong, the tooth time is implausible (below 30 or above 9,000 rpm) or the gap appears in the wrong place; fuel and spark are then cut briefly to resynchronise, and on electronic throttle P2106 limits power. Some Ford engines use P0339 instead. Typical causes are a faulty crankshaft sensor, interference in the wiring or a damaged tone wheel.
s: Reduced power on electronic throttle (Ford P2106)

P0321.d: P0321 belongs to the same signal as P0320 and P0322: the speed and reference input of the ignition, formerly the distributor's Hall pickup, today practically always the crankshaft position sensor. Range/Performance means a signal is present but implausible – wrong number of teeth between the reference gaps, erratic tooth times, or a speed that does not fit the camshaft signal. No manufacturer document available to us describes P0321 by code: Ford runs these tooth checks under P0320 or P0339 (wrong tooth count after the gap, tooth time outside 30 to 9,000 rpm, gap at the wrong position) and GM under P0336. The description therefore follows that logic and CARB's rationality requirement for crank angle sensors.

P0322.d: P0322 means the speed and reference input of the ignition – today the crankshaft position sensor – delivers no signal although the engine is turning. Ford proves the rotation with the camshaft sensor: if it shows more than one engine revolution without a crank signal (from 500 rpm, detected within 5 s), Ford sets P0322 or, depending on the engine, P0335; with electronic throttle the throttle software adds P2106 and goes into limp mode. Without a crank signal there is no ignition or injection, so the engine stalls or does not start. Saab's Motronic 2.8.1 (900 V6) sets P0322 when the engine fails to start; its inductive sensor should measure 500–600 Ω and give 2–5 V AC while cranking. Systems without a camshaft-based check may store no code at all on a total failure.
s: Engine cranks but does not start

P0323.d: P0323 stands for a speed and reference signal at the ignition input – today the crankshaft position sensor – that drops out or is disturbed for moments and then recovers. None of the manufacturer documents available to us (GM 2014–2019, Ford 2012 and 2020–2023, Saab workshop information) uses P0323; the sporadic crank sensor check runs under P0339 at Ford and under P0336 at GM. Ford's logic shows what is evaluated: teeth missing or extra for a moment and the reference gap appearing at an unexpected position, after which the module briefly cuts fuel and spark and resynchronises. Typical causes are a loose contact, chafed wiring and electrical interference. The code itself is described only by its J2012 name and CARB's monitoring requirement for crank angle sensors.

P0324.d: P0324 concerns the knock control as a whole rather than a single sensor circuit. GM and Saab's GM-based engines set it when excessive knock persists on one cylinder – knock despite ignition retard, or mechanical noise taken for knock – for more than 8–10 s; GM's 2018 engines in the first trip, older ones after two. P0325.d: The knock sensor is a piezoelectric structure-borne sound sensor bolted to the engine block; the module evaluates its signal per cylinder and retards ignition when it detects knock. Sensor A is the first sensor (bank 1 or a single sensor). With a fault the module retards ignition across the board as protection – noticeable loss of power and higher consumption. P0325 means the sensor circuit is open or the signal stays below the noise threshold. GM feeds a 20 kHz test signal into the circuit and detects an open circuit when it does not cancel out, setting the code in the first trip; Ford sees any open or short as a knock signal that is too small compared with the speed- and load-dependent noise level (at least 1,500 rpm, 35 % load, warm engine). Bulletins name moisture in the sensor (VW Touareg 3.6), engine software (GM Malibu 1.5) and chafed wiring (FCA).
s: Loss of power, sluggish response from ignition retard

P032F.d: P032F is a plausibility code: the engine module compares the torque the combustion engine actually delivers with the expected or requested torque. On hybrids the actual torque can be measured precisely through the generator; if it stays too low for a calibrated time, the code sets. Ford uses it on the 2.5 litre Escape, Corsair and Maverick hybrids: after recall 23V-380 the software detects internal engine damage such as connecting rod bearing failure and can then shut the engine down – P032F appears together with Ford's P1061; another bulletin fixes false setting by software. Stellantis lists it on the Ram 6.7 Cummins for engine stall detection. Thresholds are not published.
s: Check engine light and warning (Ford: wrench, stop safely)

P0335.d: The crankshaft position sensor reads a tone wheel with a reference gap (GM 58X, i.e. 60-2; Ford 36-1, 40-1 or 60-2) and gives the engine module speed and crank angle for injection and ignition. P0335 means it delivers no pulses although the engine demonstrably turns. GM proves the rotation via starter, camshaft pulses or airflow above 1.5 g/s and sets the code after at least 4 s of cranking or 0.3 s while running without a crank pulse (2 of 10 revolutions); petrol engines after two trips, the LML diesel in the first. Ford compares with the camshaft: more than one revolution without a crank signal, detected within 5 s. Without the signal the engine stalls or does not start; GM Global A engines (Saab 9-5 2010) keep running only with learned cam positions. A hot sensor that fails and recovers after cooling is typical.
s: Engine cranks but does not start
Engine stalls while driving or at idle
Hot-start problem: starts again after cooling down

P0336.d: P0336 means the crankshaft position sensor delivers pulses, but their pattern is implausible: the reference gap is missing or in the wrong place, the number of teeth between the gaps is wrong (58 on a 60-2 wheel) or the module keeps losing synchronisation. GM sets it after at least 4 resynchronisations in under 5 s, a gap not found within 0.4 s running or 1.5 s cranking, or a wrong tooth count in 8 of 10 revolutions, after two trips. Ford's 2023 diesel sets it when the gap of the 60-2 wheel is not recognised for 3 revolutions; GM's LML diesel uses a fault counter over tooth times. Ford petrol engines use P0320 or P0339 for the same checks. Result: misfire, jerking, brief cut-outs while the module resynchronises, and misfire detection is suspended.

P0337.d: By its J2012 name P0337 means the crankshaft position signal stays at a low level without changing state – signal wire shorted to ground, missing supply on a Hall sensor or a sensor stuck low. Few manufacturers use the code. GM 2014–2019 and Ford report all crank sensor faults under P0335/P0336 or P0320/P0339. GM's Global A engines (Saab 9-5 1.6 LLU, 2011) define P0337 as a low duty cycle: fewer than 200 reference pulses in 10 consecutive revolutions, caused among other things by an open or high resistance in the signal or ground wire, set after two trips. Older Bosch diesels (Saab 9-5 EDC16) use it differently for crank pulses missing while cam pulses are present, and shut the engine down. The consequence is as for P0335: stalling or no start.

P0338.d: By its J2012 name P0338 means the crankshaft position signal stays at a high level – signal wire shorted to supply, or an open signal output that the module's pull-up holds high on a Hall sensor. GM 2014–2019 and Ford do not use the code. GM's Global A engines in the Saab 9-5 (2010/11) and 9-4X define it as a high duty cycle, i.e. too many pulses or teeth between the reference gaps: on the 2.8 turbo V6 (LAU) a deviation of more than 8 teeth, checked once per revolution and set in the first trip; on the 1.6 (LLU) more than 200 reference pulses in 10 revolutions, and on the 2.0 turbo (LDK) a large tooth deviation over 4 revolutions, both after two trips. Behind this are usually interference pulses or a gap that is not recognised. Result: misfire, stalling, limp mode.

P0339.d: P0339 means the crankshaft position signal drops out or is disturbed for moments and then recovers. Ford's 2020–2023 petrol engines use it, depending on the engine, instead of P0320 for tooth errors: wrong tooth count after the gap, tooth time outside 30 to 9,000 rpm, gap at an unexpected position, from 500 rpm, detected within 5 s. In Ford's PCM code list (Roush workshop manual) P0339 is listed without check engine light. Saab's 9-3 diesel (T8) counts dropouts: more than 8 within 10 ms over 3 s, or more than 3 in a whole drive cycle. Honda recalled 2023 Accord Hybrids because a mis-machined sensor mounting caused no-start, rough idle, hunting idle and P0017 with P0339. Typical causes are a loose contact, a sensor failing when hot and a wrong air gap.
s: Check engine light on (not on all Ford engines)

P033A.d: The knock sensor is a piezoelectric structure-borne sound sensor bolted to the engine block; the module evaluates its signal per cylinder and retards ignition when it detects knock. Sensor D is a fourth sensor on engines with four knock sensors (McLaren 12C V8, Ford's 2020–23 systems). With a fault the module retards ignition across the board as protection – noticeable loss of power and higher consumption. P033A means the sensor circuit is open or the signal stays below the noise threshold. GM feeds a 20 kHz test signal into the circuit and detects an open circuit when it does not cancel out, setting the code in the first trip; Ford sees any open or short as a knock signal that is too small compared with the speed- and load-dependent noise level (at least 1,500 rpm, 35 % load, warm engine).
s: Loss of power, sluggish response from ignition retard

P033B.d: The knock sensor is a piezoelectric structure-borne sound sensor bolted to the engine block; the module evaluates its signal per cylinder and retards ignition when it detects knock. With a fault the module retards ignition across the board as protection – noticeable loss of power and higher consumption. P033B means the circuit is electrically sound but the signal is implausible. GM sets it when the filtered background noise stays below a threshold – typically a loose sensor or one not bolted down properly – in the first trip; Saab's GM-based engines also when excessive knock persists on several cylinders or a whole bank for 8–10 s. P033F.d: To know which stroke each cylinder is in, the engine module matches the crank angle with the camshaft phase. P033F means this synchronisation is lost while running or cannot be established. It is documented by code only at Ford (2020–2023): P033F, as an alternative to Ford's older own code, stands for a disturbed crank signal without crank/cam synchronisation, and then misfire detection is also impossible. Ford's 2012 description shows the reaction: on a crank sensor fault the module cuts fuel and spark and resynchronises – one revolution to find the gap, one more to confirm cylinder 1 via the camshaft sensor. FCA evaluates the same function in its own cam/crank synchronisation monitor under other codes. Besides the sensors, a jumped timing chain or belt can be behind it.

P0340.d: The camshaft position sensor, almost always a Hall sensor, tells the engine module which stroke cylinder 1 is in – one crank revolution alone is ambiguous – and measures the actual cam phase with variable timing. Sensor A is the intake camshaft, bank 1 the side with cylinder 1. P0340 means no or too few cam pulses arrive while the crankshaft turns in sync. GM sets it after 5.5 s (or 4 s) of cranking without a cam pulse or fewer than 4 pulses in 3 s running, petrol engines after two trips. Ford checks the ratio of cam to crank events from 200 rpm. The engine usually keeps running but starts longer and loses power as cam timing is held. Bulletins: corroded connectors on GM V8s (PIP5335C), moisture in the oil on short trips in Ford hybrids (SSM 48598).
s: Longer cranking before the engine starts
Loss of power (cam timing held in its base position)

P0341.d: P0341 means the intake camshaft sensor of bank 1 (or the only cam sensor) delivers pulses, but their number or pattern does not fit the crankshaft. GM counts the pulses while the crank is in sync: 4 to 6 in the first 12 reference events and 398 to 402 per 100 engine cycles on the 4X wheel of the cam phaser; outside that in 8 of 10 checks the code is set after two trips. Ford's 2023 diesel compares the detected segment profile of the cam wheel with the expected one (1.2 s); the Saab 9-4X V6 checks pulses per crank revolution and correlation with crank position. Ford petrol engines use P0344 instead. Result: cam phase uncertain, cam timing switched off, possibly hard starting. GM names corroded connectors at the timing cover as a sporadic cause (PIP5335C).
s: Longer cranking before the engine starts
Loss of power (cam timing held in its base position)

P0342.d: P0342 means the signal of the intake camshaft sensor of bank 1 (or the only cam sensor) stays at ground level without edges – signal wire shorted to ground, sensor supply missing or the Hall sensor faulty. Ford's 2023 diesel sets it when the signal stays at 0 V over 10 or more crank revolutions (3 s), while cranking or running. On the Saab 9-4X V6 (GM LAU) the signal must stay low without pulses for more than 1 s, or 10 s cumulatively, and the code follows after two trips; with the sensor disconnected the signal wire should show 4.8–5.2 V. Saab's Motronic 2.8.1 (900 V6) treats low and high together: no connection or short to ground or battery, about 4.5 V at idle, air gap at most 1.5 mm. GM petrol engines 2014–2019 and Ford petrol engines report this under P0340.
s: Longer cranking before the engine starts
Loss of power (cam timing held in its base position)

Causes are a signal wire shorted to positive, an open signal wire that the module's pull-up holds at 5 V, a broken sensor ground or a faulty sensor. Ford's 2023 diesel sets it when the signal stays at system voltage over 10 or more crank revolutions (3 s). On the Saab 9-4X V6 (GM LAU) the signal must stay high without pulses for more than 1 s, or 10 s cumulatively, and the code follows after two trips. Saab's Motronic 2.8.1 (900 V6) treats low and high together and allows an air gap of at most 1.5 mm. The consequences are as for P0340: longer cranking, cam timing switched off, loss of power.

P034A.d: Engines with start-stop or hybrid autostart store the crankshaft rest position when the engine stops, so that they can inject and fire correctly at once on restart. This needs a direction-sensing crank sensor, because a cylinder under compression can push the crankshaft backwards after shut-off. On restart the module compares the stored position with the one actually measured after the reference gap. GM sets P034A when they differ by more than 2 teeth in 2 of 3 autostarts or by at least 1 tooth in 4 of 5, after two trips; the diesel already at more than 1 tooth in 1 of 3. The check is suspended while a crank sensor fault is present. Result: start-stop is restricted, restarts take longer with conventional synchronisation, and the autostart may be rough.
P034A.t: Crankshaft Position Sensor - Crankshaft Start Position Incorrect

P034B.d: Direction-sensing (bidirectional) crank sensors count the rest position for start-stop even when the crankshaft rocks back after shut-off. In normal running the sensor must never report reverse rotation – if it does, the signal is disturbed. GM sets P034B after at least 3 direction reversals within 10 s at 400 to 2,000 rpm and an airflow of at least 1.5 g/s, after two trips; the diesel uses the same thresholds. GM bulletin 17-NA-317 describes the 3.6 V6 (LFY) in the 2018 Buick Enclave and Chevrolet Traverse: interference in the sensor circuit caused P034B with P0506, low idle or stalling after an autostart, transmission slip above 65 km/h and cruise control dropping out; the remedy was a revised sensor wiring. Result: start-stop disabled, possibly reduced power.
s: Low idle or stalling after an autostart
Follow-on effects such as transmission slip or cruise control dropping out (GM LFY)

P034C.d: With ion current sensing the spark plug serves as a sensor after the spark: a measuring voltage across the gap drives a current through the ions in the flame, from which the module detects combustion, misfire and knock – a Delphi patent describes coils with built-in ion sensing, and Saab's Trionic engines detected misfire this way. P034C means this measuring system works implausibly, so misfire and knock detection are no longer reliable. It is documented on the Alfa Romeo Giulia and Stelvio 2.9 V6 biturbo, where three bulletins fix it mainly with engine software; limp mode is possible. Sooted plugs or a faulty coil with ion circuit are further causes.
s: Limp mode or reduced power possible

P0350.d: P0350 is the general ignition coil circuit code without assignment to a coil: the engine module detects a fault in the primary or secondary circuit of a coil but does not report which one. This typically concerns older systems with a shared output stage or ignition module, or a shared feedback line for all coils. The monitoring works as for P0351 ff – primary-current feedback for each ignition command, or the voltage at the driver. GM and Ford report coil faults individually (P0351 ff, P2300 ff) and do not use P0350; the description follows CARB's output monitoring requirement, which allows one collective code.
s: Starting problems or stalling if a shared output stage fails

P0351.d: Modern engines have one coil-on-plug ignition coil per cylinder, with the output stage either in the engine module or in the coil itself. P0351 monitors the primary control circuit of coil A – the line from the engine module to the coil or its built-in output stage – for an open circuit or high resistance. GM's module measures the voltage with its low-side driver off and flags an open circuit above 30 kΩ in 50 of 63 samples (2018 engines in the first trip, older ones after two); Ford checks continuously within 1 s, expecting a primary-current feedback for every ignition command, and shuts off injection to that cylinder for 30 s at a time. Short circuits and the secondary side have their own codes (P2300 ff). Coil A usually serves cylinder 1, but the assignment is up to the manufacturer.
s: Misfire and rough running on cylinder 1, often also P0301
Loss of power, jerking under load
Cylinder shut off (injection off), risk to the catalyst if driven on

P0363.d: P0363 is a reaction code: the engine module has detected misfire severe enough to damage the catalyst – through its crankshaft-based misfire monitor – and has therefore shut off injection to the affected cylinder or cylinders. CARB allows exactly this: a vehicle that cuts fuel immediately on catalyst-damaging misfire may turn the check engine light on steadily instead of flashing it, and may switch fuel back on to re-check at most every 30 s. The code names no cylinder; that comes from the accompanying P0301 ff. It is documented by code only at FCA: two reprogramming bulletins for the 2017–2018 Alfa Romeo Giulia 2.0 turbo list P0363 alongside misfire and mixture codes. Ford reacts in the same way without its own code, VW uses a manufacturer code (P130A) for the hidden cylinder, and GM does not list P0363.
s: Check engine light on steadily instead of flashing
Clearly rough running, one cylinder without power
Jerking or stalling, especially when cold

P0364.d: By its J2012 name P0364 means the control circuit to the control module of a DC/AC converter (inverter) behaves implausibly – the command or enable line is present but its signal does not fit what the engine module expects. The code is a late assignment in the P03xx block: older code lists show the slot as reserved, and the other DC/AC converter codes sit in the P2DAx range (P2DA8–P2DAB). Which converter is meant – a traction inverter in a hybrid or a 120/230 V socket inverter – the name does not say, and no manufacturer document available to us uses P0364. The description is therefore limited to the code name and CARB's general requirement to monitor electronic powertrain components. Whether the check engine light comes on and what the vehicle restricts depends on the manufacturer.

P0365.d: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor (bank 1 = side with cylinder 1), usually a Hall sensor on the exhaust cam phaser. P0365 means no or too few exhaust cam pulses arrive while the crankshaft turns in sync. GM sets it after 4 s of cranking or 5.5 s without a cam pulse, or fewer than 4 pulses in 3 s running, 8 of 10 samples, after two trips; on GM's 3.6-litre V6 (Saab 9-4X) also with no pulse in 800 of 1,000 engine cycles. Ford checks the ratio of crank to cam events from 200 rpm, detected within 5 s, and collects all electrical faults here. The exhaust phaser then goes to its park position; the engine keeps running but cranks longer and loses some power. FCA advises saving the cam/crank synchronisation data before replacing the sensor, as the fault is often elsewhere.
s: Longer cranking before the engine starts
Loss of power or rough idle (exhaust cam timing in its base position)

GM expects 400 pulses per 100 engine cycles and sets the code outside 398–402, or with fewer than 4 or more than 6 pulses in the first 12 reference events at start, 8 of 10 samples, after two trips. P0367.d: Camshaft position sensor B is the exhaust camshaft sensor (bank 1 = side with cylinder 1), usually a Hall sensor on the exhaust cam phaser. The engine module holds the signal line at about 5 V and the sensor pulls it to ground with each tooth. P0367 means the line stays low without edges – typically a short to ground of the signal wire or a sensor shorted internally. A code-specific manufacturer description exists only from GM: on the Saab 9-4X 2.8 turbo V6 (LAU) the signal must stay low without pulses for more than 1 s, or 10 s cumulatively, after more than 10 crank revolutions and below 2,520 rpm, and the code follows after two trips; with the sensor disconnected the signal wire should show 4.8–5.2 V. P0370.d: Some diesel systems give the injection control a finely divided angle signal in addition to the normal reference signal, to time and meter injection precisely – the high resolution signal. GM's 6.5-litre diesel (1997) had an optical sensor in the injection pump that delivers a high resolution track and one cam reference pulse per cylinder; P0370 is set if more than 8 consecutive cam pulses pass without progress on the high resolution counter, in the first trip. The engine then runs on backup fuelling with reduced power, and injection timing control is suspended. On the 2004 Duramax LB7 the injector driver module evaluates the 57X crank signal and reports 'no crank signal' over CAN; from 60 rpm, 100 of 120 samples sets P0370, also in the first trip. Petrol engines practically do not use the code.
P0370.t: Timing Reference High Resolution Signal A

P0371.d: Some diesel systems give the injection control a finely divided angle signal in addition to the normal reference signal – the high resolution signal – for precise injection timing and metering. P0371 means signal A delivers more pulses than expected within the reference window – for example more high resolution pulses per reference pulse than the nominal ratio, which on GM's 6.5-litre diesel is 64 ± 4 per cam pulse; the usual cause is interference pulses. No manufacturer document available to us uses P0371: GM's 6.5-litre diesel (optical sensor in the injection pump) reports all faults of its high resolution track under P0370 and the Duramax LB7 uses only P0370 and P0374. The description therefore follows the J2012 name, GM's description of the signal and CARB's monitoring requirement for crank angle sensors. Typically the engine loses power and runs roughly.

P0374.d: Some diesel systems give the injection control a finely divided angle signal in addition to the normal reference signal – the high resolution signal. By its J2012 name P0374 means signal A delivers no pulses at all although the engine turns. GM's 2004 Duramax LB7 uses the code differently, for a plausibility fault: the injector driver module evaluates the 57X crank signal and reports it as implausible over CAN; from 60 rpm, 100 of 120 samples of 31.6 ms set the code, in the first trip. GM's 6.5-litre diesel with the optical sensor in the injection pump reports all faults of its high resolution track under P0370. Without the fine signal the module falls back to coarser timing, so the engine loses power and may run roughly or start poorly.

P037A.d: Diesel engines show the driver a wait-to-start lamp while the glow plugs preheat; the engine module switches it with a high-side driver. P037A means the lamp control circuit is too low – in practice a short to ground on the line to the instrument cluster. GM's diesels detect it in the driver itself: about 0.5 Ω to ground with the lamp commanded, only with a lamp configured, ignition on, more than 11 V and not while cranking. The 2015 engines need 3 s of fault, the 2016/2018 engines 10 of 15 samples; the check engine light follows after two trips. The glow plugs keep working; only the indication is missing, so the driver may start too early. CARB requires monitoring of the wait-to-start lamp circuit. Ford reports lamp faults under P0381 and does not use P037A.

Check engine light on (GM after two trips)

P037B.d: P037B is the counterpart of P037A: the control circuit of the wait-to-start lamp is too high, i.e. the line carries voltage although the engine module's driver is off, or the driver sees a short to battery voltage. GM's 2015 diesels check in the off state and set the fault after 1 s with more than 11 V; the 2016/2018 engines evaluate a short of about 0.5 Ω to a voltage source in the driver, 10 of 20 samples at 100 ms. In both cases the check engine light comes on after two trips. The lamp then stays on permanently or cannot be switched off, so the driver no longer gets a usable preheat signal; the driver may protect itself when commanded. There is no limp mode. Ford and Saab do not use P037B; CARB requires monitoring of the lamp circuit and of output components for shorts.
