P08CB.t: Pressure Control Solenoid M Control Circuit High

c: Shift solenoid J faulty (coil or valve)
Contaminated or degraded transmission fluid restricting the valve
Connector or harness fault between TCM and solenoid
Transmission control module output fault
P08CC.d: Base code for the tenth on/off shift solenoid of an automatic transmission; which valve gets the letter J is decided by the manufacturer. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Ford's gasoline OBD summary ends its shift solenoid list at SS E, the Genesis 8-speed bulletin stops at solenoid F, and GM and Toyota label their later valves as pressure control or clutch solenoids, so J stays unused in the known sources. CARB requires automatic transmission solenoids to be checked for functional response and circuit faults. A manufacturer reporting the fault type through a DTC suffix, as Toyota does for pressure control solenoid L, would store such faults under this base code instead of P08CD to P08D4. Expect harsh, missing or substitute-gear shifts.
s: Check engine or transmission warning light on
Transmission may hold a substitute gear

c: Solenoid or its shift valve held in the off position by debris or varnish
Low fluid level or weak supply pressure to the valve
Worn clutch pack or leaking seal in the circuit served by the valve
Solenoid coil too weak to move the valve
P08CD.d: Set when shift solenoid J is switched on but the gear or clutch it controls does not respond, so the valve behaves as if stuck in its off position. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The closest documented analogue is GM's P0751 on the 6-speed transmissions: the TCM commands first gear and flags shift solenoid A stuck off when slip reaches 400 rpm with the gear ratio out of window, a two-trip fault. Ford sets P0751 to P0771 when the obtained gear or shift pattern shows a solenoid functionally failed off after three solenoid events. CARB requires this kind of functional check. P08CE is the opposite fault, P08CF and P08D1 to P08D4 cover the circuit. The driver notices slipping, flare or a missing gear.
s: Check engine or transmission warning light on
Engine flare or slipping during or after a shift
A gear is missing or skipped
Transmission may hold a substitute gear

c: Solenoid or its shift valve held in the applied position by debris or varnish
Contaminated transmission fluid after internal wear
Control circuit shorted so the solenoid stays energised
TCM output driver does not switch off
P08CE.d: Set when shift solenoid J is switched off but its clutch or shift valve stays applied, so the valve behaves as if stuck in its on position. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's P0752 on the 6-speed transmissions is the nearest documented counterpart: with third gear commanded, the TCM flags shift solenoid A stuck on when the gearbox slip reaches 400 rpm while first or second gear is actually obtained, and the MIL comes on after one trip. Ford sets its stuck-on codes P0752 to P0772 from the gear or shift pattern actually reached. CARB requires such functional monitoring. P08CD is the opposite fault. Because an applied clutch can tie up the gearbox, drivers may feel a wrong gear, a harsh engagement or limp mode.
s: Check engine or transmission warning light on
Wrong gear or harsh engagement, possible binding feel

c: Solenoid coil open or shorted internally
Damaged harness, corroded or loose connector at the transmission
Fault in the internal transmission harness or solenoid body
TCM output driver fault
P08CF.d: General electrical fault of shift solenoid J, used when a manufacturer does not split the circuit fault into open, low, high or range codes. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The analogue for solenoid A, P0753, is used by Hyundai for Genesis G80 and G90 8-speed transmissions as Shift Control Solenoid Valve A Electrical; bulletin 21-AT-016HG lists electrical codes for valves A to F and has the solenoid replaced after checking the harness, without any J valve. Ford's electrical check flags a solenoid when driver feedback disagrees with the commanded state for 0.5 to 5 seconds. CARB requires circuit monitoring when a functional check is not feasible. P08D1 to P08D4 are the detailed circuit codes. Shift quality usually drops at once.

c: Loose or corroded connector losing contact under vibration or heat
Chafed harness with intermittent short or break
Valve sticking now and then due to contaminated fluid
Solenoid coil failing only when hot
P08D0.d: Reserved for a shift solenoid J fault that comes and goes instead of being present continuously, typically brief circuit dropouts or erratic valve response. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and the intermittent codes of the earlier shift solenoids, such as P0754 for solenoid A, are not used in the GM and Ford sources checked either; those makers report dropouts through their open, short or functional codes. Ford runs its solenoid electrical checks continuously with 0.5 to 5 second filters, so short interruptions are caught there. CARB requires circuit monitoring of transmission output components in general. P08CF and P08D1 to P08D4 are the permanent electrical faults. Drivers notice occasional harsh shifts or a passing warning light.
s: Warning light that comes and goes
Sporadic limp mode that clears after restart

c: Solenoid coil resistance out of specification
High resistance at connector pins or internal harness
Unstable supply voltage to the TCM or solenoid feed
Faulty current sensing in the TCM output stage
P08D1.d: Set when the control circuit of shift solenoid J is electrically intact but its measured values, usually solenoid current or driver feedback, lie outside the expected window for the commanded state. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The analogue for solenoid A, P0972, is likewise not used in the GM and Ford sources checked; Ford reports such current faults by its own electrical current check, which flags feedback current out of range for 0.5 seconds. CARB requires output circuits to be checked for faults beyond plain opens and shorts. P08D2 and P08D3 cover low and high circuit voltage, P08D4 an open circuit, P08CF a general electrical fault. Shift quality may suffer because the valve no longer moves as intended.
s: Check engine or transmission warning light on

P08D2.d: Set when the TCM sees too little voltage on the control line of shift solenoid J, typically because the line or the coil is shorted to ground. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; J would be a tenth on/off valve, which none of the known transmission sources assigns. GM's analogue for solenoid A, P0973 on the 6-speed units, fails when the output driver reports a ground short for 1.2 of 1.5 seconds and lights the MIL after one trip; Ford names the same fault on its solenoids a short to ground. CARB requires such circuit checks. P08D3 is the high-side fault, P08D4 the open circuit. The TCM usually switches the valve off and runs a substitute gear.

P08D3.d: Logged when the control line of shift solenoid J reads higher than the commanded state allows, pointing to a short to battery voltage or, on some designs, an open coil. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. In GM's tables the high code for solenoid A, P0974, covers both an open circuit and a short to power, fails after 1.2 of 1.5 seconds and needs two trips for the MIL, while Ford keeps opens apart and uses its high code for shorts to power only. Which reading applies to J therefore depends on the maker. CARB requires the circuit check. P08D2 is the low-side counterpart, P08D4 the dedicated open-circuit code. Transmission connector not fully seated after service
P08D4.d: Dedicated code for an open control circuit of shift solenoid J: the TCM drives the valve but no current flows through wire, connector or coil. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The known analogues show why: Ford files an open circuit under the base code of each solenoid (P0750 for solenoid A) and GM includes it in the high-voltage code P0974, so neither needs a separate open code. Ford detects such electrical faults when driver feedback disagrees with the command for 0.5 to 5 seconds. CARB requires open and short checks on transmission outputs. P08D2 and P08D3 are the short-circuit codes. An unpowered valve rests in its default state, so a gear may be missing or locked.

TCM output fault
P08D5.d: Base code for shift solenoid K, the eleventh on/off shift valve in SAE's lettering. Which valve carries the letter is up to the manufacturer, and none documents K publicly: Ford's gasoline OBD summary lists shift solenoids only up to SS E, Hyundai's bulletin 21-AT-016HG for the Genesis 8-speed ends at shift control solenoid F, and GM's 2016 to 2025 tables contain no code of the K group. Ford shows how a base code can be used: its P0750 stands for an open circuit of solenoid A. CARB requires functional and circuit monitoring of shift solenoids. P08D6 to P08DD split the fault into functional and circuit types. Expect harsh or missing shifts and possibly a fixed substitute gear.

Low fluid level or weak line pressure
Leaking seal or worn clutch pack in the circuit fed by the valve
P08D6.d: Indicates that shift solenoid K was commanded on but the gear or clutch behind it never engaged, as if the valve stayed in its off position. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A documented model is GM's P0751 for solenoid A on the 6-speed units: with first gear commanded, the TCM counts a fault when slip reaches 400 rpm and the measured ratio sits in a fixed window that points to the wrong gear, and it needs two trips to light the MIL. Ford infers a solenoid failed off from the obtained gear or shift pattern over three solenoid events. CARB requires this functional check. The reverse fault is P08D7. Typical signs are engine flare during shifts and a skipped gear.

P08D7.d: Stored when shift solenoid K is switched off but the circuit it feeds stays pressurised, so a clutch remains applied. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's P0752 for solenoid A is the documented analogue: with third gear commanded, the TCM fails the valve when gearbox slip reaches 400 rpm while the transmission actually sits in first or second, and the MIL lights after a single trip. Ford flags stuck-on solenoids from the gear actually reached during its mechanical check. CARB demands this functional monitoring. P08D6 is the opposite fault, P08D8 and P08DA to P08DD the circuit faults. Drivers may notice a wrong starting gear, binding, harsh engagement or emergency mode.

P08D8.d: Collective electrical fault for shift solenoid K, used by makers that do not split circuit faults into low, high, open or range codes. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The pattern exists for earlier letters: Hyundai stores P0753 (shift control solenoid valve A electrical) on the Genesis G80 and G90 8-speed and, per bulletin 21-AT-016HG, replaces the solenoid once the harness checks out, with valves listed only up to F. Ford's electrical check fails a solenoid when the driver feedback contradicts the command for 0.5 to 5 seconds. CARB requires circuit monitoring of transmission outputs. P08DA to P08DD are the detailed codes. The TCM usually reacts at once with altered shifting.

Transmission may lock into a limp-home gear

c: Loose or fretted terminal in the transmission connector
Chafed wire that touches only under vibration
Solenoid coil dropping out at high fluid temperature
P08D9.d: Meant for a shift solenoid K fault that appears and vanishes, such as a connector losing contact over bumps or a coil dropping out when hot. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and none of the sources checked even uses the intermittent code of solenoid A, P0754; GM and Ford catch brief interruptions with their open, short and functional codes instead. Ford runs its electrical checks continuously with 0.5 to 5 second filters. CARB asks for circuit monitoring of output components without prescribing an intermittent code. P08DA.d: Points to a control circuit of shift solenoid K that is neither open nor shorted, yet whose measured values, usually coil current, do not fit the commanded state. P08DE.d: Base code for shift solenoid L, which in SAE's lettering would be the twelfth on/off shift valve of an automatic transmission. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. It must not be confused with pressure control solenoid L, which Toyota uses on the 2024 Tacoma under its own code family. Ford's gasoline summary stops at shift solenoid E, Hyundai's Genesis 8-speed bulletin at F, and GM's 2016 to 2025 OBD tables show no L shift solenoid. For a maker using base codes, Ford's practice is the model: P0750 there means an open circuit. CARB requires shift solenoids to be monitored. The detailed fault types are P08DF to P08E6. P08DF.d: Functional fault of shift solenoid L: the TCM switches the valve on, but speed sensor data show that the intended clutch did not take up, so the valve acts as if stuck off. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The detection logic is known from the analogue for solenoid A: Ford compares the obtained gear or shift pattern over three solenoid events, and GM's P0751 counts repeated slip of at least 400 rpm in a ratio window that does not match first gear, with the MIL after two trips. P08E0.d: Functional fault of shift solenoid L in the opposite direction: although switched off, the valve keeps its circuit applied, leaving engaged a clutch that should be released. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. As a model, GM's P0752 for solenoid A sets after one trip when gearbox slip reaches 400 rpm with third gear commanded but first or second actually engaged, and Ford's mechanical check reads a stuck-on solenoid from the gear the transmission really obtains. CARB requires such functional checks. Electrical causes are rare here; a seized spool or an output stage that never switches off is more likely. P08DF is the stuck-off fault. P08E1.d: General electrical malfunction of shift solenoid L, intended for transmissions whose TCM does not distinguish or separately report low, high and open circuit faults. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The equivalent electrical code is in real use for lower letters, for example P2709 for shift control solenoid valve F on the 2017 and 2018 Genesis G80 and G90 8-speed, where Hyundai's bulletin 21-AT-016HG calls for harness checks and solenoid replacement. Ford fails a solenoid electrically when the driver feedback disagrees with the command for 0.5 to 5 seconds. CARB requires the circuit check. c: Loose terminal or poor pin tension in the connector
Insulation chafed at a bracket or edge
Coil that fails intermittently when hot
P08E2.d: Reserved for an unstable fault of shift solenoid L that is detected, disappears and may return, typically from a loose terminal, a chafed wire that only touches under vibration or a heat-sensitive coil. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The intermittent codes of the lower letters, beginning with P0754 for solenoid A, are absent from the GM and Ford documents checked as well; those systems record short dropouts as ordinary circuit or functional faults, Ford with continuous checks filtered over 0.5 to 5 seconds. CARB asks for circuit monitoring in general. For diagnosis, freeze frame data and a wiggle test help more than a static resistance check. Symptoms appear only now and then.

c: Coil resistance drifting with temperature
Corroded pins adding resistance
TCM output stage losing drive strength
P08E3.d: Plausibility fault in the control circuit of shift solenoid L: the circuit is not open or shorted, but voltage or current during actuation is implausible for the commanded state. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and the matching code for solenoid A, P0972, is likewise absent from the GM and Ford documents checked. Ford's electrical current check, which flags feedback current out of range for 0.5 seconds, shows how such a test works. Practical causes are coil resistance drifting with temperature, corroded pins adding resistance or a TCM output stage losing drive strength. P0917.d: Set when the gear shift position signal on circuit A of an automated manual gearbox stays above its highest valid value for longer than a calibrated time. The signal line may be shorted to the sensor supply or to battery voltage, the sensor ground may be open, or the sensor itself may be faulty. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The Aisin AI and Nissan/Aichi patents show the shift stroke or shift position sensor as the feedback that confirms an engaged gear; with a reading above the valid band the controller can no longer tell neutral from an engaged gear. CARB requires out-of-range checks on such inputs. P0916 is the opposite low fault, P091D and P095D are the high faults of circuits B and C, P0919 a shift movement that misses its target. Shifting is usually locked.
s: Check engine or transmission warning light on
Gearbox stays in one gear or in neutral
Warning message about the transmission on the dashboard
P0917.t: Gear Shift Position Circuit A High

c: Connector at the shift sensor or actuator unit losing contact under vibration
Chafed or partially broken sensor wire near the gearbox
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Shift position sensor with an internal contact or track fault
P0918.d: Flags a gear shift position signal on circuit A that drops out or jumps for short moments in an automated manual gearbox. The module sees implausible steps or brief losses that are too short or too irregular for a lasting low or high fault. Typical triggers are terminals that lose contact under vibration, a chafed harness moving with the powertrain, or moisture at the actuator connector. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Patents from Aisin AI and Nissan/Aichi show the shift stroke sensor as the feedback that confirms an engaged gear. CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs. P0914, P0916 and P0917 are the steady electrical faults of circuit A, P0915 the plausibility fault. Shifts may abort or the gearbox may briefly fall back to neutral.
s: Gear changes abort now and then or the gearbox drops to neutral
Fault often appears on rough roads or in wet weather
P0918.t: Gear Shift Position Circuit A Intermittent

c: Stiff or jammed shift rail, shift fork or synchroniser
Worn shift motor or leaking shift cylinder that no longer delivers full force
Low pressure in the hydraulic supply on hydraulically actuated units
Shift positions not relearned after actuator or module replacement
P0919.d: Set when the control module of an automated manual gearbox drives the shift actuator towards a gear, but the measured shift position does not reach the target within the allowed time and tolerance. Sensor and actuator circuits can be electrically intact; the fault concerns the closed loop as a whole. Usual reasons are a stiff or jammed shift rail or synchroniser, a weak actuator, low hydraulic pressure on hydraulic units, or a sensor offset. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A Hyundai/Kia patent detects jammed shift actuators from motor current, and an Isuzu patent controls the shift motor by stroke ranges using a shift stroke sensor. CARB requires functional checks on such outputs. P0909 is the same error in the select direction, P0920 to P0927 the actuator circuits. Gears may not engage.
s: Gear does not engage or engages only after a delay
Gearbox remains in neutral or locks in one gear

c: Loose or corroded connector at the shift position sensor
Damaged signal, supply or ground wire of sensor circuit B
Faulty shift position sensor B
Faulty sensor input in the transmission control module
P091A.d: Circuit B is a second channel reporting the shift position of an automated manual gearbox, for instance a redundant sensor track or a separate sensor on another shift rail. This general circuit code sets on an electrical fault on that signal that matches none of the more specific B variants. No manufacturer documents the code publicly, and which physical sensor carries the letter B depends on the design. Patents from Aisin AI and Nissan/Aichi describe shift stroke sensors as the feedback for gear engagement, an Aisin AI patent also covers the fallback when a stroke sensor fails. CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs. P091B to P091D are the B siblings, P0914 and P095A the same signal on circuits A and C. Shifting may be restricted.
s: Transmission or engine warning light on
Slower or restricted gear changes in fallback mode
Gearbox may hold a gear or stay in neutral

c: Worn or drifting shift position sensor, channels A and B disagree
Bent sensor bracket or displaced magnet on the shift rail
Gear positions not relearned after actuator or module replacement
Increased contact resistance in the sensor circuit
P091B.d: Plausibility fault of the shift position signal on circuit B in an automated manual gearbox. The voltage stays within its electrical limits, yet the value does not fit: it disagrees with circuit A, does not change while the shift actuator moves, or does not match the learned gear positions. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A Nissan/Aichi patent notes that sensor mountings on shift parts can deform under vibration and falsify the reading, and an Aisin AI patent describes how the control continues when a stroke sensor is no longer trusted. CARB requires rationality checks on such inputs. P091A, P091C and P091D are the electrical faults of circuit B, P0915 the same check on circuit A. Gear changes may be limited.
s: Fallback mode with fewer available gears
P091B.t: Gear Shift Position Circuit B Range/Performance

c: Signal wire of circuit B shorted to ground
Open or shorted sensor supply line
Faulty shift position sensor B
P091C.d: Set when the shift position signal on circuit B of an automated manual gearbox stays below its lowest valid value for longer than a calibrated time. Usually the signal line is shorted to ground, the sensor supply is missing, or the sensor has failed internally. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Patents from Aisin AI and Nissan/Aichi present the shift stroke or shift position sensor as the feedback that confirms an engaged gear; with a reading below the valid band that confirmation is lost on this channel. CARB requires out-of-range checks on such inputs. P091D is the opposite high fault, P0916 and P095C are the low faults of circuits A and C, P091B the plausibility fault of circuit B. The gearbox may run in fallback mode.
s: Transmission or engine warning light on
Restricted gear changes or a held gear
Engine start may be blocked if neutral cannot be confirmed
P091C.t: Gear Shift Position Circuit B Low

c: Signal wire of circuit B shorted to supply or battery voltage
Open sensor ground
Faulty shift position sensor B
P091D.d: Set when the shift position signal on circuit B of an automated manual gearbox stays above its highest valid value for longer than a calibrated time. The signal line may be shorted to sensor supply or battery voltage, the sensor ground may be open, or the sensor may be faulty. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Patents from Aisin AI and Nissan/Aichi present the shift stroke or shift position sensor as the feedback for gear engagement, so a reading above the valid band leaves the module unable to judge this channel. CARB requires out-of-range checks on such inputs. P091C is the opposite low fault, P0917 and P095D are the high faults of circuits A and C, P091B the plausibility fault of circuit B. Shifting is usually restricted.
s: Transmission or engine warning light on
Restricted gear changes or a held gear
Engine start may be blocked if neutral cannot be confirmed
P091D.t: Gear Shift Position Circuit B High

c: Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the shift actuator or valve
Broken drive wire between module and actuator
Open solenoid coil or motor winding in the actuator
Faulty driver stage in the transmission control module
P0920.d: Concerns the drive circuit that moves the shift mechanism of an automated manual gearbox in the forward shift direction. Depending on design this is one of two solenoid valves on a double-acting shift cylinder or one rotation direction of an electric shift motor. The code sets when the module finds this output open or electrically faulty, e.g. no current while the driver is on. No manufacturer documents the code publicly. A ZF patent feeds each chamber of a double-acting cylinder through its own 3/2 solenoid valve, an Isuzu patent turns the shift motor forward or reverse by shift direction. CARB requires circuit checks on outputs. P0921 to P0923 are the siblings, P0924 the reverse direction. Gears in this direction can no longer be engaged.
s: Some gears cannot be selected, the gearbox skips them or stays in neutral
Vehicle may only move off in a limited set of gears

c: Sticking shift valve, worn shift motor or stiff shift linkage
Solenoid or motor resistance out of specification
Increased contact resistance in connector or wiring
Insufficient hydraulic pressure on hydraulic units
P0921.d: Plausibility fault in the drive circuit of the forward shift actuator of an automated manual gearbox. The circuit is neither open nor shorted, but current, voltage or the resulting movement do not fit the command, for example a current that is too high for the requested stroke or a shift position that hardly changes. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A Hyundai/Kia patent explains that jamming raises the motor load of a shift actuator and must be caught early, and a ZF patent shows double-acting shift cylinders with one solenoid valve per chamber. CARB requires functional checks on such outputs. P0920, P0922 and P0923 are the clear electrical faults, P0925 the reverse direction, P0919 the missed target. Forward shifts become slow or fail.
s: Slow, harsh or aborted gear changes in one direction
Fallback mode with fewer available gears
P0921.t: Gear Shift Forward Actuator Circuit Range/Performance

c: Drive wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Internal short in solenoid coil or shift motor
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the connector
P0922.d: Set when the drive circuit of the forward shift actuator of an automated manual gearbox shows a voltage that is too low for the current switching state. This usually points to a short to ground on a valve or motor line, or to an internal short in the actuator. Many controllers then switch the output off to protect the driver stage. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A ZF patent drives each chamber of a double-acting shift cylinder through its own solenoid valve, and an Isuzu patent runs an electric shift motor in both directions, so a fault can affect one shift direction only. CARB requires circuit checks on outputs. P0923 is the opposite high fault, P0920 the open circuit, P0926 the reverse direction. Gears in this direction are blocked.
s: Certain gears can no longer be engaged
Gearbox may stay in neutral or hold one gear
P0922.t: Gear Shift Forward Actuator Circuit Low

c: Drive wire shorted to battery voltage
Driver stage in the control module stuck on
Open coil or winding read as high on some circuit designs
P0923.d: Set when the drive circuit of the forward shift actuator of an automated manual gearbox shows a voltage that is too high for the current switching state. Typical reasons are a valve or motor line shorted to battery voltage, or a driver stage in the module that no longer switches off; depending on circuit design an open load can also read high. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A ZF patent describes double-acting shift cylinders whose chambers each have a 3/2 solenoid valve, and an Isuzu patent drives a shift motor forward or reverse by shift direction. CARB requires circuit checks on outputs. P0922 is the opposite low fault, P0920 the open circuit, P0927 the reverse direction. An actuator that stays energised can hold or force a gear, so shifting is usually locked.
s: Gearbox locks in one gear or refuses to shift
Possible grinding when a gear is pushed unintentionally
P0923.t: Gear Shift Forward Actuator Circuit High

c: Loose, corroded or unplugged connector at the shift actuator or valve
Broken drive wire between module and actuator
Open solenoid coil or motor winding in the actuator
Faulty driver stage in the transmission control module
P0924.d: Concerns the drive circuit that moves the shift mechanism of an automated manual gearbox in the reverse shift direction, i.e. opposite to the forward actuator. It does not mean the reverse gear itself. Depending on design this is the second solenoid valve of a double-acting shift cylinder or the second rotation direction of an electric shift motor. The code sets when the module finds this output open or electrically faulty. No manufacturer documents the code publicly. A ZF patent assigns one 3/2 solenoid valve to each cylinder chamber, an Isuzu patent reverses the shift motor depending on shift direction. CARB requires circuit checks on outputs. P0925 to P0927 are the siblings, P0920 the forward direction. Gears in this direction cannot be engaged.
s: Some gears cannot be selected or the gearbox stays in neutral
Gear changes out of the current gear may fail

c: Sticking shift valve, worn shift motor or stiff shift linkage
Solenoid or motor resistance out of specification
Increased contact resistance in connector or wiring
Insufficient hydraulic pressure on hydraulic units
P0925.d: Plausibility fault in the drive circuit of the reverse shift actuator of an automated manual gearbox, the actuator that moves the shift mechanism opposite to the forward direction. The circuit is neither open nor shorted, but current, voltage or the resulting shift movement do not match the command. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A Hyundai/Kia patent detects jammed shift actuators from rising motor current, and a ZF patent shows double-acting shift cylinders with one solenoid valve per chamber, so each direction can be judged on its own. CARB requires functional checks on such outputs. P0924, P0926 and P0927 are the clear electrical faults, P0921 the forward direction, P0919 the missed target. Shifts in this direction become slow or fail.
s: Slow, harsh or aborted gear changes in one direction
Fallback mode with fewer available gears
P0925.t: Gear Shift Reverse Actuator Circuit Range/Performance

c: Drive wire chafed through and shorted to ground
Internal short in solenoid coil or shift motor
Water or corrosion bridging pins in the connector
P0926.d: Set when the drive circuit of the reverse shift actuator of an automated manual gearbox, the one moving the shift mechanism opposite to the forward direction, shows a voltage that is too low for the current switching state. This usually means a valve or motor line shorted to ground or an internal short in the actuator; the module often switches the output off to protect itself. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A ZF patent drives each chamber of a double-acting shift cylinder through its own solenoid valve, an Isuzu patent runs the shift motor in both directions. CARB requires circuit checks on outputs. P0927 is the opposite high fault, P0924 the open circuit, P0922 the forward direction. Gears in this direction are blocked.
s: Certain gears can no longer be engaged
Gearbox may stay in neutral or hold one gear
P0926.t: Gear Shift Reverse Actuator Circuit Low

c: Drive wire shorted to battery voltage
Driver stage in the control module stuck on
Open coil or winding read as high on some circuit designs
P0927.d: Set when the drive circuit of the reverse shift actuator of an automated manual gearbox shows a voltage that is too high for the current switching state. Common reasons are a valve or motor line shorted to battery voltage or a driver stage that no longer switches off; on some circuit designs an open load also reads high. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A ZF patent describes double-acting shift cylinders with a 3/2 solenoid valve on each chamber, and an Isuzu patent reverses an electric shift motor according to shift direction, so the reverse direction has its own output. CARB requires circuit checks on outputs. P0926 is the opposite low fault, P0924 the open circuit, P0923 the forward direction. A permanently energised actuator can force a gear, so shifting is usually locked.
s: Gearbox locks in one gear or refuses to shift
Possible grinding when a gear is pushed unintentionally
P0927.t: Gear Shift Reverse Actuator Circuit High

c: Internal fault in the electronic shifter module, often logged together with P0607 (documented by FCA)
Shift lock solenoid coil open
Broken wire, poorly crimped or pushed-out terminal on the shift lock circuit
P0928.d: The module that drives the shift lock (brake transmission shift interlock, BTSI) sees no continuity on control circuit A, so it cannot reliably release the selector from Park. FCA/Chrysler uses the code as P0928-00 BTSI Control: bulletin 08-072-14 (2013-14 Ram 1500, 2014 Durango with 8-speed) and 21-034-15 (2015 Chrysler 300 rotary shifter) name it when the selector will not leave Park or the knob turns without the brake applied; the cure there is a new electronic shifter. P0929 is the plausibility fault, P0930 and P0931 the low and high faults of circuit A, P092A the same open fault on circuit B. The driver usually cannot shift out of Park until the fault clears or the manual release is used.
s: Selector lever will not move out of Park even with the brake pressed
Problem may disappear after the ignition is switched off and the modules go to sleep
Rotary or electronic shifter can be moved without the brake applied
Shift position flashes or a message asks to return the selector to Park
P0928.t: Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit A/Open

c: Gear shift module software that misjudges the actuator position (Ford reprogramming bulletins)
Worn or binding lock actuator inside the shifter assembly
Poor pin fit or damaged pin at the shifter connector
P0929.d: Set when the shift lock actuator on circuit A is electrically present but does not respond as commanded, for example it fails to reach the locked or released position. Ford stores it in the gear shift module (GSM): SSM 51057 and 53039 list P0929:77 (commanded position not reachable) on Mach-E, Escape, Bronco Sport, Maverick and Transit, fixed by GSM software or replacement; TSB 25-2045 adds P0929:00, :07 and :9A on 2021-24 F-150 together with a selector that will not leave or enter Park, and checks pin 3 of connector C211. Ford shows the wrench lamp, not the MIL. P0928, P0930 and P0931 are the pure electrical faults of circuit A, P092B the same fault on circuit B.
s: Wrench or transmission warning lamp on
Selector will not leave Park or will not go back into Park
Clicking from the shifter or a selector that does not stow or unstow
P0929.t: Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit A Range/Performance

c: Broken wire or loose terminal on circuit B at the shifter
Open coil in the second lock solenoid
Shifter connector not fully seated after console work
P092A.d: Reports an open on control circuit B of the shift lock. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and none says which lock is B. One possible use is a second lock actuator: GHSP patents describe shifters where a further solenoid holds the lever in Neutral below a set speed unless the brake is pressed, beside the usual Park lock. CARB requires output circuits to be checked for continuity but may exempt safety-only systems. The FCA recall on the BTSI solenoid shows how such a lock fails in practice. P0928 is the same open fault on circuit A, P092B the plausibility fault, P092C and P092D the low and high faults of circuit B. Expect a lever that is locked in a position or no longer locked.
s: Selector lever locked in one position although the brake is pressed
Lock no longer engages, lever moves freely without brake
Warning message about the shifter or transmission
P092A.t: Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit B/Open

c: Lock pin or actuator binding inside the shifter assembly
Shifter module software misjudging the actuator response
Weak battery or poor supply leaving the solenoid too little force
P092B.d: Set when the actuator on shift lock circuit B is wired correctly but does not reach or report the commanded lock or release state. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The closest documented case is Ford P0929 on circuit A, where the gear shift module logs that the commanded position was not reached and the cure is new GSM software or a new module. CARB asks for a functional check of output components where feasible. GHSP patents show that a shifter can carry a second lock solenoid, for instance a Neutral lock. P092A, P092C and P092D are the open, low and high faults of circuit B, P0929 the matching fault on circuit A. The lever may stay locked, or the lock may engage late.
s: Lever releases late or only after several tries
Lever stays locked in one position
Transmission or wrench warning lamp on
P092B.t: Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit B Range/Performance

c: Circuit B wire chafed to ground near the shifter
Shorted turns in the second lock solenoid
Liquid spilled into the shifter causing leakage to ground
P092C.d: The voltage on shift lock control circuit B is lower than expected, usually because the wire or the solenoid has a path to ground. No manufacturer documents this code publicly or names the lock behind circuit B. GHSP patents describe shifters with a second solenoid next to the Park lock, for example one that holds the lever in Neutral unless speed is low and the brake is applied. CARB requires output circuits to be checked for shorts but allows safety-only systems to be left out. P092D is the high fault, P092A the open and P092B the plausibility fault of circuit B; P0930 is the low fault on circuit A. A shorted lock circuit can leave the lever locked or let it move without the brake.
s: Lever locked in a position despite brake applied
Lock does not engage, lever moves without brake
P092C.t: Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit B Low

c: Circuit B wire shorted to a supply voltage
Poor crimp or loose terminal at the second lock solenoid
Open coil in the second lock solenoid
P092D.d: The module sees a higher voltage on shift lock circuit B than the commanded state allows, such as a short to supply or, with a low-side driver, an open coil. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The documented counterpart on circuit A is FCA P0931 in recall 16V-249, where a badly crimped BTSI solenoid terminal on 2016 Grand Cherokees set the high fault and kept the lever in Park. GHSP patents show that a shifter may carry a second lock solenoid, so circuit B can be a separate lock. CARB requires circuit fault checks on outputs, with an exemption path for safety-only systems. P092C is the low, P092A the open fault of circuit B; P0931 is the same fault on circuit A.
s: Lever will not release from its locked position
Warning message about the shifter or transmission
P092D.t: Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit B High

c: Shift lock control wire chafed through to ground in the console or under the carpet
Shorted turns in the shift lock solenoid coil
Spilled liquid in the shifter area causing leakage to ground
P0930.d: The voltage on control circuit A of the shift lock solenoid stays below the expected level, typically a short to ground or a driver output pulled low. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. FCA uses the sibling codes on the same brake transmission shift interlock (P0928 BTSI Control, P0931 on the 2016 Grand Cherokee). CARB requires output components to be checked for circuit continuity and shorts, while a safety-only system may be exempt, which is why these faults often do not light the MIL. P0928 is the open, P0931 the high fault, P0929 the plausibility fault of circuit A; P092C is the low fault on circuit B. Depending on the design the selector stays locked in Park or is no longer locked at all.
s: Selector lever stuck in Park although the brake is pressed
Selector can be moved out of Park without pressing the brake
Shift lock override slot needed to move the lever
P0930.t: Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit A Low

c: Poorly crimped or loose terminal on the shift lock solenoid harness (FCA recall 16V-249)
Control wire shorted to a supply voltage
Open shift lock solenoid coil seen as high voltage by a low-side driver
P0931.d: The control module reads a voltage on shift lock circuit A that is higher than the commanded state allows. FCA documents the code directly: in recall 16V-249 the Jefferson North plant found 2016 Jeep Grand Cherokee (WK) vehicles with active or stored P0931-00 whose selector would not release from Park. The cause was a badly crimped terminal on the BTSI solenoid harness from shifter supplier GHSP; FCA replaced the gear selector and warned that losing the solenoid could leave the lever locked in Park or Neutral. So a poor connection, not only a short to battery, can show up as High. P0930 is the low, P0928 the open fault of circuit A; P092D is the high fault on circuit B.
s: Selector lever will not release from Park
Lever may lock in Park or Neutral unexpectedly after stopping
Fault comes and goes with vibration or temperature
P0931.t: Gear Shift Lock Solenoid/Actuator Control Circuit A High

c: Fault in the solenoid pack or valve body module that carries the pressure sensor (open solenoid, internal lead frame)
Poor crimp or solder joint at the sensor connector terminals
5 V reference or sensor ground interrupted
Transmission or powertrain control module fault
P0932.d: General electrical fault in the circuit of the sensor that reports hydraulic pressure in the gearbox, usually line pressure in an automatic or system pressure in an automated manual or dual-clutch unit. The module sees a signal it cannot use at all, without a clear low or high pattern. Chrysler names it Line Pressure Sensor Circuit Fault; an ALLDATA case on a 2003 Grand Cherokee 4.7 automatic shows it together with P0935, caused by an open line pressure solenoid in the solenoid pack. CARB requires circuit checks on such transmission inputs. P0934 and P0935 are the low and high faults, P0933 the plausibility fault, P0936 the intermittent one. Expect harsh shifts, often with line pressure forced to maximum.
s: Warning light or transmission warning on
Harsh engagements and firm shifts from maximum line pressure
Possible limp mode with limited gears

c: Open circuit or fault in the line pressure control solenoid causing real excess pressure
Pressure sensor drifting or reading offset
Worn or sticking valves in the valve body
Wrong fluid level or degraded fluid
P0933.d: The pressure reading is electrically valid but does not fit the operating state. Chrysler RFE, RLE and TES transmissions set it when measured line pressure is more than 25 psi (172 kPa) above the commanded value while staying below the highest pressure ever used in that gear; Sonnax notes that a maximum-pressure condition from an open pressure control solenoid circuit can trigger it and mislead toward the sensor. Ferrari lists P0933 on its DCT as an invalid hydraulic pressure sensor signal, read in the NCR gearbox ECU. Neighbours: P0932, P0934 and P0935 are circuit faults, P0936 intermittent, P0869 a true high line pressure. The driver notices firm or harsh shifts.
s: Harsh or firm engagements and shifts
Shift quality does not adapt and may stay rough

c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
5 V reference open or shorted
Pressure sensor or the solenoid pack carrying it failed
Control module fault
P0934.d: The pressure sensor signal sits below its valid window. Chrysler RFE transmissions feed the line pressure sensor with a 5 V reference and expect 0.35 to 4.75 V; P0934 sets when the signal stays at or below 0.35 V for 0.18 s, monitored continuously with the engine running. Typical reasons are a signal wire shorted to ground, a lost 5 V reference or a failed sensor. Ferrari also uses P0934 on its DCT, described as hydraulic pressure sensor signal too low. P0935 is the opposite high fault, P0932 the general circuit fault, P0933 plausibility and P0936 intermittent. Without a usable pressure signal the control usually raises pressure to a safe maximum, so shifts turn harsh.
s: Harsh shifts due to default maximum pressure

c: Sensor ground open or poor terminal contact
Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Pressure sensor or solenoid pack failed internally
Control module fault
P0935.d: The pressure sensor signal sits above its valid window. On Chrysler RFE transmissions the line pressure sensor normally reads between 0.35 and 4.75 V; P0935 sets when the signal stays at or above 4.75 V for 0.18 s with the engine running. That pattern points to a signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage, an open sensor ground or a sensor failed internally. An ALLDATA case on a 2003 Grand Cherokee logged it with P0932. Ferrari lists P0935 on its DCT as hydraulic pressure sensor signal too high. P0934 is the low counterpart, P0932 the general circuit fault, P0933 plausibility, P0936 intermittent. Expect harsh shifts and possibly a limp mode.

c: Poor crimp or solder joint at the sensor connector
Chafed harness making intermittent contact
Moisture or corrosion in the connector
Sensor with an internal intermittent fault
P0936.d: The hydraulic pressure signal drops out or jumps for short periods, too briefly or irregularly for a lasting low or high fault. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The underlying sensor is the same one Chrysler uses for line pressure on RFE units and Ferrari for system pressure on its DCT, where the steady faults appear as P0934 and P0935. Gears Magazine names poor solder joints and crimps at the sensor terminals as a frequent source of intermittent pressure sensor codes. CARB requires circuit checks on such transmission inputs. P0932 to P0935 cover the general, plausibility, low and high faults. The driver may see a warning that comes and goes and occasional harsh shifts.

c: Connector at the temperature sensor loose, corroded or oil-soaked
Damaged sensor wiring near the gearbox or cooler lines
Temperature sensor failed
P0937.d: General electrical fault in the circuit of the temperature sensor for the hydraulic fluid of an automated gearbox, without a clear low or high pattern. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Ferrari shows where such a sensor sits: its DCT carries a radiator outlet and gearbox inlet oil temperature sensor reported under P0938 to P0940 in the NCR gearbox ECU. The control needs this value to correct pressure and clutch fill for viscosity. CARB requires circuit checks on transmission sensors. P0938 is the plausibility fault, P0939 and P0940 low and high, P0941 intermittent; P0711 to P0713 cover the main transmission fluid temperature sensor. Shift quality may suffer and a warning appears.
s: Rougher shifts or clutch engagement, especially when cold

c: Temperature sensor drifting or reacting sluggishly
Signal lost through connector or wiring fault (as in Ferrari's no-signal case)
Real temperature anomaly from a cooler or thermostat fault
P0938.d: By J2012 wording the hydraulic oil temperature reading is electrically valid but implausible, for example frozen, rising too slowly after a cold start or disagreeing with other temperature values. Ferrari uses P0938 on its DCT for the radiator outlet and gearbox inlet oil temperature sensor, but describes it in its bulletin as no signal, an electrical fault rather than a plausibility check; the code is read in the NCR gearbox ECU. CARB asks for rationality checks on temperature inputs. P0937 is the general circuit fault, P0939 and P0940 the low and high faults, P0941 intermittent. A wrong temperature value leads to poorly matched clutch and shift pressures and may limit the cooling strategy.
s: Shift and clutch quality inconsistent with operating temperature

c: Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Temperature sensor shorted internally
Control module input fault
P0939.d: The hydraulic oil temperature sensor signal sits below its valid window. With the usual NTC thermistor, a low voltage corresponds to an implausibly hot reading and typically comes from a signal wire shorted to ground or a sensor shorted internally. Ferrari uses P0939 on its DCT for the radiator outlet and gearbox inlet oil temperature sensor, described as signal too low and read in the NCR gearbox ECU. CARB requires out-of-range checks on transmission sensors. P0940 is the high counterpart, P0937 the general circuit fault, P0938 plausibility and P0941 intermittent. Because the module believes the oil is very hot, it may reduce torque, change shift strategy or show an overheat warning.
s: Reduced performance or altered shift behaviour
P0939.t: Hydraulic Oil Temperature Sensor Circuit Low

c: Accumulator solenoid coil open
Connector unplugged or wire broken between module and solenoid
Fault in the internal transmission harness or lead frame
Output driver in the control module failed
P093A.d: The control circuit of the solenoid that opens or locks a hydraulic accumulator in the gearbox is open. Such accumulators store pressurised fluid, for example to keep clutches applied during engine stop-start, as GM's patents on a stop-start accumulator and an accumulator with solenoid valve describe. No manufacturer documents P093A publicly. GM uses its own P171A for the same fault on the surge accumulator solenoid: failed if circuit impedance exceeds 200 kOhm in 32 of 40 samples, Type B with MIL after two trips. P093B and P093C are the low and high faults, P093D the performance fault. Stop-start is usually disabled, and the first restart may engage with a jolt.
s: Jolt or slip when driving off after an engine restart

c: Solenoid control wire shorted to ground
Solenoid coil shorted internally
Output driver in the control module failed
P093B.d: The control circuit of the hydraulic accumulator solenoid reads low, usually a control wire shorted to ground or a coil with very low resistance. No manufacturer documents P093B publicly. GM covers the same fault on its surge accumulator solenoid with P171B: failed short to ground when circuit impedance drops below 0.5 Ohm in 32 of 40 samples, Type B with MIL after two trips. The accumulator holds pressurised fluid so clutches stay applied during an engine auto-stop, as GM's stop-start accumulator patent explains. P093A is the open-circuit fault, P093C the high fault and P093D the performance fault. A grounded control line can leave the valve permanently energised, and stop-start is typically switched off.

c: Solenoid control wire shorted to battery voltage
Damaged internal transmission harness or lead frame
Output driver in the control module failed
P093C.d: The control circuit of the hydraulic accumulator solenoid reads high, typically a control wire shorted to battery voltage so the driver cannot switch the valve as commanded. No manufacturer documents P093C publicly. GM covers the same fault on its surge accumulator solenoid with P171C: failed short to voltage when the circuit impedance criterion of 0.5 Ohm is met in 6 of 8 samples, Type B with MIL after two trips. GM's patent on an accumulator with solenoid valve shows how the valve holds or releases the stored fluid. P093A is the open circuit, P093B the low fault and P093D the performance fault. Stop-start is usually disabled; a valve that never closes cannot keep the accumulator charged during an auto-stop.
s: Jolt when pulling away after a restart

c: Accumulator solenoid stuck open (drains) or closed (no fill)
Accumulator piston or bore leaking
Leakage at clutch seals or a worn valve body
Missing or misplaced check ball after a rebuild
P093D.d: The accumulator solenoid circuit is electrically sound, but the accumulator system does not deliver the expected hydraulic result. No manufacturer documents P093D publicly. GM's comparable P171D on the 9-speed transmission watches turbine speed during an engine auto-start: if it exceeds a predicted value because holding clutches slip from too little stored pressure, it counts a failure, enabled between 0 and 110 °C transmission fluid temperature, Type B. Gears Magazine names a solenoid stuck open or closed, a leaking accumulator piston, clutch or valve body leakage and misplaced check balls as causes. P093A to P093C are the electrical faults. Stop-start is disabled and the restart may feel like a bang.
s: Lurch or bang when the engine restarts
Firm shifts with adaptive learning frozen

c: Open signal or ground wire, or connector unplugged
Temperature sensor open internally
Signal wire shorted to a voltage source
P0940.d: The hydraulic oil temperature sensor signal sits above its valid window. With an NTC thermistor this matches an extremely cold reading, typically from an open circuit, an unplugged connector, a broken ground or a short to a voltage source. Ferrari uses P0940 on its DCT for the radiator outlet and gearbox inlet oil temperature sensor, described as an electrical fault with signal too high, read in the NCR gearbox ECU. CARB requires out-of-range checks on transmission sensors. P0939 is the low counterpart, P0937 the general circuit fault, P0938 plausibility and P0941 intermittent. With a substitute value the gearbox works on, but clutch and shift pressures are no longer matched to the real oil temperature.
s: Shifts or clutch engagements feel rough once warm
P0940.t: Hydraulic Oil Temperature Sensor Circuit High

c: Loose contact at the sensor connector under vibration or heat
Chafed wiring near hot gearbox or cooler parts
Sensor with an intermittent internal fault
P0941.d: The hydraulic oil temperature signal jumps or drops out briefly, too short or irregular for a lasting low or high fault. Since fluid temperature changes slowly, a sudden step is a clear sign of an electrical problem rather than a real temperature change. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Ferrari's DCT bulletin shows the related sensor at the radiator outlet and gearbox inlet, with its steady faults under P0938 to P0940. CARB requires circuit checks on transmission sensors. P0937 is the general circuit fault, P0938 plausibility, P0939 and P0940 low and high. For the driver this means a warning that may come and go and shift quality that changes from one moment to the next.
P0941.t: Hydraulic Oil Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent

c: Fluid loss at the reservoir cap or hydraulic power unit seals
Worn pump motor or faulty pump relay
Damaged wiring, connectors or power supply of the pump
Transmission control module fault
P0942.d: General fault of the unit that generates and stores hydraulic pressure for an automated gearbox or its auxiliary oil supply: motor-driven pump, accumulator and pressure control. Toyota sets P0942 on the 2001 to 2005 MR2 Spyder sequential gearbox together with the SMT warning light and a buzzing pump, or with gears that can no longer be changed; fluid seeping from the reservoir cap or the seal of the hydraulic power unit is a known cause, fixed with new seal rings. Ferrari reads P0942 on its DCT differently, as system pressure command signal too low. CARB requires functional checks of transmission outputs. P0943 and P0944 are the cycling and pressure-loss faults, P0945 to P0948 the pump control circuit.
s: Transmission or gearbox warning light on
Pump buzzing or running for long periods
Gears cannot be changed or shifts are delayed
Auto stop-start disabled or engine restarts immediately

c: Accumulator has lost its gas precharge
Internal leakage at valves, seals or actuator cylinders
Faulty pressure switch or pressure sensor giving wrong cut-in point
Low or aerated hydraulic fluid
P0943.d: In a hydraulic pressure unit the pump charges an accumulator up to a cut-out pressure and switches off until pressure falls to the cut-in point. By J2012 wording this code means the pump switches on again too soon, so the interval between charging cycles is shorter than expected. Typical reasons are internal leakage across valves or seals, or an accumulator that has lost its gas precharge and stores too little oil. Audi patents describe such accumulator and leakage checks based on charging switch-over times and pressure decay. No manufacturer documents this exact meaning publicly; Ferrari uses P0943 on its DCT for a system pressure command signal that is too high. CARB requires functional checks of transmission outputs. P0942 is the general fault, P0944 the loss of pressure.
s: Pump can be heard switching on unusually often
P0943.t: Hydraulic Pressure Unit Cycling Period Too Short

c: Pump loses prime (air drawn in through filter, seal or strainer pipe)
Blocked oil strainer or suction tube
Worn or failed pump (mechanical or electric)
Leaking check valve or internal leak in the valve body
P0944.d: The pump runs but the expected hydraulic pressure does not build or collapses. Stellantis names it Loss of Hydraulic Pump Prime: a 2023 STAR case lists it with P0868 and a slow engagement after the vehicle has stood, both set as the only transmission codes with the MIL on, and the fix was a new transmission; an FCA defect file from 2015 also shows it beside line pressure low. Mercedes uses P0944 on the 722.9 automatic with electric auxiliary oil pump for stop-start, as internal fault of that pump; stop-start stops working, and a leaking check valve between converter housing and pump is one cause. Ferrari reads it on its DCT as no system pressure signal with pressure loss. P0943 covers short cycles, P0868 low fluid pressure.
s: Check engine or transmission warning light on
Slow engagement after the vehicle has been parked
Auto stop-start not available or engine restarts at once
Slipping, no drive or limp mode
P0944.t: Hydraulic Pressure Unit Loss of Pressure

c: Pump relay coil open or relay not seated
Open control wire or loose terminal between module and relay
Failed output stage in the control module
P0945.d: The control module drives the motor of the hydraulic pump through a relay or a direct output. This code reports a general circuit fault or an open in that control path, so the pump cannot be switched reliably. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. The layout is shown by a ZF patent for an automated gearbox, in which a motor-driven pump draws oil from a reservoir and charges a pressure accumulator behind a one-way valve, with shut-off valves feeding the shift cylinders. CARB requires circuit checks on transmission outputs. P0946 is the plausibility fault, P0947 and P0948 low and high; P094E covers the pump supply instead of the control side. Without the pump the gearbox soon runs out of pressure.
s: Pump does not run, pressure is not built
Gears cannot be changed or auto stop-start disabled

c: Relay contacts welded or sticking
Pump supply or control wire shorted to battery voltage
Faulty pump state feedback or control module
P0946.d: The pump control circuit is electrically intact, but its behaviour does not match the command, for example a pump that keeps running after being switched off, or one that switches but is not followed by the expected feedback. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. In the hydraulic unit of an automated gearbox, as shown in a ZF patent, the pump only has to run until the accumulator is charged; a relay that sticks or switches late upsets that cycle. CARB requires functional checks on transmission outputs. P0945 is the general circuit or open fault, P0947 and P0948 the low and high faults, P094B a pump stuck on regardless of the relay. A pump that never stops drains the battery and wears quickly.

c: Relay control wire chafed and shorted to ground
Shorted relay coil
Damaged output stage in the control module
P0947.d: The voltage on the control line of the hydraulic pump relay or driver is lower than the module expects for the commanded state. Usually the line is shorted to ground or the relay coil is shorted, so the output may be overloaded and the pump runs when it should not, or the driver shuts down. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. The hydraulic unit it belongs to, a motor-driven pump that charges an accumulator for the shift and clutch cylinders of an automated gearbox, is described in a ZF patent. CARB requires circuit checks on transmission outputs. P0948 is the high counterpart, P0945 the open fault, P0946 plausibility. Pressure supply for shifting may fail.
s: Pump runs continuously or not at all
Gearbox in limp mode or stop-start disabled

c: Relay control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open relay coil seen as high level by the driver
Control module fault
P0948.d: The control line of the hydraulic pump relay or driver shows a higher voltage than expected, typically because it is shorted to battery voltage or the relay coil is open on a low-side driver. The pump then cannot be switched on, or the module sees it as active when it is not. J2012 places this code with the pump control circuit; Ferrari however reads P0948 on its DCT as no signal from the system pressure output, an unrelated use. The pump and accumulator unit of an automated gearbox is described in a ZF patent. CARB requires circuit checks on transmission outputs. P0947 is the low counterpart, P0945 the open fault and P0946 the plausibility fault. Expect a warning and possible loss of pump pressure.
s: Gear changes not possible or stop-start disabled

c: Relearn not run after clutch, actuator or control unit replacement
Adaptation values erased by software update or battery disconnection
Learning aborted by low voltage or worn clutch outside the learn window
P0949.d: Status code for an automatically shifted manual gearbox: the control unit has not yet finished learning its adaptation values, above all the clutch touch point and the end positions of the shift actuators. Such learning runs after a new control unit, clutch or actuator, after a software update and sometimes after the battery was disconnected; Hyundai and Kia patents show how the touch point is found and corrected from shaft speed changes. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. The code is a reminder rather than a hardware fault; launch and shifts may be jerky until learning is done. P0950 to P0954 cover the manual control circuit, P0806 to P0808 the clutch position sensor. MIL use depends on the maker.
s: Gearbox warning or message to perform teach-in
Restricted gear selection until learning completes
P0949.t: Auto Shift Manual Adaptive Learning Not Complete

c: Internal fault of the pump controller or driver stage
Pump motor drawing excess current (worn bearings, fluid in motor)
High resistance in supply or ground of the driver
P094A.d: Concerns the electronic driver that powers the motor of a hydraulic or electric oil pump, often a separate pump controller. The driver reports, or the module infers, that it cannot deliver the commanded speed or current although the circuit is not open or shorted. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Hyundai shows what such a driver monitors on its wet 8-speed DCT pumps: overcurrent, current and Hall sensor faults and internal faults, filed under its own P193D and P1C2E codes. Mercedes reports an internal fault of the 722.9 auxiliary oil pump under P0944 instead. CARB requires functional checks on outputs. P094B and P094C are stuck pump faults, P094D overheating, P094E supply; P0C29 is the equivalent for auxiliary fluid pumps of automatics.

c: Pump relay contacts welded closed
Leakage or lost accumulator charge keeps pressure below cut-out
Shorted driver stage or supply wire shorted to battery voltage
P094B.d: The hydraulic pump keeps running although the module has switched it off, or it never reaches its cut-out point. Causes are a welded relay or shorted driver, or a pump that cannot reach cut-out pressure because of leakage. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. In the pump and accumulator unit of an automated gearbox, described in a ZF patent, the pump should rest once the accumulator is charged. Toyota links a constantly buzzing pump on the MR2 sequential gearbox to fluid loss at the hydraulic power unit, reported under P0942. CARB requires functional checks on outputs. P094C is the opposite fault, P0946 the relay plausibility fault, P0943 the too-short cycle. Battery drain and pump wear follow.
s: Pump audible after the vehicle is switched off

c: Air in the pump after service or a suction leak
Seized or failed pump motor
Blocked strainer or leaking check valve
Supply or relay fault stopping the pump
P094C.d: The pump is commanded on but does not deliver: it does not turn, turns too slowly or produces too little pressure. The module judges this from pressure or speed feedback. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Mercedes reports a comparable condition of the electric auxiliary oil pump on the 722.9 automatic under P0944; its test plan checks connector and fuse, supply voltage, CAN lines and software, then a check valve in the converter housing, before the pump is replaced. Hyundai lists a stuck high-flow pump on its 8-speed DCT as P193E71. CARB requires functional checks on outputs. P094B is the opposite fault, P094A the driver, P0944 the pressure loss of the whole unit.
s: Engine restarts at once or stop-start not available

c: Pump running too long because of leakage or a stuck relay
Defective pump controller board
Very hot transmission fluid or blocked cooling
P094D.d: The hydraulic or electric oil pump, or its integrated controller, has become too hot. The temperature is usually measured on the controller board and the pump is derated or switched off to protect it. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Hyundai lists the same condition for the high-flow pump of its wet 8-speed DCT as P193D4B, over temperature, and P1C2E92 for the high-pressure pump motor control. Kia recalled stop-start oil pump controllers in 2023 because a damaged capacitor could short and overheat the board, harness and connector. CARB requires functional checks on outputs. P094A is the driver fault, P094B a pump that never stops, a common reason for heat build-up.
s: Burning smell near the pump in severe cases

c: Blown pump fuse
Open or corroded supply wire or connector
Weak battery or poor main ground lowering pump supply voltage
P094E.d: Fault in the power feed of the hydraulic or electric oil pump: fuse, supply wire, connector or relay output. The module sees missing or implausible supply at the pump or its controller. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. Mercedes shows the checks that belong to it on the electric auxiliary oil pump of the 722.9 automatic, although it reports that pump under P0944: connector and fuse first, then supply voltage and CAN lines. Hyundai lists an open circuit of its DCT high-flow pump as P193D13. CARB requires circuit checks on outputs. P0945 to P0948 concern the control side, P094A the driver, P0562 general low system voltage. Without supply the pump stops and stop-start is usually blocked.
s: Stop-start disabled or gearbox in limp mode

c: Failed up/down switch or sensor in the selector lever or paddles
Damaged wiring or corroded connector at the shifter (e.g. after spilled liquid)
Clockspring or steering column wiring fault on paddle-shift vehicles
P0950.d: General electrical fault in the circuit that carries the driver's manual up and down requests to the transmission control, as used by tip-shift gates on automatics and by automated manual gearboxes. A Chrysler patent shows the classic design: a transverse gate beside the drive positions with a proximity switch that signals upshift on one side and downshift on the other. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly. The module typically checks the switch signals for states that cannot occur. P0951 to P0954 are the range, low, high and intermittent faults, P0955 onward the mode select circuit. Usually manual shifting is disabled while normal automatic driving remains available; MIL use varies.
s: Manual or tip shifting does not respond

c: Sticking or worn up/down tip switch, request signal stays active
Displaced magnet or damaged Hall sensor board in the selector lever
Spilled liquid or dirt in the shifter causing cross-talk between contacts
Faulty input stage in the transmission or shifter control module
P0951.d: Plausibility fault in the circuit that reports the driver's manual upshift and downshift requests, typically the tip gate of an automatic selector lever or steering wheel paddles. The signal is electrically valid but makes no sense, for example both requests active together or a request held far longer than any tap. A Volkswagen patent explains that the Hall elements in such tip gates are hard to diagnose and proposes checking all sensors and lines while the lever sits in P or R. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; CARB requires rationality checks on such inputs. P0950 is the general circuit fault, P0952 to P0954 the low, high and intermittent faults. Usually only manual shifting is disabled.
s: Tip shifting or paddles do not respond or respond erratically
Unwanted gear changes in manual mode
Warning message, automatic mode keeps working
P0951.t: Auto Shift Manual Control Circuit Range/Performance

c: Signal wire of the up/down circuit chafed through and shorted to ground
Tip switch stuck in the closed position
Moisture or spilled drink in the shifter creating a leakage path to ground
Low supply voltage to a Hall-type tip sensor
P0952.d: The control unit sees the voltage on the manual up/down request circuit below its expected window, typically a signal wire shorted to ground or a switch stuck in the grounded state. In many tip gates the moving contact switches to ground, as a Nissan patent shows, so a short to ground can mimic a permanently held request; a Volkswagen patent describes checking the Hall tip sensors for shorts and breaks while the lever is in P or R. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs. P0953 is the high counterpart, P0950 the general and P0951 the plausibility fault. In practice manual shifting is locked out while D keeps shifting automatically.
s: Gear indicator shows no manual gear or a warning message
Normal automatic driving in D still possible
P0952.t: Auto Shift Manual Control Circuit Low

c: Signal wire shorted to a voltage-carrying wire in the shifter harness
Broken wire or unplugged connector on a pulled-up input
Missing ground of the tip switch or Hall sensor
Faulty input stage in the transmission control module
P0953.d: Voltage on the manual up/down request circuit lies above its expected window. Common reasons are a signal wire shorted to battery voltage or, where the input is pulled up internally, a broken wire or a switch that never closes. A Volkswagen patent names a short to plus and a line break as faults its tip-gate diagnosis detects with the lever in P or R; a Chrysler patent shows the classic AutoStick-style gate with one switch for up and one for down. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs. P0952 covers the low side, P0954 dropouts, P0950 the general fault. Manual shifting is usually disabled, automatic mode remains.
s: Tip gate or paddles have no effect
Warning or message about manual mode
P0953.t: Auto Shift Manual Control Circuit High

c: Loose or spread pins in the selector lever connector
Harness broken internally where it moves with the lever or steering column
Worn or oxidised tip switch contacts
P0954.d: The manual up/down request signal drops out or flickers for short moments, so a single tap may arrive twice, late or not at all. Unlike P0952 and P0953 the voltage is not stuck outside its window; it jumps between states without a matching lever movement. Typical triggers are loose pins in the shifter connector, worn contacts or a harness that flexes with the lever. A Chrysler patent shows how simple contact switches in the gate signal each request, a Volkswagen patent how Hall tip sensors and their lines are checked. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; CARB requires circuit checks. P0950 is the general fault. The driver notices missed or doubled manual shifts.
s: Manual shifts occasionally ignored or executed twice
Fault comes and goes, often over bumps
P0954.t: Auto Shift Manual Control Circuit Intermittent

c: Failed manual mode switch or microswitch in the selector lever
Corroded or loose connector at the selector lever assembly
Damaged wiring between selector lever and transmission control module
P0955.d: Fault in the circuit that tells the transmission control whether the driver has moved the selector lever from D into the manual gate. A Nissan patent shows a dedicated manual mode switch with two contacts on separate inputs, so a break or a short to ground can be told apart; a Hyundai patent uses a microswitch on the lever. Genesis bulletins for 2017-18 G80 and G90 automatics list Auto Shift Manual Mode Circuit for the cable-shift version, with a check engine light and a part from the shift lever group as repair, though the table prints the code as P0995 and P095500. So at least Hyundai uses ASM for the manual mode of a torque converter automatic. P0956 to P0959 are the detailed variants, P0950 the up/down request circuit.
s: Manual mode cannot be selected or is not displayed
Check engine or transmission warning light on

c: Mode switch or its actuating foot misaligned on the lever
Worn switch contacts giving contradictory states on both inputs
Transmission range sensor out of adjustment, disagrees with the mode signal
Worn selector lever bushings allowing side play
P0956.d: The manual mode signal is electrically valid but contradicts other information, for example manual mode reported while the range sensor reads P, R or N, or the mode switch never changing although the up/down requests arrive. A Hyundai patent uses a microswitch with two opposing contacts and treats identical or missing signals on both inputs as a defect; a Nissan patent likewise compares two contacts of the manual mode switch. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly, and Hyundai's mode circuit fault is only documented as the general code P0955. CARB requires rationality checks on such inputs. P0957 to P0959 cover low, high and intermittent faults. Manual mode is usually blocked.
s: Manual mode drops out or will not engage
Display shows manual mode while lever is in D, or the reverse
P0956.t: Auto Shift Manual Mode Circuit Range/Performance

c: Mode signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
Mode switch stuck in the grounded position
Liquid or dirt in the selector lever housing
P0957.d: Voltage in the manual mode circuit, the signal that reports the selector lever in the manual gate, is below the expected range. Mostly the signal line has a short to ground or the switch contact hangs in its grounded position. A Nissan patent describes a manual mode switch whose moving contact is grounded and explains how the control unit spots a contact shorted to earth from its two inputs. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; Hyundai's mode circuit fault appears in Genesis bulletins only as the general code. CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs. P0958 is the high counterpart, P0955 the general and P0956 the plausibility fault. Expect manual mode to be unavailable or stuck on.
s: Manual mode not available or permanently indicated
P0957.t: Auto Shift Manual Mode Circuit Low

c: Broken mode signal wire or disconnected shifter plug
Missing ground at the mode switch
Mode signal shorted to a voltage-carrying wire
P0958.d: The manual mode signal from the selector lever reads above its expected range. Possible causes are a short to supply voltage or, with an internally pulled-up input, an open circuit or missing switch ground that keeps the line high. A Nissan patent explains how two separately wired contacts let the control unit recognise a break in the manual mode switch, and a Hyundai patent shows the lever microswitch that reports the change from D to M. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; Hyundai's mode fault is only documented as P0955. CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs. P0957 is the low side, P0959 the intermittent variant. Usually the gearbox stays in automatic mode.
s: Manual gate has no effect, gearbox stays in automatic mode
No manual gear shown on the display
P0958.t: Auto Shift Manual Mode Circuit High

c: Loose pins in the selector lever connector
Worn or bouncing mode microswitch
Harness damaged where it moves with the lever
P0959.d: The signal reporting the selector lever in the manual gate drops out or toggles briefly while the lever is not moved, so the transmission control switches between manual and automatic mode on its own. The voltage is not stuck out of range as with P0957 or P0958 but jumps. Loose connector pins at the lever, a harness that flexes with the shifter or a worn microswitch are typical. A Hyundai patent shows such a microswitch actuated by the lever's sideways movement, a Nissan patent the two-contact mode switch. No manufacturer documents this exact code publicly; CARB requires circuit checks. P0955 is the general fault, P0954 the intermittent fault of the up/down circuit.
s: Manual mode switches on or off by itself
Gear display flickers between D and manual gear
Fault often appears on rough roads
P0959.t: Auto Shift Manual Mode Circuit Intermittent

c: Loose or corroded connector at shift position sensor C
Damaged signal, supply or ground wire of sensor circuit C
Faulty shift position sensor C
Faulty sensor input in the transmission control module
P095A.d: Circuit C is a third channel reporting the shift position inside an automated manual gearbox, for example a further sensor track or a sensor on another shift rail or selector shaft. This general circuit code sets on an electrical fault of that signal that fits none of the more specific C variants. No manufacturer documents the code publicly, and which sensor carries the letter C depends on the design. A Nissan/Aichi patent describes shift stroke sensors as the feedback for engaging gears, an Aisin AI patent the fallback when a stroke sensor fails. CARB requires circuit checks on such inputs. P095B to P095D are the C siblings, P0914 and P091A the same signal on circuits A and B. Shifting may be restricted.
s: Transmission or engine warning light on
Slower or restricted gear changes in fallback mode
Gearbox may hold a gear or stay in neutral

c: Worn or drifting shift position sensor C disagreeing with the other channels
Bent sensor bracket or displaced magnet on the shift rail
Gear positions not relearned after actuator or module replacement
Increased contact resistance in the sensor circuit
P095B.d: Plausibility fault of the shift position signal on circuit C of an automated manual gearbox. The voltage is electrically acceptable, but the value does not fit: it contradicts the other position channels, stays put while the shift actuator moves, or misses the learned gear positions. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A Nissan/Aichi patent points out that sensor mountings on shift parts can give way under vibration and distort the reading; an Aisin AI patent explains how control carries on when a stroke sensor can no longer be trusted. CARB requires rationality checks on such inputs. P095A, P095C and P095D are the electrical faults of circuit C, P0915 and P091B the same check on A and B.
s: Fallback mode with fewer available gears
