Possible no-start countdown after ignore period

c: Pump motor open
Connector unplugged or corroded
Pin pushed back out of connector body

c: Heater element failed
Wiring open or connector loose
P20EB.d: A general electrical fault on the reductant tank heater "A" control circuit. AdBlue freezes at -11 C, so the tank heater must work for cold-start dosing.
s: Check engine light or NOx warning on
Possible no-start countdown after ignore period
P20EB.t: Reductant Control Module Power Relay De-Energized Performance - Too Late

c: Uncontrolled or over-long DPF regeneration
Leaking exhaust fuel injector or injector dripping
Exhaust temperature sensor reading too high
P20EC.d: P20EC means the temperature of the SCR NOx catalyst on bank 1, measured or modelled from the exhaust temperature sensors, has exceeded the limit that protects the catalyst coating. Typical triggers are an over-long or uncontrolled particulate filter regeneration, excess fuel in the exhaust or a faulty temperature sensor. Repeated overheating ages the catalyst and lowers its NOx conversion.

c: Uncontrolled or over-long DPF regeneration
Leaking exhaust fuel injector or injector dripping
Exhaust temperature sensor reading too high
P20ED.d: P20ED means the temperature of the SCR NOx pre-catalyst on bank 1, measured or modelled from the exhaust temperature sensors, has exceeded the limit that protects the catalyst coating. The pre-catalyst is a smaller SCR stage mounted close to the engine on some systems. Typical triggers are an over-long or uncontrolled particulate filter regeneration, excess fuel in the exhaust or a faulty temperature sensor. Repeated overheating ages the catalyst and lowers its NOx conversion.

c: SCR catalyst aged or poisoned
NOx sensor drift
Exhaust leak between upstream and downstream NOx sensors
P20EE.d: The SCR catalyst on bank 1 is no longer reducing NOx to the level the ECU expects, even with proper reductant dosing and quality. Often the result of catalyst poisoning by sulphur or hydrocarbons, thermal aging, or a leak between the upstream and downstream NOx sensors.
s: Sulfur (rotten egg) smell from exhaust under load

c: Pre-catalyst aged or poisoned
Poor reductant quality or dosing
NOx sensor drift
P20EF.d: P20EF means the SCR pre-catalyst on bank 1, a smaller SCR stage ahead of the main catalyst on some systems, converts less NOx than the monitor requires. The module compares the NOx signals before and after the stage with the dosed reductant. Causes are similar to P20EE for the main catalyst: an aged or poisoned catalyst, poor reductant quality or dosing, or a drifting NOx sensor.
s: Possible engine power limitation after repeated detection
P20EF.t: SCR NOx Pre-Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 1)

c: Runaway DPF regeneration upstream
Temperature sensor drift high
P20F0.d: SCR NOx Catalyst Over Temperature (Bank 2): the component is overheating, typically from extended load or slip.
s: Sulfur (rotten egg) smell from exhaust under load

c: Runaway regeneration upstream
P20F1.d: SCR NOx Pre-Catalyst Over Temperature (Bank 2): the component is overheating, typically from extended load or slip.
s: Sulfur (rotten egg) smell from exhaust under load

c: SCR catalyst thermally aged
Catalyst poisoning from sulphur or oil ash
P20F2.d: SCR NOx Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 2): the control module has detected this fault condition.

P20F2.t: SCR NOx Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 2)

c: Pre-catalyst thermally aged
P20F3.d: SCR NOx Pre-Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold (Bank 2): the control module has detected this fault condition.

c: Dosing nozzle clogged with crystallised DEF
Pump weak — flow under target
P20F4.d: The DEF consumption observed over the dosing window is below the model expectation — typically a clogged dosing nozzle, weak pump, or leak between pump and injector that recirculates DEF back to the tank.

Possible no-start countdown after ignore period

c: Injector seat leaks DEF into exhaust

P20F5.d: The DEF consumption observed over the dosing window is above the model expectation — typically a leaking injector seat, leaking line fitting, or a pressure-control valve that vents constantly to the tank.

c: Valve seat eroded or contaminated
Valve plunger seized open
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement

Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

Throttle position signal invalid

Throttle motor not controllable

Pedal position sensor signal implausible

Idle too high or too low

c: ECU internal processor fault
ECU software flash corrupted
Module software outdated, reflash may resolve

c: ECU internal performance fault
ECU connector pins corroded
Module software outdated, reflash may resolve

s: Reduced throttle response, possible limp mode

c: Carbon deposits on throttle plate
Throttle position sensor drift
Idle/throttle relearn not performed
P2109.d: The ECU detects that the throttle position sensor A signal at the closed-throttle stop does not match the learned minimum value. The mechanical or electrical zero reference of the throttle has drifted out of the expected range, often after cleaning, replacement or wear.
s: Reduced throttle response, possible limp mode
Idle too high or too low

c: Motor winding open
Open wire to motor
Pin pushed back out of connector body

c: Motor brushes worn
Carbon buildup at throttle plate
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P210B.d: Throttle actuator B motor responds electrically but does not move the throttle plate as commanded — typically high-resistance brushes, partial winding fault, or a sticky throttle bore.
s: Reduced throttle response, possible limp mode
Idle too high or too low
P210B.t: Throttle Actuator B Control Motor Circuit Range/Performance

c: Short to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P210C.d: Throttle actuator B motor drive line stuck low — short to ground. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.

Idle too high or too low

c: One potentiometer track worn — voltage drift
Water in pedal connector
P210E.d: The redundant throttle or accelerator pedal position channels C and F disagree by more than the allowed tolerance. Drive-by-wire systems compare two or three independent channels to detect a faulty potentiometer track.
s: Reduced throttle response, possible limp mode
Idle too high or too low

P210F.d: Throttle B control has detected an unsafe condition and forced an RPM limit. Common protective response when motor current, throttle position feedback, or supply voltage on the B path is out of spec.

Idle too high or too low

c: Underlying TAC fault triggers rpm cap
Throttle response time out of spec
P2110.d: The TAC monitor caps engine speed at a fixed limp-home rpm because it can no longer trust the throttle response. Driver may notice a hard rev limit well below redline.
s: Reduced throttle response, possible limp mode
Idle too high or too low

c: Throttle plate seized open
Return spring broken
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
P2111.d: The throttle plate cannot be commanded back to the closed/idle position. Idle speed runs high or the engine cannot decelerate properly — safety-critical fault that usually triggers immediate limp mode.
s: Reduced throttle response, possible limp mode
Idle too high or too low
P2111.t: Throttle Actuator Control System — Stuck Open

c: Throttle plate seized closed
Throttle motor seized or gear broken
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
P2112.d: The throttle plate cannot be commanded open. The engine stays at idle or stalls under load. Often caused by a seized motor, broken gear, or heavy carbon coking inside the throttle bore.
s: Reduced throttle response, possible limp mode
Idle too high or too low
P2112.t: Throttle Actuator Control System — Stuck Closed

c: Carbon deposits or ice keep the throttle plate off its rest stop
Position sensor B worn or drifted at the low end of its track
Minimum position not relearned after cleaning or part replacement
Corroded connector shifting the sensor B signal
P2113.d: The engine computer checks whether position signal B reports a plausible value when the throttle or pedal rests against its lower mechanical stop. At key-on many systems learn this minimum and compare it with a tolerance window; a reading outside that window sets the code. Ford and GM label their second throttle position sensor as B, so on those layouts B means the throttle body, but neither maker publishes P2113 itself. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; Subaru uses the A version (P2109). Ice, coking or a bent stop are typical triggers. P0220-P0223 cover the B circuit, P2109 and P2114-P2117 the other letters. The driver may see a warning lamp and reduced power.
s: Engine or ETC warning lamp on
P2113.t: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor B Minimum Stop Performance

c: Position sensor C worn or drifted near its rest position
Deposits, ice or a damaged stop prevent the rest position
Rest position not relearned after repair
Connector or wiring fault shifting the C signal
P2114.d: This code reports that position signal C does not show a believable value while its throttle or pedal sits on the lower stop. The controller learns or expects a minimum reading within a tolerance band and flags a fault when the learned value falls outside it. Letter C is rarely assigned: Ford and GM use A/B for the throttle and D/E/F for the pedal, so C appears only on layouts with a third sensor. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; the logic follows the A version P2109 (Subaru) and the Delphi minimum-learn patent. P2113 and P2115-P2117 are the same test for other letters, P2136/P2137 compare C against A or B. Expect a warning lamp and possibly limited power.
s: Engine or ETC warning lamp on
P2114.t: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor C Minimum Stop Performance

c: Pedal blocked by floor mat or weak return spring
Worn pedal sensor track D at the idle end
Aftermarket pedal tuning module or wrong pedal part
Corroded or loose pedal connector
P2115.d: Here the controller judges position signal D at the released (minimum) end of travel. On Ford and GM drive-by-wire systems D is the first accelerator pedal sensor, so the code means the pedal's idle reading is outside the expected window, for example because the pedal does not return fully or its sensor track has shifted. No manufacturer documents P2115 publicly; Ford and GM publish only circuit and correlation codes for D (P2120-P2123, P2138). P2116 and P2117 are the E and F counterparts, P2109 and P2113 refer to A and B. The engine may not return to idle cleanly, and the ECU may limit pedal response.
s: Engine does not drop to normal idle when the pedal is released
P2115.t: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor D Minimum Stop Performance

c: Pedal held off its stop by floor mat or sticking pivot
Worn or contaminated sensor track E
Moisture or corrosion at the pedal connector
P2116.d: The code covers the rest-position check of signal E. Ford, GM and Mitsubishi assign E to the second accelerator pedal sensor, which on many pedals runs at roughly half the voltage of sensor D (GM: APP 2 between 0.16 and 2.3 V). If the reading with the pedal released lies outside the learned or calibrated window, P2116 can be stored. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Circuit faults of the same sensor are reported separately (P2125, P2127-P2129) and disagreement between D and E as P2138; P2115 and P2117 handle D and F. Typical effects are a warning lamp, an unsteady idle and limited throttle response.
P2116.t: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor E Minimum Stop Performance

c: Pedal does not return fully to its stop
Worn third sensor track F
Poor contact at the pedal connector
P2117.d: P2117 is the minimum-stop check for signal F. Ford lists F as the third accelerator pedal sensor on its older Gen2 throttle systems (circuit codes P2132/P2133, range P2131), while most current pedals carry only D and E, so the code can only occur on three-track pedals. The ECU flags it when the F reading at the released position lies outside the expected band. No manufacturer documents P2117 publicly. Siblings are P2115 (D) and P2116 (E); P2139 and P2140 compare F with D or E. A sticking pedal or a worn track usually lies behind it, with a warning lamp and reduced pedal response as the visible result.
P2117.t: Throttle/Pedal Position Sensor F Minimum Stop Performance

c: Plate binding from carbon
Motor windings aged or open
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P2118.d: The current draw of the throttle motor lies outside the expected range — either much higher (binding plate) or much lower (worn brushes, open winding) than calibrated.
s: Reduced throttle response, possible limp mode
Idle too high or too low
P2118.t: Throttle Actuator Control Motor Current Range/Performance

c: Carbon deposits make the throttle plate stick
Water or ice in the intake behind the throttle body
Weak return spring or worn gear in the throttle body

P2119.d: This is a mechanical performance check of the electronic throttle body. GM calls it Throttle Closed Position Performance: after the motor is de-energized the return springs must bring the plate into its default (limp) position, e.g. 1.32-1.90 V on TP sensor 1 in GM's 2006 tables; 15 failed samples in a row set it. A Bosch-based GM ECM times the spring return at key-on (fault above 0.56 s). Toyota, Lexus, Ford (Ranger/Bronco, ice behind the throttle) and Mitsubishi use the code too. Unlike P2101 (position error while driven) or P2118 (motor current), P2119 points at a sticking or iced plate or a weak spring; the engine may enter limp mode.

P2125.d: P2125 reports a general electrical fault in signal circuit E. GM uses it as Accelerator Pedal Position Sensor 2 Circuit: the ECM looks for a continuous or intermittent open or short in the sensor 2 circuit with a counter at 12.5 ms per count (19 of 39 counts). In GM's 2006 tables sensor 2 is valid between about 0.16 and 2.3 V. GM bulletin 14636 lists P2125 among the pedal codes caused by a broken solder joint inside the pedal (2009-2011 Impala, LaCrosse). Range/Performance is P2126, explicit low or high voltage P2127/P2128, dropouts P2129, and the D/E comparison P2138. With one pedal track lost the ECU usually limits engine power.

P2126.d: Signal E is electrically intact but its value does not fit the situation. Ford's 2012 OBD summary uses P2126 for the second pedal sensor on Gen2 throttle systems: it sets when sensors D and E disagree by more than 1.1 degrees, as a non-MIL fault with the wrench lamp. Mitsubishi lists P2126 as accelerator pedal sensor E on the 2022 Outlander. Many newer systems report the same disagreement as P2138 instead. P2125 is the general circuit fault, P2127/P2128 are voltage below or above limits, P2129 covers dropouts. P2129.d: P2129 is meant for short dropouts or spikes in signal circuit E that do not last long enough for a steady low or high fault. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM and Ford, which assign E to the second pedal sensor, catch such glitches inside their circuit codes instead: GM counts failures every 12.5 ms and flags the APP sensor 2 circuit after 19 of 39 counts (P2125/P2127/P2128), Ford uses 0.25/4.75 V limits. c: Air leak after the air mass sensor, often at the crankcase ventilation

Fuel pressure too low
P2187.d: P2187 means the long-term fuel trim of bank 1 has to add more fuel than allowed in the idle and low-load range. Many systems, especially Bosch ones, split mixture adaptation into an additive part, which dominates at low airflow, and a multiplicative part for load. An air leak adds a fixed amount of unmeasured air, which matters most at idle, so it shows up in the additive part. GM's 3.6 V6 engines set the code above 7 % (2005) or 6.1 % (2008 LLT, at 520 to 1120 rpm, 1.7 to 7.8 g/s and coolant above 60 °C), and GM's 2024 tables above about 5.5 %, over two trips. On the Opel/GM 2.0 turbo in the Saab 9-5 (2010) the weighted long-term trim must exceed its limit for 4 s continuously or 50 s in total (Type B). Audi traced P2187 with P2279 on 2.0 TFSI engines to a crankcase ventilation valve that let boost into the crankcase; Mazda found A/F sensor wiring on the CX-7 2.3 turbo shorted after brake fluid was spilled on it.
s: Rough or hunting idle, hissing from the engine bay

c: Leaking injector or fuel pressure too high
Fuel vapour from the purge valve or oil-diluted crankcase gases

P2188.d: P2188 means the long-term fuel trim of bank 1 has to remove more fuel than allowed in the idle and low-load range, the additive part of the mixture adaptation on Bosch-type systems. GM's 2008 3.6 LLT sets it below -6.0 % at 520 to 1120 rpm and 1.7 to 7.8 g/s, with closed loop and coolant above 60 °C. On the Opel/GM 2.0 turbo in the Saab 9-5 (2010) the weighted long-term trim must stay below its limit for 4 s or 50 s in total (Type B); Saab's test gives -22 to 0 % as normal trim and 19 to 42 kPa manifold pressure at idle. At idle the extra fuel typically comes from sources the ECM does not meter: Mercedes lists for the M132 engine a leaking PCV valve, leaking injectors or excessive fuel pressure, wrong intake pressure readings, a restricted or worn throttle and a contaminated oxygen sensor. A saturated charcoal canister purging at idle has the same effect. Stellantis found an airflow straightener in the air box clipped in wrong, which disturbed the air mass reading and set P2188 and P2190.

c: Intake gasket or runner leak on the bank 2 side
Shared vacuum leak, usually with P2187 present too
Bank 2 front sensor, its wiring or an injector on that bank
P2189.d: P2189 is the bank 2 version of P2187: on engines with a front oxygen sensor per bank, the long-term trim of bank 2 has to add more fuel than allowed at idle and low load. GM's 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 set it when the additive correction exceeds 7 %, the 2008 3.6 LLT above 6.1 % at 520 to 1120 rpm, airflow of 1.7 to 7.8 g/s, engine load of 11 to 45 % and coolant above 60 °C, and GM's 2024 tables above about 5.5 % over two trips. Because both banks share the throttle, crankcase ventilation and brake booster vacuum, a leak there normally lifts the idle trim on both banks, setting P2187 and P2189 together. A code on bank 2 alone points to something only that bank sees: an intake manifold gasket or runner leak on that side, an injector on that bank, or the bank 2 front sensor or its wiring. Comparing both banks' trims at idle and at 2500 rpm narrows it down.

P2190.d: P2190 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2188: the long-term trim of bank 2 has to remove more fuel than allowed at idle and low load. GM's 2008 3.6 LLT sets it below -6.0 % in the same window it uses for P2188 (520 to 1120 rpm, 1.7 to 7.8 g/s, closed loop, coolant above 60 °C, catalyst heating not active), and GM's 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 treat it in the same additive adaptation range. A rich fault on bank 2 only usually lies in that bank: a leaking injector, or a bank 2 front sensor reading lean so the ECM keeps leaning the mixture. Fuel pressure, purge vapour and air-mass errors act on both banks and tend to set P2188 and P2190 together. Stellantis is an example: an airflow straightener clipped in wrong in the air box upset the air mass reading and logged P2188 and P2190 together, sometimes with P0111 and an unstable idle; refitting it correctly cured it.

P2195.d: P2195 means the front oxygen or air-fuel sensor on bank 1 reports a lean mixture that the ECM does not believe, either because it stays lean or because it disagrees with other evidence. On GM's Bosch-based 2005 V6 the rear sensor has to read rich (above 0.85 V) while the front A/F sensor reads leaner than lambda 1.08 and the short-term trim sits at its maximum of 1.25, for about 100 s or 50 s in total. Ford checks narrow-band sensors for fewer than 5 switches in 30 s and wide-band sensors for 30 s at the short-term trim limit; from 2019 a sensor whose filtered lambda changes by less than 0.0001 for 30 s sets P2195 if the value is at or above 1. On the Opel/GM 2.0 turbo in the Saab 9-5 (2010) the code sets within 4 s continuously or 50 s in total. Ford replaced the heated oxygen sensors for P2195 and P2197 on 2015 to 2017 Explorer and F-150 3.5 GTDI. An exhaust leak ahead of the sensor can also make it read lean.
s: Possible rough running or higher consumption from wrong fuelling
P2195.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean (Bank 1, Sensor 1)

c: Front oxygen or A/F sensor contaminated or aged

P2196.d: P2196 means the front oxygen or air-fuel sensor on bank 1 reports a rich mixture that the ECM does not accept. On GM's Bosch-based 2005 V6 this is a cross-check with the rear sensor: the rear sensor reads lean (below 0.15 V) while the front A/F sensor reads richer than lambda 0.92 and the short-term trim has pulled to its minimum of 0.75, for about 100 s or 50 s in total. Ford sets it for a narrow-band sensor that hardly switches and stays rich, a wide-band sensor that sits 30 s at the short-term trim limit, or, from 2019, a filtered lambda below 1 that changes by less than 0.0001 for 30 s; Ford blocks the stuck-rich test while fuel is boiling off the oil after a cold start. On the Opel/GM 2.0 turbo in the Saab 9-5 (2010) the code sets within 4 s continuously or 50 s in total. Because the ECM leans the engine to follow the false signal, a rear sensor reading lean and a lean real mixture often accompany it.
P2196.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich (Bank 1, Sensor 1)

c: Bank 2 front oxygen or A/F sensor aged or contaminated

P2197.d: P2197 is the bank 2 version of P2195 on engines with a front sensor per bank: the bank 2 front oxygen or A/F sensor keeps reporting lean in a way the ECM rejects. GM's Bosch-based 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 flag it when the bank 2 rear sensor reads rich (above 0.85 V) while the front sensor reads leaner than lambda 1.08 with short-term trim at its 1.25 maximum, a contradiction a real lean mixture would not produce. Ford applies its switching, trim-limit and, from 2019, stuck-lambda tests to bank 2 the same way, with a 30 s window. Ford's 2017 bulletin for 2015 to 2017 Explorer and 2015 to 2016 F-150 3.5 GTDI lists P2195 and P2197 with P2626 and P2629, the pumping-current trim circuits of the A/F sensors, and fixes them with new heated oxygen sensors. If only bank 2 is affected, an exhaust manifold leak on that side ahead of the sensor is worth ruling out before replacing the sensor.
s: Possible rough running or higher consumption
P2197.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean (Bank 2, Sensor 1)

c: Bank 2 front oxygen or A/F sensor contaminated or aged

P2198.d: P2198 is the bank 2 counterpart of P2196: the bank 2 front oxygen or A/F sensor reports rich in a way the ECM does not accept. On GM's Bosch-based 2005 2.8 and 3.6 V6 the bank 2 rear sensor must read lean (below 0.15 V) while the front sensor reads richer than lambda 0.92 and the short-term trim has dropped to its 0.75 minimum; the code then sets after about 100 s, or 50 s cumulatively, over two trips. Ford uses the same lack-of-switching, trim-limit and stuck-lambda logic as on bank 1, sets the stuck-rich code when the frozen lambda value is below 1, and suspends the stuck-rich test during cold starts while fuel boils off the oil through the crankcase ventilation. A sensor contaminated by oil or coolant, or one whose signal or reference wiring has a fault, gives this pattern; since the ECM leans bank 2 to follow the false reading, the rear sensor of that bank usually shows lean at the same time.

Possible no-start countdown after ignore period

c: Connector intermittent contact
Harness chafed near exhaust
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration
P2204.d: The bank 1 NOx sensor signal drops out intermittently. Typical cause is a marginal connector, harness chafing near hot exhaust components, or thermal-cycling solder joints inside the smart sensor.
s: Check engine light or NOx warning on
Possible no-start countdown after ignore period

c: Heater element open
Heater short to supply or ground
P2205.d: The heater inside the bank 1 NOx sensor cannot be controlled — open, short, or failed driver. Without proper heater operation the sensor never reaches its operating temperature and reports invalid data.
s: Check engine light or NOx warning on
Possible no-start countdown after ignore period

c: Internal heater or control-unit fault in the NOx sensor
Heater wiring chafed to ground near the exhaust
Moisture or corrosion in the sensor connector
P2206.d: A NOx sensor needs its ceramic element heated to several hundred degrees before it can measure. P2206 means the heater control circuit of the first (upstream) NOx sensor on bank 1 reads low, typically a short to ground or a driver output stuck low. CARB requires diesel OBD to detect heater circuit opens and shorts that conflict with the commanded state. GM's 3.0L Duramax (LZ0) lists it as NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit Low; Volvo and Mack trucks treat P2206 on the inlet sensor as an internal sensor failure and replace the sensor. P2205 is the general heater circuit fault, P2207 the high side, P2208-P2211 the heater sense circuit. The SCR system loses NOx feedback.
s: SCR or emissions warning on the display
P2206.t: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit Low (Bank 1)

c: Heater element inside the NOx sensor burnt open
Open circuit or short to voltage in the heater wiring
Loose or heat-damaged connector
P2207.d: P2207 is the high-side counterpart of P2206: the heater control circuit of the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1 shows a voltage that is too high for the commanded state, typically an open heater element or a short to supply voltage. CARB requires the diesel OBD system to flag such circuit faults that contradict the command. GM lists P2207 as NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit High for the 2024 Silverado/Sierra 3.0L diesel (LZ0). Without heating the sensor never becomes ready, so SCR dosing runs without NOx feedback. P2205 is the general heater circuit code, P2206 the low side, and P2208-P2211 concern the heater feedback circuit. P22A5 is the same fault on sensor 2.
s: NOx readiness or SCR efficiency faults may follow
P2207.t: NOx Sensor Heater Control Circuit High (Bank 1)

c: Internal fault in the NOx sensor or its control unit
Damaged wiring between sensor element and sensor control unit
Water ingress in the connector
P2208.d: Besides the control line, the NOx sensor heater has a sense or feedback path through which the controller checks how the heater actually responds (current, resistance or element temperature). P2208 marks a general fault in this sense circuit of the upstream sensor on bank 1. GM calls it NOx Sensor Heater Feedback Circuit (3.0L LZ0 diesel); Volvo and Mack class P2208 on the inlet sensor as a sensor failure that requires replacement. CARB demands heater performance monitoring within the supplier's limits. P2209 is the plausibility check of the same feedback, P2210/P2211 low or high values, P2212 dropouts; P2205-P2207 concern the control side. MIL on, driveability normal.
s: NOx sensor reports no valid value

c: Aged NOx sensor element that heats up too slowly
Low supply voltage or poor ground to the sensor
Prolonged cold or wet exhaust delaying dew-point release
P2209.d: P2209 is the performance check of the NOx sensor heater: the feedback is electrically present but shows that the element does not reach or hold operating temperature as expected. VW's 2014 TDI specification books (Passat, Touareg) set it when NOx control has not become active more than 180 s after the dew point was passed. Ford's 2023 diesel OBD summary uses P2209 as NOx signal readiness, judged by the ratio of actual to expected sensor on-time. GM names it Heater Feedback Performance. CARB requires both heater performance and NOx sensor activity monitoring. P2208 is the circuit fault, P2210/P2211 low or high values. MIL after confirmation, no limp mode.
s: NOx sensor not ready for long periods after start
P2209.t: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Range/Performance (Bank 1)

c: Fuse, harness break, or short
P220A.d: The supply voltage rail to the NOx sensor on bank 1 sensor 1 is faulty — typically a fuse, harness break, or short. NOx sensors need a clean stable supply for the heater and the wide-band measurement cell.
s: Check engine light or NOx warning on
Possible no-start countdown after ignore period
P220A.t: NOx Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

Possible no-start countdown after ignore period
P220B.t: NOx Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

P2210.d: P2210 means the heater feedback signal of the upstream NOx sensor on bank 1 sits below its permitted range. Typical electrical causes are a short to ground in the sense line or a failed measuring stage in the sensor electronics. GM lists the code as NOx Sensor Heater Feedback Circuit Low for the 2024 Silverado/Sierra 3.0L diesel (LZ0). CARB requires the OBD system to detect heater circuit faults that conflict with the commanded state. P2211 is the opposite direction, P2208 the general sense-circuit fault, P2209 a plausible but poor heating result, and P2206 a low reading on the control side. The sensor then delivers no usable NOx value; the MIL comes on.
s: No NOx reading in live data
P2210.t: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit Low (Bank 1)

c: Interrupted heater element in the NOx sensor
Open sense line or short to voltage
Loose or heat-damaged connector
P2211.d: P2211 flags a heater feedback signal above its permitted range on the upstream NOx sensor of bank 1. An open sense line, a short to supply voltage or an interrupted heater element that the electronics reads as maximum resistance are the usual reasons. GM lists it as NOx Sensor Heater Feedback Circuit High for the 3.0L Duramax (LZ0) in the 2024 Silverado/Sierra. Under CARB rules such circuit faults must be detected regardless of operating conditions. P2210 is the low direction, P2208 the general fault, P2209 the performance check and P2207 the high fault on the control side. The NOx sensor stays unready, SCR control falls back on modelled values, and the MIL lights up.
P2211.t: NOx Sensor Heater Sense Circuit High (Bank 1)

Connector with intermittent contact under vibration
Harness routed against vibrating component

P2226.d: The ECU detects a general fault in the barometric pressure sensor circuit. The atmospheric pressure value used for altitude compensation and fuel/air calculation is not available or implausible.

Connector corroded

P2227.d: The barometric pressure sensor delivers an electrically valid signal that does not match the operating point — for example pressure jumps that do not match altitude changes, or values stuck near full scale.

Signal shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2228.d: The barometric (ambient) pressure sensor reports a voltage below the valid window. The ECU uses this signal to compensate fuel and boost calculations for altitude — a stuck-low value tricks the ECU into thinking the car is at high altitude.

c: Signal shorted to supply
Sensor ground open
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2229.d: The barometric pressure sensor reports a voltage above the valid window. Usually a short to supply or an open ground.

c: Sensor failed
P222A.d: A general electrical fault on barometric pressure sensor B — open, shorted, or out of plausibility. The sensor measures atmospheric pressure for altitude compensation; sensor B is a redundant or secondary unit.

c: Sensor drift
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
Sensor mounting loose - signal damping
P222B.d: Barometric sensor B reads in range but plausibility check fails — slow response or stuck reading. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P222B.t: Barometric Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

c: Short to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

P222C.d: Barometric sensor B below lower plausibility — short to ground. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.

c: Open signal line
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P222D.d: Barometric sensor B above upper plausibility — open signal or short to B+. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.

Harness routed against vibrating component

P222F.d: Barometric pressure sensors A and B disagree by more than the allowed tolerance. Used for redundancy on hybrid and emission-critical systems.

c: Engine harness chafed against an engine component (e.g. vacuum pump pulley, cam cover)
Loose or corroded pin at the BARO sensor or ECM connector
Barometric pressure sensor with an internal contact problem
P2230.d: P2230 flags a barometric pressure (BARO) signal that is electrically present but jumps or drops out for short moments instead of sitting permanently low or high. The engine computer uses BARO for air-charge, fuelling and boost calculations. Ford's 2020-2023 gasoline OBD summary lists P2230 with P2227-P2229 among the BARO faults that inhibit auto start-stop. GM bulletins for 2014-2017 trucks and SUVs with the 5.3/6.2 L V8 and for the 2012-2013 Equinox/Terrain 2.4 L trace P2230 to engine harness wires chafed through. Exact thresholds are not published. P2228/P2229 are steady low/high signals, P2227 a plausibility fault. Drivers usually notice only the warning light; start-stop may stay off.
s: Check engine light, often coming and going
Other sensor codes stored at the same time if a shared harness is damaged

c: Internal short between heater and sensing element in the oxygen sensor
Heater and signal wires melted or chafed together (exhaust heat, routing)
Moisture or contamination bridging pins in the sensor connector
P2231.d: P2231 means the engine computer sees the heater supply of the upstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 leaking into the sensor's signal path - typically an internal short in the sensor or two neighbouring wires touching in the harness. VW's 2014 specification books for the Passat and Tiguan set it when the front sensor signal changes by more than 190 microamps, i.e. the measured sensor current is distorted. CARB requires circuit faults of every fuel-control oxygen sensor to be detected. P2232/P2233 cover sensors 2 and 3 of bank 1, P2234 the first sensor of bank 2. Because the mixture feedback can no longer be trusted, the engine may run on open-loop fuelling with higher consumption and emissions.
s: Higher fuel consumption due to open-loop fuelling
Rough idle or hesitation in some cases
P2231.t: O2 Sensor Signal Circuit Shorted to Heater Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

c: Reference line shorted to positive

P2246.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

Pin pushed back out of connector body

P224C.d: The drive circuit for the shutoff valve at the alternative-fuel tank A is open. Bi-fuel vehicles (CNG, LPG, hydrogen) use a high-pressure shutoff valve at the tank for safety; with this fault the alternative fuel cannot be drawn from the tank.
P224C.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit/Open

c: Valve seized closed
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play
P224D.d: Alternative-fuel shutoff valve A is electrically OK but does not open when commanded. Vehicle remains on petrol/diesel only.
P224D.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off

c: Short to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P224E.d: Shutoff valve A drive line stuck low — short to ground. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P224E.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit Low

c: Short to B+
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P224F.d: Shutoff valve A drive line stuck high — short to B+. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P224F.t: Alternative Fuel Tank Shutoff Valve A Control Circuit High

c: Reference line shorted to positive
Connector corroded with leakage
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P2250.d: Bank 2 counterpart to P2246. The reference voltage at bank 2, sensor 1 is above the upper threshold, usually due to a short to positive or connector leakage.
P2250.t: O2 Sensor Reference Voltage Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

c: Vs− line open
Wide-band sensor failed
P2251.d: The negative current control line (Vs−) of the wide-band lambda sensor on bank 1 sensor 1 is open or out of range. Used as the virtual ground reference for the Nernst cell.
P2251.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

c: Vs negative line shorted to ground
Nernst cell return open inside sensor
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2252.d: The negative-current (Vs negative) line on the bank 1, sensor 1 wide-band oxygen sensor is below the lower threshold. This line is the return path for the Nernst cell; loss of the signal blocks the lambda calculation.
P2252.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

c: Vs negative line shorted to positive
Internal short in sensor
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2253.d: The Vs negative line on bank 1, sensor 1 reads above the upper threshold. Often a short to positive or a damaged ECU sensor amplifier.
P2253.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit High (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

c: Broken reference ground wire or pushed-out pin between sensor and ECM
Internal open circuit in the wide-band sensor
Corroded sensor connector with high contact resistance
P2254.d: P2254 concerns the negative current control line - also called reference ground, virtual ground or COM - of the wide-band air-fuel sensor ahead of the catalyst on bank 2. Ford's OBD summaries (2012 and 2020-2023) set it for an open line: with Bosch sensors the PCM briefly injects a reference current and flags the line if lambda barely moves, within about 10 s; with NTK sensors the interface chip reports the open line directly. VW's 2014 Passat and CC books set it when the front signal sits at 1.47-1.52 V while the cell resistance exceeds 950 ohms. P2251 is the same fault on bank 1, P2255/P2256 are low/high faults. Closed-loop mixture control on bank 2 is lost.
s: Higher fuel consumption from open-loop fuelling on bank 2
Possible rough running or failed emissions test
P2254.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit/Open (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

c: Reference ground wire shorted to ground (chafed against exhaust or body)
Internal fault in the wide-band sensor
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
P2255.d: P2255 reports that the negative current control line (reference ground) of the bank 2 upstream wide-band sensor reads too low, typically a short to ground. No manufacturer publicly documents P2255 with thresholds. Ford's OBD summaries assign shorts to ground on any wide-band sensor line to P0151 and use P2254 only for an open line, and VW's 2014 specification books likewise list only P2254. The code therefore appears mainly where the sensor interface separates short-circuit faults by line. CARB requires circuit and out-of-range faults of fuel-control sensors to be detected and, where feasible, stored as separate codes. P2252 is the bank 1 counterpart, P2256 the high-side fault. Mixture control on bank 2 becomes unreliable.
P2255.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit Low (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

c: Reference ground wire shorted to heater supply or battery voltage
Internal short in the wide-band sensor
Fault in the sensor interface of the ECM
P2256.d: P2256 means the negative current control line (reference ground) of the bank 2 upstream wide-band sensor reads too high, typically a short to battery or heater voltage. No manufacturer publicly documents P2256 with thresholds. Ford's OBD summaries send a short to battery on any wide-band sensor line to P0152 and reserve P2254 for the open line; VW's 2014 books also list only P2254 for this circuit. CARB requires fuel-control sensors to be checked for circuit continuity and out-of-range values, with separate codes where feasible. P2253 is the bank 1 counterpart, P2255 the low-side fault, P2254 the open circuit. A short to voltage can damage the sensor or the interface, so the wiring should be checked before a new sensor is fitted.
s: Repeat failure of a new sensor if the wiring short remains
P2256.t: O2 Sensor Negative Current Control Circuit High (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

c: Control wire shorted to ground
Faulty SAI relay
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2257.d: The control circuit of the secondary air injection system A reads a voltage below specification. Either the relay output is shorted to ground or the wiring/load is faulty.
P2257.t: Secondary Air Injection System Control A Circuit Low

c: Control wire shorted to battery
Open relay coil
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2258.d: The control circuit A of the secondary air injection system shows a voltage above the calibrated upper threshold. Likely a short to battery voltage or an open in the relay coil/output.
P2258.t: Secondary Air Injection System Control A Circuit High

c: Short to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P2259.d: The drive line for secondary air injection (AIR) control circuit B is stuck low. Secondary air is pumped into the exhaust manifold during cold start to speed up catalyst light-off.
P2259.t: Secondary Air Injection System Control B Circuit Low

c: Sensor calibration memory corrupt
Module software outdated, reflash may resolve
Supply voltage outside specification
P225A.d: The factory calibration memory of the NOx sensor on bank 1 sensor 1 cannot be read or contains a checksum error. Each NOx sensor ships with a unique calibration table programmed at the factory.
s: Check engine light or NOx warning on
Possible no-start countdown after ignore period

c: Sensor calibration memory corrupt
Module software outdated, reflash may resolve
Supply voltage outside specification
P225B.d: The factory calibration memory of the NOx sensor on bank 1 sensor 2 cannot be read or contains a checksum error. Each NOx sensor ships with a unique calibration table programmed at the factory.
s: Check engine light or NOx warning on
Possible no-start countdown after ignore period

c: Sensor poisoned by silicon, sulphur, or oil ash
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
Sensor element contaminated by oil, soot or coolant
P225C.d: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck High (Bank 1 Sensor 1): the component is electrically intact but its response does not match the command.
s: Check engine light or NOx warning on
Possible no-start countdown after ignore period
P225C.t: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck High (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

c: Sensor aged or condensate damaged
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
Sensor element contaminated by oil, soot or coolant
P225D.d: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1): the component is electrically intact but its response does not match the command.
s: Check engine light or NOx warning on
Possible no-start countdown after ignore period
P225D.t: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck Low (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

c: Sensor poisoned
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
Sensor element contaminated by oil, soot or coolant
P225E.d: The NOx sensor on bank 1 sensor 2 reads suspiciously high for too long — biased upward or stuck. Common after sensor poisoning by silicon, sulphur, or oil ash.
s: Check engine light or NOx warning on
Possible no-start countdown after ignore period
P225E.t: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck High (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

c: Sensor aged
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
Sensor element contaminated by oil, soot or coolant
P225F.d: The NOx sensor on bank 1 sensor 2 reads suspiciously low for too long — biased downward or stuck. Common after sensor element ageing, condensate damage from cold start, or wiring fault that pulls the signal down.
s: Check engine light or NOx warning on
Possible no-start countdown after ignore period
P225F.t: NOx Sensor Performance - Signal Biased/Stuck Low (Bank 1 Sensor 2)

c: Short to B+
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P2260.d: AIR system control B drive line stuck high — short to B+. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P2260.t: Secondary Air Injection System Control B Circuit High

c: Stuck bypass valve
Leak in vacuum/pressure actuator
P2261.d: The ECU detects a mechanical fault in the turbocharger or supercharger bypass valve. The valve does not open or close as commanded, causing boost-pressure errors and reduced engine response.
s: Possible blue or black smoke from exhaust
Whistling or hissing sound from intake

c: Charge pipe loose or split
Turbocharger mechanical damage
Wastegate stuck open
P2262.d: The ECU does not detect any meaningful boost pressure increase under load even though the turbocharger is commanded. Likely a mechanical defect in the turbo, charge-air piping or wastegate.
s: Possible blue or black smoke from exhaust
Whistling or hissing sound from intake
P2262.t: Turbo Boost Pressure Not Detected - Mechanical

c: Charge-air hose or cooler duct leaking or pulled off
Variable-geometry vanes or actuator sticking
Restricted exhaust, for example a heavily loaded particulate filter
Boost pressure sensor reading wrong
P2263.d: P2263 means boost pressure measured in the intake manifold stays too far from the target set by the closed-loop boost control. CARB requires diesel OBD to detect underboost, overboost and slow response of the boost control. On the 2014 Cruze 2.0 diesel the allowed underboost deviation runs from 35 to 85 kPa with injection quantity and speed, and the code sets as Type A once the condition holds for 15 s; GM's 2018 diesels need 400 failures in 500 samples and name leaks after the compressor or in the manifolds, and exhaust obstructions, as targets. Ford's 2023 diesels count deviations above 35 kPa at 1500 rpm or more, typically over 100 s. The Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) waits for more than 200 s out of range and stores it as Type C. GM's Cruze bulletin found a charge-air cooler duct pulled off the throttle body, with P0299, P2002 and P2463 alongside. The engine usually limits torque.
s: Hissing or whistling from the charge-air system

c: Defective water-in-fuel sensor
Wiring or connector fault
P2264.d: The ECU detects an electrical fault in the diesel water-in-fuel sensor circuit. Until repaired, water contamination in the fuel filter cannot be detected, risking damage to the high-pressure pump and injectors.

c: Sensor drift or contamination
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
Sensor mounting loose - signal damping
P2265.d: The ECU detects that the water-in-fuel sensor signal is implausible compared to operating conditions. The reading does not change as expected during fuel filter purge or warm-up.
P2265.t: Water in Fuel Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

c: Short to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P2266.d: The water-in-fuel sensor at the diesel fuel filter reads below lower plausibility — short to ground. The sensor warns the driver to drain the filter when condensate accumulates.
P2266.t: Water in Fuel Sensor A Circuit Low

c: Open signal line
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P2267.d: Water-in-fuel sensor reads above upper plausibility — open signal or short to B+. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P2267.t: Water in Fuel Sensor A Circuit High

c: Intermittent connector
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration
Harness routed against vibrating component
P2268.d: Water-in-fuel sensor signal jumps or drops out intermittently. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P2268.t: Water in Fuel Sensor A Circuit Intermittent

c: Condensate accumulated in filter — drain required
P2269.d: The water-in-fuel sensor at fuel filter A has detected water above the warning threshold. The fuel filter must be drained; running the engine on water-contaminated diesel can damage the high-pressure pump and injectors.
P2269.t: Water in Fuel Condition - Sensor A

c: Lamp drive failed
P226A.d: A general electrical fault on the drive line for the dashboard water-in-fuel warning lamp.
P226A.t: Water in Fuel Lamp Control Circuit

c: Wastegate or VGT stuck closed
P226B.d: Boost pressure on turbo A exceeds the upper threshold and the cause is mechanical (wastegate stuck closed, VGT vanes stuck closed) rather than electrical drive fault.
s: Possible blue or black smoke from exhaust
Whistling or hissing sound from intake
P226B.t: Turbocharger/Supercharger A Boost Pressure Too High - Mechanical

c: VGT vanes stiff or worn
P226C.d: Turbocharger Boost Control A Slow Response: the control module has detected this fault condition. This affects turbo/supercharger boost-pressure control.
s: Charging may not start or interrupts
P226C.t: Turbocharger Boost Control A Slow Response

c: Substrate cracked or melted from runaway regen
Substrate removed by tampering
P226D.d: The DPF substrate on bank 1 has been detected as cracked, melted, or removed. Differential pressure across the filter is too low for the measured exhaust flow — the soot trap no longer works.
s: Check engine light or DPF warning light on

c: Substrate cracked, melted, or removed
P226E.d: The DPF substrate on bank 2 has been detected as cracked, melted, or removed. Differential pressure across the filter is too low for the measured exhaust flow — the soot trap no longer works.
s: Check engine light or DPF warning light on

c: VGT vanes stiff or worn
P226F.d: Turbocharger Boost Control B Slow Response: the control module has detected this fault condition. This affects turbo/supercharger boost-pressure control.
s: Charging may not start or interrupts
P226F.t: Turbocharger Boost Control B Slow Response

c: Downstream sensor failed stuck lean
Exhaust leak after catalyst
P2270.d: The downstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 reports a constant lean signal during a forced-rich command from the ECU. Suggests either a sensor that has lost its rich-side response, or a catalyst that is so degraded that no rich exhaust reaches the downstream sensor (cross-check P0420).
P2270.t: O2 Sensor Signal Stuck Lean (Bank 1, Sensor 2)

c: Downstream sensor failed stuck rich
Downstream sensor contaminated
P2271.d: The downstream oxygen sensor on bank 1 reports a constant rich signal during a forced-lean command. Suggests a failed downstream sensor or a sensor contaminated by oil/coolant from upstream engine wear.
P2271.t: O2 Sensor Signal Stuck Rich (Bank 1, Sensor 2)

c: Downstream sensor failed stuck lean
Exhaust leak after catalyst
P2272.d: The downstream oxygen sensor on bank 2 reports a constant lean signal during a forced-rich command from the ECU. Suggests either a sensor that has lost its rich-side response, or a catalyst that is so degraded that no rich exhaust reaches the downstream sensor (cross-check P0420).
P2272.t: O2 Sensor Signal Stuck Lean (Bank 2, Sensor 2)

c: Downstream sensor failed stuck rich
P2273.d: The downstream oxygen sensor on bank 2 reports a constant rich signal during a forced-lean command. Suggests a failed downstream sensor or a sensor contaminated by oil/coolant from upstream engine wear.
P2273.t: O2 Sensor Signal Stuck Rich (Bank 2, Sensor 2)

c: Sensor aged or contaminated
P2274.d: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean (Bank 1 Sensor 3): the control module has detected this fault condition.
P2274.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean (Bank 1 Sensor 3)

c: Sensor coated with carbon or fuel residue
P2275.d: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich (Bank 1 Sensor 3): the control module has detected this fault condition.
P2275.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich (Bank 1 Sensor 3)

c: Sensor aged
P2276.d: O2 sensor at bank 2 sensor 3 reports a lean reading suspiciously stable for too long. Sensor 3 is typically downstream of the second catalyst on systems with three-stage aftertreatment.
P2276.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Lean (Bank 2 Sensor 3)

c: Sensor coated
P2277.d: O2 sensor at bank 2 sensor 3 reports a rich reading suspiciously stable for too long. Sensor 3 is typically downstream of the second catalyst on systems with three-stage aftertreatment; sensor coated with carbon or fuel residue is the typical cause.
P2277.t: O2 Sensor Signal Biased/Stuck Rich (Bank 2 Sensor 3)

c: Wiring crossover after sensor replacement
P2278.d: The PCM detects that the O2 sensor signals from bank 1 sensor 3 and bank 2 sensor 3 are swapped — typically a wiring crossover after sensor replacement.
P2278.t: O2 Sensor Signals Swapped Bank 1 Sensor 3 / Bank 2 Sensor 3

c: Leaking crankcase breather or PCV pressure-regulating valve
Leak at intake manifold, hoses or seals after the air mass sensor
Camshaft timing offset
ECM calibration needing an update
P2279.d: P2279 means the ECM has concluded that air enters the engine without being measured or expected, for example because the air mass sensor, manifold pressure and throttle position no longer agree with its air model. Volkswagen and Audi use it widely. On the 2013 to 2016 Audi A6, A7 and A8 4.0 TFSI, a leaking pressure-regulating valve in the crankcase breather module set P2279 with P0507 and a metallic whistle at warm idle; a fabric-reinforced membrane fixed it. On 2.0 TFSI engines (BPY, CCTA and others) a check valve that did not seal under boost let pressure into the crankcase, logging P2279, P2187 and P1297 with oil leaking at the filler cap. For the 2.5 litre five-cylinder Volkswagen advises checking cam timing first, since a timing offset changes the air the engine draws. Diesels set it too: the Mercedes OM651 2.2 in the international Jeep Compass and Patriot logged it with limp mode and got a new air filter and software.
s: Whistling at idle, unstable or high idle speed

c: Sensor failed
P227A.d: A general electrical fault on barometric pressure sensor C — open, shorted, or out of plausibility. The sensor measures atmospheric pressure for altitude compensation; sensor C is a redundant or secondary unit.

c: Sensor drift
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window

c: Open signal line

P227D.d: Barometric sensor C above upper plausibility — open signal or short to B+. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.

c: Cracked intake boot
P227F.d: Restriction or leak detected in the intake plumbing between the air filter and the mass-air-flow sensor on bank 2 — typically a cracked intake boot or torn filter element.

c: Clogged air filter element
Foreign object in intake
P2280.d: The ECU detects an excessive intake restriction. Either the air filter is heavily clogged or an obstruction in the intake duct is reducing airflow below the expected level.
P2280.t: Air Flow Restriction / Air Filter Restriction

c: Cracked or torn intake hose
Loose hose clamp
P2281.d: The ECU detects unmetered air entering between the mass airflow sensor and the throttle body. The actual airflow into the engine is greater than what the MAF measures, leading to lean conditions.
P2281.t: Air Leak Between MAF and Throttle Body

c: Leaking intake manifold gasket
Cracked vacuum hose
P2282.d: The ECU detects unmetered air entering downstream of the throttle body. Typical sources are leaking intake-manifold gaskets, vacuum hoses or PCV components.
P2282.t: Air Leak Between Throttle Body and Intake Valves

c: Sensor failed
P2283.d: A general electrical fault on the injector control pressure (ICP) sensor — used on HEUI (Hydraulically actuated Electronically controlled Unit Injector) systems on heavy-duty diesel engines such as the Ford Powerstroke 6.0/7.3 and Caterpillar engines. ICP measures the high-pressure oil that actuates the injectors.

c: ICP sensor drift
Leak in high-pressure oil system
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P2284.d: The injector control pressure (ICP) sensor on HEUI diesel systems reports a value that does not match expected operating range or commanded pressure. Affects fuel injection timing and quantity.
P2284.t: Injector Control Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

c: Signal shorted to ground
Open 5 V supply
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2285.d: The voltage of the injector control pressure sensor is below the calibrated minimum. The signal indicates either a short to ground or a sensor that has lost its supply.
P2285.t: Injector Control Pressure Sensor Circuit Low

c: Signal shorted to supply
Open ground wire
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2286.d: The voltage of the injector control pressure sensor is above the calibrated maximum. Likely a short to supply voltage or an open ground in the sensor circuit.
P2286.t: Injector Control Pressure Sensor Circuit High

c: Intermittent connector contact
Sensor failing under load
Harness routed against vibrating component
P2287.d: The injector control pressure sensor signal is intermittently lost or out of range. Often caused by intermittent wiring faults or a failing sensor that drops out under vibration or temperature.

c: IPR stuck closed
P2288.d: ICP is above the upper threshold during operation. Typically the injection pressure regulator (IPR) is stuck closed or the high-pressure oil pump runs above target.

c: Check valve stuck
P2289.d: ICP remains above threshold after engine shutdown — pressure does not bleed off as expected, indicating a stuck check valve or sensor offset error.

Power loss especially at high load or rpm

c: Long-term drift upward

Power loss especially at high load or rpm

c: IPR stuck open
HP oil pump weak
P2290.d: ICP is below the lower threshold — typically IPR stuck open, leaking high-pressure oil rail, or weak HP oil pump.

c: HP oil rail does not pressurise
P2291.d: During cranking, ICP does not build up enough to fire injectors. Typical no-start condition on HEUI engines from a stuck-open IPR or weak HP oil pump.
P2291.t: Injector Control Pressure Too Low - Engine Cranking

c: Air in HP oil rail
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration
Harness routed against vibrating component
P2292.d: ICP signal is unstable or jumps — connector or sensor issue, or air in the high-pressure oil rail. A flow-deviating injector throws off cylinder balance — adjacent cylinders run leaner/richer to compensate, often masking the root cause until the trim limit is hit.

c: Pressure regulator worn or sticking
High-pressure pump weak
Rail pressure sensor drift
P2293.d: The high-pressure fuel pressure regulator (volume control or pressure control valve on a direct-injection rail) is not maintaining commanded pressure. Often the rail-pressure sensor reading drifts away from the setpoint under load.
s: Hard start, no start, or stalling under load
Power loss especially at high load or rpm

c: Regulator solenoid open or shorted
Wiring break to regulator
P2294.d: Electrical fault on the control line to the high-pressure fuel pressure regulator solenoid. Without a working drive signal the rail cannot maintain pressure and the engine may not start or runs in limp-home.
s: Hard start, no start, or stalling under load
Power loss especially at high load or rpm

c: Drive line shorted to ground
Solenoid coil internally shorted
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2295.d: Drive voltage to the second fuel pressure regulator solenoid is below the lower limit. On common-rail diesels and direct-injection petrol engines this affects high-pressure fuel control directly.
s: Hard start, no start, or stalling under load
Power loss especially at high load or rpm
P2295.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator 2 Control Circuit Low

c: Drive line shorted to supply
ECU driver stage failed
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2296.d: Drive voltage to the second fuel pressure regulator solenoid is above the upper limit — short to supply or open ground side. The driver protection trips, regulator falls back to default.
s: Hard start, no start, or stalling under load
Power loss especially at high load or rpm
P2296.t: Fuel Pressure Regulator 2 Control Circuit High

c: Sensor slow or coated
P2297.d: During engine deceleration with closed throttle (DFCO), the O2 sensor on bank 1 sensor 1 should swing fully lean as the manifold fills with fresh air. Code is set when the swing does not happen — usually a slow or coated sensor.
P2297.t: O2 Sensor Out of Range During Deceleration (Bank 1 Sensor 1)

c: Sensor slow or coated
P2298.d: During engine deceleration with closed throttle (DFCO), the O2 sensor on bank 2 sensor 1 should swing fully lean as the manifold fills with fresh air. Code is set when the swing does not happen — usually a slow or coated sensor.
P2298.t: O2 Sensor Out of Range During Deceleration (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

c: Brake light switch stuck on
Accelerator pedal sensor drift
P2299.d: The ECU detects simultaneous brake and accelerator activation beyond a permitted threshold. Modern brake-throttle override safety logic forces idle in this state — usually triggered by a stuck brake light switch or a faulty pedal sensor.
P2299.t: Brake Pedal Position / Accelerator Pedal Position Correlation

c: Regulator leaks or pump weak
P229A.d: Fuel Pressure Regulator B Exceeded Control Limits - Pressure Too Low: the control module has detected this fault condition. This controls fuel-rail pressure.

c: Hose or fitting leak
Leaking pressure regulator, low-pressure shut-off valve or injector seal
Pressure sensor drift faking a pressure loss
P240D.d: The control module has detected a leak on the low-pressure side of the alternative fuel system, the part downstream of the pressure regulator that feeds gas to the fuel rail. On GM's bi-fuel Impala, for example, the regulator brings CNG down from tank pressure to about 470–900 kPa. Monitors usually infer a leak from pressure that falls while the shut-off valves are closed, or from rail pressure that cannot be held. Bi-fuel systems then close the gas valves and continue on gasoline. Natural gas and LPG are flammable, so the lines, fittings and regulator should be checked for leaks before the gas mode is used again.
s: Check engine or alternative fuel warning light on
Gas mode unavailable, engine runs on gasoline only
Gas smell near the tank, lines or engine bay
P240D.t: Alternative Fuel Low Pressure System Leak

c: Hose, fitting or cylinder valve leak
Tank solenoid valve not sealing
Pressure sensor drift faking a pressure loss
P240E.d: The control module has detected a leak on the high-pressure side of the alternative fuel system, between the tank and the pressure regulator, where CNG is stored at up to about 25 MPa (3,600 psi). This section includes the tank valves, the high-pressure lines and filter and the inlet of the regulator. Monitors usually infer a leak from tank or line pressure that drops while no gas is being used. Bi-fuel systems then close the tank solenoid valves and continue on gasoline. Because of the stored pressure and the flammable gas, the system should be checked by a qualified shop before the gas mode is used again.
s: Check engine or alternative fuel warning light on
Gas mode unavailable, engine runs on gasoline only
Gas smell near the tank, lines or engine bay
P240E.t: Alternative Fuel High Pressure System Leak
