P2414.d: Same as P237A but on the upstream sensor B1S1 (pre-catalyst). A drifted or sluggish lambda sensor lets the mixture run lean or rich without correction — fuel economy and emissions suffer immediately.
P2414.t: O2 Sensor Exhaust Sample Error Bank 1 Sensor 1

c: Exhaust leak ahead of or near the sensor (manifold, gasket, flex pipe)
Sensor loose or installed incorrectly
Aged or contaminated wide-band sensor
P2415.d: P2415 indicates that the upstream air-fuel sensor on bank 2 is not reading a representative exhaust sample - typically because outside air is drawn in through a leak near the sensor or the sensor is not seated correctly, so the reading is implausibly lean. VW's 2014 specification books for the Passat, CC and Touareg evaluate the sensor signal voltage against two bands, 3.70-4.81 V and a lower band of 2.51-3.00 V or 3.0-3.70 V, the band being switched with the gain factor used for the sensor characteristic. P2414 is the identical check on bank 1. CARB requires fuel-control sensors to be monitored for every parameter that affects emissions. Expect a warning light and possibly rough running and higher consumption.
s: Ticking exhaust noise when a leak is present
Higher fuel consumption or uneven running
P2415.t: O2 Sensor Exhaust Sample Error (Bank 2 Sensor 1)

c: Sensor 2 and sensor 3 connectors swapped after a repair
Wrong sensor type or harness length fitted in one position
Wires crossed in a harness repair
P2416.d: P2416 means the engine computer concludes that the two downstream oxygen sensors of bank 1 - sensor 2 after the first catalyst and sensor 3 after a second catalyst, as used mainly on SULEV/PZEV vehicles - are connected the wrong way round. No manufacturer publicly documents the detection logic for P2416. By analogy with P0040, which VW sets when the lambda controllers of the two front sensors move beyond their limits in opposite directions, the check compares the expected and actual response of each sensor. The usual cause is swapped connectors after a sensor replacement or harness repair. CARB requires secondary oxygen sensors to be monitored for proper function. P2417 is the bank 2 counterpart, P0041 a swap between banks.
s: Check engine light shortly after an exhaust or sensor repair
Catalyst monitor not completing or giving implausible results
P2416.t: O2 Sensor Signals Swapped (Bank 1 Sensor 2 / Bank 1 Sensor 3)

c: Sensor 2 and sensor 3 connectors swapped after a repair
Wrong sensor type or harness length fitted in one position
Wires crossed in a harness repair
P2417.d: P2417 is set when the engine computer finds that the two downstream oxygen sensors on bank 2 - sensor 2 behind the first catalyst and sensor 3 behind a second one - respond as if their wiring were exchanged. Such three-sensor layouts are typical of V-engines built to SULEV/PZEV limits. No manufacturer publicly documents the detection logic for P2417; the closest documented analogue is P0040, which VW sets when two sensors drive their lambda controllers past opposite limits. In practice the fault follows a repair in which plugs or harness branches were mixed up. CARB requires secondary oxygen sensors to be checked for proper function. P2416 is the same check on bank 1, P0041 a swap between the banks.
s: Check engine light shortly after an exhaust or sensor repair
Catalyst monitor for bank 2 not completing
P2417.t: O2 Sensor Signals Swapped (Bank 2 Sensor 2 / Bank 2 Sensor 3)

c: Broken control wire or unplugged valve connector
Open solenoid coil in the switching valve
Corroded connector near the tank (road salt, splash water)
P2418.d: P2418 is the electrical check of the control circuit of the EVAP switching valve - an extra valve in the evaporative system whose job depends on the design. Ford calls it EVAP switching valve or vapor blocking valve; its 2012 and 2020-2023 OBD summaries check the driver continuously and set P2418 when a short, open or intermittent fault persists for more than 5 s, so at Ford this one code covers all circuit faults. Karma's Revero and GS-6 bulletin uses P2418 for the open control circuit of the rear fuel tank isolation valve driven by the ECM. P2419/P2420 separate low and high circuit faults, P2450 is the mechanical stuck-open fault. While the valve cannot be controlled, leak tests are suspended and fuel vapour odour or refuelling trouble may follow.
s: Possible fuel vapour odour or slow refuelling
P2418.t: EVAP System Switching Valve Control Circuit/Open

c: Control wire shorted to ground (chafed near tank or frame)
Shorted coil in the switching valve or leak check module
Water ingress into the leak check module
P2419.d: P2419 reports that the control circuit of the EVAP switching valve reads low - usually the control line is shorted to ground, or the driver stage measures too little voltage. Karma's Revero/GS-6 bulletin lists P2419 for the rear fuel tank isolation valve controlled by the ECM. Subaru's bulletin 09-103-23 for 2015 Legacy and Outback with an evaporative leak check module (ELCM) tells technicians to look for P2419 and P2420 whenever the ELCM pump fault P2404 is stored, because the switching valve sits in the same module. Ford, by contrast, reports every circuit fault of this valve as P2418. CARB requires output components to be checked for circuit faults. P2420 is the high-side fault, P2418 the open circuit. The leak test is suspended and the warning light comes on.
s: Often stored together with leak detection pump codes
P2419.t: EVAP System Switching Valve Control Circuit Low

c: Harness swapped during repair
P241A.d: The pre- and post-catalyst lambda signals on bank 1 are swapped - the upstream sensor responds like a downstream sensor and vice versa. Typically the harness was reversed during a sensor change.
P241A.t: O2 Sensor Signals Swapped Bank 1 Sensor 1 and Sensor 2

c: Harness swapped during repair
P241B.d: The pre- and post-catalyst lambda signals on bank 2 are swapped - the upstream sensor responds like a downstream sensor and vice versa. Typically the harness was reversed during a sensor change.
P241B.t: O2 Sensor Signals Swapped Bank 2 Sensor 1 and Sensor 2

c: Ice in throttle bore
P241C.d: The throttle actuator on bank 2 cannot move because of ice formation - typical for very cold ambient temperature with humid intake. Engine de-ices on warm-up.
s: Reduced throttle response, possible limp mode
Idle too high or too low
P241C.t: Throttle Actuator Control System Ice Blockage Bank 2

c: AdBlue tank empty or out of compliance
P241D.d: The SCR inducement strategy (mandatory regulatory measure to enforce AdBlue refilling and emissions compliance) has reached the final stage and shut down the engine. Refill AdBlue and clear inducement fault to restart.
s: Check engine light or NOx warning on
Possible no-start countdown after ignore period

c: Valve stuck closed
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play
P241E.d: The valve that routes engine coolant to heat the AdBlue lines is stuck closed - AdBlue lines do not warm up and may freeze in cold weather, blocking dosing.
s: Check engine light or NOx warning on
Possible no-start countdown after ignore period
P241E.t: Reductant Heater Coolant Control Valve Stuck Closed

c: Cooler fouled with soot or scaled
P241F.d: The temperature drop across EGR cooler B is below the calibrated threshold - cooler is fouled with soot, has internal scaling, or coolant flow is restricted. Recirculated gas reaches the intake hotter than designed, increasing NOx and combustion temperatures.
P241F.t: EGR Cooler B Efficiency Below Threshold

c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Switching valve coil with too low resistance (overcurrent)
Faulty driver stage in the ECM
P2420.d: P2420 means the control circuit of the EVAP switching valve reads high - typically a short to battery voltage on the control line or an overcurrent detected by the driver stage. Karma lists P2420 for the rear fuel tank isolation valve of the Revero and GS-6, which the ECM operates, and Subaru's bulletin 09-103-23 for 2015 Legacy/Outback with an evaporative leak check module (ELCM) includes P2420 among the codes to check alongside the pump fault P2404. Ford instead reports all circuit faults of its switching valve as P2418. CARB requires output components to be monitored for circuit faults. P2419 is the low-side fault and P2418 the open circuit. The evap leak monitor cannot run until the circuit is repaired.
P2420.t: EVAP System Switching Valve Control Circuit High

c: Vent valve mechanically stuck open
Dust/debris preventing valve seat
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
P2421.d: The evaporative emission system vent valve does not close on command. The ECU detects that the evap system cannot hold pressure or vacuum because the canister is permanently vented to atmosphere.
s: Possible smell of fuel near tank or engine bay

c: Vent valve seized closed
Drive circuit open
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
P2422.d: The vent valve at the canister end of the EVAP system cannot open. Without ambient air entering the canister, fresh fuel cannot purge the stored vapors and refueling may trigger ORVR issues. Common with rusted or rodent-damaged vent valves.
s: Possible smell of fuel near tank or engine bay
P2422.t: EVAP Canister Vent Valve Stuck Closed

c: Catalyst aging / thermal damage
Oxygen sensor drift
P2423.d: The ECU determines that the hydrocarbon adsorption catalyst on bank 1 no longer holds enough HC during cold start to meet emission targets. Often due to ageing or thermal damage.
s: Sulfur (rotten egg) smell from exhaust under load
P2423.t: HC Adsorption Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 1

c: Catalyst adsorber aged
P2424.d: The hydrocarbon adsorption catalyst on bank 2 - which traps HC during cold-start until the main catalyst lights off - is degraded; HC slip during cold start is above the calibrated threshold.
s: Sulfur (rotten egg) smell from exhaust under load
P2424.t: HC Adsorption Catalyst Efficiency Below Threshold Bank 2

c: Open in valve or wiring
Pin pushed back out of connector body
Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor
P2425.d: The valve that admits coolant flow to the EGR cooler has an open control circuit - cooling cannot be enabled and EGR temperatures stay too high.
P2425.t: EGR Cooling Valve Control Circuit Open

c: Control line shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P2426.d: Same as P2425 with the control line shorted to ground. EGR mixes inert exhaust into intake to lower combustion peak temperature — too little raises NOx, too much causes misfires and rough running.
P2426.t: EGR Cooling Valve Control Circuit Low

c: Control line shorted to supply
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P2427.d: Same as P2425 with the control line shorted to supply. EGR mixes inert exhaust into intake to lower combustion peak temperature — too little raises NOx, too much causes misfires and rough running.
P2427.t: EGR Cooling Valve Control Circuit High

c: DPF blocked or active regeneration
P2428.d: An EGT sensor on bank 1 reports a temperature above the safety threshold for prolonged operation - typical for blocked DPF, restricted exhaust, or excessive fuelling. Risk of catalyst, DPF or turbo damage.
P2428.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Too High Bank 1

c: DPF blocked or active regeneration
P2429.d: An EGT sensor on bank 2 reports a temperature above the safety threshold for prolonged operation - typical for blocked DPF, restricted exhaust, or excessive fuelling. Risk of catalyst, DPF or turbo damage.
P2429.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Too High Bank 2

c: Open in sensor or wiring
P242A.d: A general circuit fault is detected on the EGT sensor at bank 1 sensor 3 (typically just downstream of the turbo or before the catalyst). The ECU loses thermal protection feedback for the catalyst and DPF.
P242A.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Bank 1 Sensor 3

c: Sensor element drifted
P242B.d: Same as P242A with the signal in plausible range yet not matching the engine model.
P242B.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Range or Performance Bank 1 Sensor 3

c: Signal shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P242C.d: Same as P242A with the signal voltage below the plausible range. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P242C.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Low Bank 1 Sensor 3

c: Signal shorted to supply
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P242D.d: Same as P242A with the signal voltage above the plausible range. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P242D.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit High Bank 1 Sensor 3

c: Intermittent contact at connector
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration
Harness routed against vibrating component
P242E.d: Same as P242A with intermittent or erratic signal. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P242E.t: Exhaust Gas Temperature Sensor Circuit Intermittent or Erratic Bank 1 Sensor 3

c: DPF full of ash
P242F.d: The diesel particulate filter on bank 1 reports backpressure attributable to ash (non-combustible residue from oil and fuel additives, not removable by regeneration). The filter has reached the end of its service life and needs cleaning or replacement.
s: Check engine light or DPF warning light on
P242F.t: Particulate Filter Restriction Ash Accumulation Bank 1

c: Open in sensor or wiring
P2430.d: A general circuit fault on the secondary air injection (AIR) system flow or pressure sensor on bank 1 - the sensor that verifies air pump flow during cold-start enrichment compensation.
P2430.t: AIR System Air Flow or Pressure Sensor Circuit Bank 1

c: Defective SAI sensor
SAI sensor wiring fault
P2431.d: The ECU detects a general fault in the secondary air injection system air flow or pressure sensor circuit. The diagnostic cannot verify proper SAI operation.
P2431.t: Secondary Air Injection System Air Flow/Pressure Sensor Circuit

c: Clogged SAI passages
SAI sensor drift
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P2432.d: The signal of the SAI air flow or pressure sensor is implausible during operation. The reading does not change as expected when the air pump is commanded.
P2432.t: Secondary Air Injection System Air Flow/Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

c: Signal shorted to supply
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P2433.d: Same as P2430 with the signal voltage above the plausible range. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P2433.t: AIR System Air Flow or Pressure Sensor Circuit High Bank 1

c: Intermittent contact at connector
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration
Harness routed against vibrating component
P2434.d: Same as P2430 with intermittent or erratic signal. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P2434.t: AIR System Air Flow or Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent or Erratic Bank 1

c: Open in sensor or wiring
P2435.d: AIR System Air Flow or Pressure Sensor Circuit Bank 2: an electrical fault is present in the circuit.
P2435.t: AIR System Air Flow or Pressure Sensor Circuit Bank 2

c: Sensor element drifted
P2436.d: Same as P2430 on bank 2 with the signal in plausible range yet not matching the engine model.
P2436.t: AIR System Air Flow or Pressure Sensor Circuit Range or Performance Bank 2

c: Signal shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P2437.d: AIR System Air Flow or Pressure Sensor Circuit Low Bank 2: the signal voltage is below the expected range. Often a short to ground or high resistance in the wiring.
P2437.t: AIR System Air Flow or Pressure Sensor Circuit Low Bank 2

c: Signal shorted to supply
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P2438.d: Same as P2433 on bank 2. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P2438.t: AIR System Air Flow or Pressure Sensor Circuit High Bank 2

c: Intermittent contact at connector
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration
Harness routed against vibrating component
P2439.d: Same as P2434 on bank 2. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P2439.t: AIR System Air Flow or Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent or Erratic Bank 2

c: DPF full of ash
P243A.d: The diesel particulate filter on bank 2 reports backpressure attributable to ash (non-combustible residue from oil and fuel additives, not removable by regeneration). The filter has reached the end of its service life and needs cleaning or replacement.
s: Check engine light or DPF warning light on
P243A.t: Particulate Filter Restriction Ash Accumulation Bank 2

c: DPF heavily clogged
P243B.d: Particulate Filter Restriction Forced Limited Power Bank 2: the control module has detected this fault condition.
s: Check engine light or DPF warning light on
P243B.t: Particulate Filter Restriction Forced Limited Power Bank 2

c: Short-trip operation
P243C.d: The DPF on bank 2 needs regeneration more often than calibrated. Possible causes are an oil-burning engine, fuel-injector leak, short-trip operation, or a sensor offset.
s: Check engine light or DPF warning light on

c: Regeneration too slow
P243D.d: Regenerations on bank 2 take longer than calibrated to complete - typically a low EGT during the cycle (cold weather, short trips) or a partially aged catalyst before the DPF.
s: Check engine light or DPF warning light on

c: Regeneration aborted before completion
P243E.d: Particulate Filter Regeneration Incomplete Bank 2: the control module has detected this fault condition.
s: Check engine light or DPF warning light on

c: Soot loading critical
P243F.d: Particulate Filter Restriction Soot Accumulation Too High Bank 2: the control module has detected this fault condition.
s: Check engine light or DPF warning light on
P243F.t: Particulate Filter Restriction Soot Accumulation Too High Bank 2

c: Switching valve stuck open by carbon or corrosion
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play
P2440.d: The switching/check valve in the secondary air injection plumbing on bank 1 is stuck in the open position. With the valve permanently open, exhaust gas can back-feed into the air pump and corrode it, while the downstream O2 sensor sees ambient air constantly.
P2440.t: Secondary Air Injection System Switching Valve Stuck Open (Bank 1)

c: Switching valve stuck closed by carbon
Vacuum control line leak
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
P2441.d: The switching valve on bank 1 will not open when commanded, so no secondary air reaches the exhaust during cold start. Catalyst light-off is delayed and emissions during the cold-start window rise.
P2441.t: Secondary Air Injection System Switching Valve Stuck Closed (Bank 1)

c: Switching valve stuck open
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play
P2442.d: The switching/check valve in the secondary air injection plumbing on bank 2 is stuck in the open position. With the valve permanently open, exhaust gas can back-feed into the air pump and corrode it, while the downstream O2 sensor sees ambient air constantly.
P2442.t: Secondary Air Injection System Switching Valve Stuck Open (Bank 2)

c: Switching valve stuck closed
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play
P2443.d: The switching valve on bank 2 will not open when commanded, so no secondary air reaches the exhaust during cold start. Catalyst light-off is delayed and emissions during the cold-start window rise.
P2443.t: Secondary Air Injection System Switching Valve Stuck Closed (Bank 2)

c: Pump seized by corrosion
Pump relay failed
Pump fuse blown
P2444.d: The secondary-air pump does not run when commanded during cold start. Often a seized pump (after exhaust back-feed corroded the impeller), a blown fuse, or a failed relay.
P2444.t: Secondary Air Injection System Pump Stuck Off (Bank 1)

c: Pump relay stuck closed
Drive line shorted to supply
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
P2445.d: The secondary-air pump continues to run after the cold-start window, when the ECU has commanded it off. Usually a stuck-closed relay welding the pump permanently to battery voltage.
P2445.t: Secondary Air Injection System Pump Stuck On (Bank 1)

c: Pump seized from condensate corrosion
Relay failed open
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
P2446.d: Bank 2 secondary air pump does not deliver air when commanded. The catalyst light-off process is delayed and cold-start emissions rise.
P2446.t: Secondary Air Injection Pump Stuck Off (Bank 2)

c: Relay stuck closed
Driver stage shorted on
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
P2447.d: Bank 2 secondary air pump runs continuously. Either a stuck-on relay or a shorted control output keeps the pump powered when it should be off.
P2447.t: Secondary Air Injection Pump Stuck On (Bank 2)

c: AIR switching valve stuck open
P2448.d: The secondary air injection system on bank 1 delivers more flow than calibrated when the pump is commanded on - typically a stuck-open switching valve allowing free flow.
P2448.t: AIR System High Air Flow Bank 1

c: AIR switching valve stuck open
P2449.d: The secondary air injection system on bank 2 delivers more flow than calibrated when the pump is commanded on - typically a stuck-open switching valve allowing free flow.
P2449.t: AIR System High Air Flow Bank 2

c: Cracked or missing DPF substrate
Leak in pressure sensing line
P244A.d: The differential pressure across the DPF is below the calibrated minimum even at higher loads. Often a sign of a damaged or missing filter substrate, or a leak in the sensing line.
s: Check engine light or DPF warning light on
P244A.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Differential Pressure Too Low

c: Sensor zero-point drift
P244B.d: At engine off, the DPF differential pressure sensor does not return to zero within the allowed offset window. The static offset is too large to be ignored.
s: Check engine light or DPF warning light on
P244B.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Differential Pressure Sensor Offset

c: Engine load too low for regeneration
P244C.d: During an attempted regeneration of the bank 1 DPF the EGT did not reach the temperature window needed for soot oxidation. Regeneration could not start or was held. Driving in higher load is needed.
s: Check engine light or DPF warning light on
P244C.t: Exhaust Temperature Too Low For Particulate Filter Regeneration Bank 1

c: Engine load too high - filter overheating risk
P244D.d: Same as P244C with the EGT too high - regeneration paused to protect filter substrate from melt damage.
s: Check engine light or DPF warning light on
P244D.t: Exhaust Temperature Too High For Particulate Filter Regeneration Bank 1

c: Engine load too low for regeneration
P244E.d: During an attempted regeneration of the bank 2 DPF the EGT did not reach the temperature window needed for soot oxidation. Regeneration could not start or was held. Driving in higher load is needed.
s: Check engine light or DPF warning light on
P244E.t: Exhaust Temperature Too Low For Particulate Filter Regeneration Bank 2

c: Engine load too high - filter overheating risk
s: Check engine light or DPF warning light on
P244F.t: Exhaust Temperature Too High For Particulate Filter Regeneration Bank 2

c: Mechanical failure of valve
Contamination preventing motion
P2450.d: The EVAP switching valve does not respond to commands as expected. The valve is mechanically stuck or unable to switch between purge and vent paths, blocking proper leak diagnosis.
s: Possible smell of fuel near tank or engine bay

c: Valve stuck closed
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play
P2451.d: The EVAP switching valve - which directs vapor flow between purge and leak-detection paths - is stuck in the closed position. The diagnostic cycle cannot complete.
s: Possible smell of fuel near tank or engine bay
P2451.t: EVAP System Switching Valve Stuck Closed

c: Sensor offset drifted or moisture inside the sensor
Sensor hose blocked by soot or condensate
Corroded connector or terminals
P2452.d: The pressure sensor A of the particulate filter, usually a differential sensor with hoses to the filter inlet and outlet, tells the ECM how loaded the filter is. Despite its generic circuit title, P2452 is in practice an offset check made when no exhaust flows. Ford's 2023 diesels run it in after-run and set the code when the sensor still reads more than 1 kPa. GM's 2018 diesels check the filter inlet pressure at the start of the drive cycle, after at least 10 s engine off, and set it as a Type B code when the offset is too big. A sensor that has drifted, moisture inside it or a hose holding pressure all give such an offset. Audi saw P2452 together with P2453, P2454, P2456 and P2002 on the 2009 to 2011 Q7 TDI and traced it to moisture entering the differential pressure sensor G505 through poor internal sealing; the fix was a sensor with better sealing. The soot model then works with wrong values, so regeneration timing suffers.
s: Regeneration too early, too late or inhibited
P2452.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit

c: Sensor hose disconnected, split, kinked or blocked
Sensor skewed or stuck, for example from moisture ingress
High resistance in sensor wiring or ECM grounds
P2453.d: P2453 means the particulate filter pressure signal is electrically fine but does not behave like a real filter pressure. Manufacturers use two kinds of test. With the engine off there should be almost no pressure difference: GM's 2009 Duramax fails above 4.1 kPa, the 2014 Cruze 2.0 diesel above 3.2 kPa in after-run, and the Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) checks once at least 60 s after shutdown. With the engine running the signal has to follow changes in exhaust flow: the Duramax expects it to rise and fall when the flow changes by more than 200 m³/h per second, and Ford's 2023 diesels fail a reading under 1 kPa at 500 m³/h or more, which points to a disconnected or split hose. Saab adds that kinked braided hoses do not recover their shape. Audi (Q7 TDI) found moisture in sensor G505, Chrysler (2.8 diesel) checked sensor and connector, and Stellantis found open circuits and bad PCM grounds. Without a valid signal the soot load is estimated, often followed by P2463.
s: DPF warning, regeneration inhibited or too frequent
P2453.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance

c: Signal wire open or shorted to ground, connector unplugged
Internal sensor failure, for example from moisture
5 V reference shorted by another sensor on the same supply
P2454.d: The particulate filter pressure sensor is a three-wire part: the ECM feeds it 5 V and ground and reads a signal that rises with the pressure difference across the filter. P2454 means that signal sits below the lowest plausible value. Ford's 2023 diesels fail below 0.10 V within 2 s, where 0.45 V corresponds to zero pressure difference; GM's 2018 diesels fail below 3 % of the supply with 80 of 160 samples. On the Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) an open circuit sets P2454 as well as a short to ground, after 2 s, so a disconnected plug reads low there. A shorted 5 V reference can also pull the signal down and usually sets P0641 alongside. Audi (Q7 TDI 2009 to 2011) saw P2454 from moisture inside sensor G505, and Chrysler lists it on the 2.8 diesel Town and Country with a sensor and connector check. Without the signal the filter load is estimated and regeneration may be limited.
P2454.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit Low

c: Signal wire shorted to 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor low-reference (ground) circuit open
Internal sensor failure
P2455.d: P2455 means the particulate filter pressure sensor signal sits above the highest plausible value, at the top of the 5 V range. Ford's 2023 diesels and the Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) both use 4.9 V as the limit, Ford within 2 s and Saab after 1 s; on Ford's 6.7 L the signal follows roughly 0.082 V per kPa above 0.45 V, so 4.9 V would be about 54 kPa. Typical faults are a signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage, or an open low-reference (ground) circuit, which Saab lists among the circuit faults for this code. A real pressure that high from a blocked filter is unusual and would normally first raise soot codes such as P2463. Chrysler lists P2455 on the 2.8 diesel Town and Country with a sensor and connector check. The ECM falls back to a modelled soot load and may limit regeneration.
P2455.t: Diesel Particulate Filter Pressure Sensor A Circuit High

c: Connector intermittent
Wiring chafed against bracket
Harness routed against vibrating component
P2456.d: The DPF differential-pressure sensor delivers an intermittent signal — usually a marginal connector or a chafed wiring section that breaks contact during temperature or vibration.
s: Check engine light or DPF warning light on
P2456.t: DPF Differential Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent

c: Cooler internally clogged with soot
Cooler cracked, coolant entering exhaust
P2457.d: The EGR cooler does not lower exhaust gas temperature as expected — typically internal coolant fouling, a partial blockage, or a cracked cooler that mixes coolant with exhaust gas.

c: ECM calibration that needs an update (documented by Volkswagen)
Short trips that keep regenerations from finishing
Oxidation catalyst too weak to reach regeneration temperature
P2458.d: During a regeneration the engine raises exhaust temperature, mostly by late post-injection burned in the oxidation catalyst, until the soot in the particulate filter oxidises. P2458 means a regeneration took longer than the calibrated limit, so the filter was not cleaned in the expected time. CARB asks diesel OBD to detect regenerations that do not complete as intended. On the Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) the ECM runs the check with coolant at 73 to 96 °C and sets the code when regeneration times are too long; it is a Type C code there, stored without the MIL. Volkswagen saw P2458 with the MIL on 2011 Jetta and Golf 2.0 TDI (CJAA) and fixed it with an ECM software update, so the calibration is worth checking before parts are replaced. Otherwise the regeneration is slowed by low exhaust temperature, a weak oxidation catalyst, faulty temperature or pressure readings, or trips too short to finish. P2459 covers regenerations that happen too often.
s: DPF warning or MIL, depending on the manufacturer
Cooling fan and raised idle running on after shutdown

c: High soot output from the engine (injectors, EGR, air leaks)
Differential pressure reading too high (sensor, blocked or swapped hoses)
Filter loaded with ash or defective from manufacture
P2459.d: P2459 means the particulate filter is being regenerated more often than the calibration expects. CARB requires diesel OBD to flag regeneration so frequent that emissions would exceed the limit; frequent regeneration also dilutes oil and costs fuel. Ford's 2023 diesels set it when the average distance between completed regenerations falls below about 40 km. GM's 2014 Cruze 2.0 diesel compares the soot load that triggered a regeneration with a table built from the engine-out soot model, and GM's 2018 diesels flag a ratio of 10 or more between the pressure-based soot estimate and the engine-out model, citing dirty combustion, a leak in the intake or exhaust, or an inefficient filter. The Opel/GM 2.0 CDTi in the Saab 9-5 (2010) instead counts too many interrupted regenerations, as a Type C code. Stellantis replaced the filter on 2022 to 2023 Ram 2500/3500 6.7 Cummins over a manufacturing issue; left alone, the engine eventually derates.
s: Higher fuel consumption and rising oil level
Reduced engine power if the fault persists

c: Open in valve or wiring
Pin pushed back out of connector body
Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor
P245A.d: The EGR cooler bypass valve on bank 1 - routes EGR around the cooler during cold-start to keep cabin and engine warm-up fast - has an open control circuit.
P245A.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit Open Bank 1

c: Bypass valve sticking due to soot
P245B.d: Same as P245A with the actuator electrically intact yet not delivering the commanded position. EGR mixes inert exhaust into intake to lower combustion peak temperature — too little raises NOx, too much causes misfires and rough running.
P245B.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit Range or Performance Bank 1

c: Control line shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P245C.d: Same as P245A with the control line shorted to ground. EGR mixes inert exhaust into intake to lower combustion peak temperature — too little raises NOx, too much causes misfires and rough running.
P245C.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit Low Bank 1

c: Control line shorted to supply
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P245D.d: Same as P245A with the control line shorted to supply. EGR mixes inert exhaust into intake to lower combustion peak temperature — too little raises NOx, too much causes misfires and rough running.
P245D.t: EGR Cooler Bypass Control Circuit High Bank 1

c: Open in sensor or wiring

P2463.d: P2463 means the soot load in the particulate filter has passed the level at which the engine still regenerates it on its own. GM's 2009 Duramax sets it at 70 g or more for 5 minutes, the 2014 Cruze 2.0 diesel at more than 32 g for 30 s, both as Type A codes; GM's 2018 diesels use the pressure-based soot model with 120 failures in 150 samples. On the Cruze the ECM then turns on the MIL, reduces engine power and blocks normal regeneration, so a dealer service regeneration is needed. GM's bulletin on the related driver messages notes that the filter cleans itself about once per tank and needs driving above 50 km/h; extended idling and stop-and-go traffic keep it from finishing. The underlying cause is not always the driving: Stellantis traced P2463 with P2453 to broken differential pressure sensor wiring and PCM grounds, Mack to a failed aftertreatment fuel doser. Check those before regenerating, or the code returns.

MIL on and reduced engine power

c: Purge valve sticking
P24DC.d: Same as P24DB with the actuator electrically intact yet not delivering the commanded purge flow. Valve B is the second purge valve on systems that use two. The purge valve opens a path so that, after the engine is switched off, the dosing system can draw the remaining urea solution out of the dosing valve and lines; this protects them from freezing, as DEF freezes at about −11 °C, and from crystal deposits. If the valve cannot be controlled, the lines may stay filled, which risks frozen or blocked dosing parts and later SCR faults.
s: Check engine light or NOx warning on
