c: Corroded or loose sensor connector
Chafed or vibrating harness near the exhaust
Aged ceramic sensor element drifting under heat cycles
P24E5.d: The ammonia (NH3) slip sensor downstream of the SCR catalyst delivers an intermittent or erratic signal. The ECM expects a smooth voltage proportional to ammonia concentration in the tailpipe — sudden jumps, dropouts or noise mean the wiring, connector or sensing element is failing. Used to close-loop the AdBlue/DEF dosing strategy.

c: Burnt-out heater winding inside the sensor
Broken wire or unplugged connector
Failed heater driver stage in the dosing module
P24E6.d: The heater inside the ammonia (NH3) slip sensor warms the sensing cell to operating temperature so it can read tailpipe ammonia. The ECM detects an open in the heater control circuit — no current flows when the heater should be active, so the sensor never reaches its working point and SCR closed-loop control is suspended.

c: Heater control wire shorted to ground
Internal short across the heater element
Low-side driver pulled down in the control module
P24E7.d: The heater control circuit of the ammonia (NH3) slip sensor reads below the expected voltage range. Either the wiring is shorted to ground or the heater driver in the SCR/dosing module is stuck low. The sensor element never warms up, NH3 readings stay invalid and the SCR strategy falls back to open-loop dosing.

c: Heater control wire shorted to battery voltage
High-side driver stuck on
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P24E8.d: The heater control circuit of the NH3 slip sensor reads above the expected voltage range. Typically a short to battery voltage or a heater driver stuck high — duty-cycle control is lost, the heater either runs continuously or not at all, and the sensor element risks overheating before the ECM disables it.

c: Aged heater with increased resistance
Poor thermal contact between heater and sensing cell
P24E9.d: The heater of the NH3 slip sensor is electrically intact, but the warm-up profile or steady-state temperature feedback does not match the ECM model. The sensor takes too long to reach operating temperature or drifts away from setpoint, so SCR closed-loop control is delayed or held off.

c: Open or shorted supply wire
Failing supply rail inside the dosing module
P24EA.d: The supply rail that powers the NH3 slip sensor electronics (typically 5 V or 12 V from the dosing/SCR module) is out of tolerance. Without a stable supply the sensor cannot deliver a valid ammonia reading, and the ECM disables the closed-loop SCR strategy.

c: Supply line shorted to ground
High-resistance ground at the SCR module
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P24EB.d: The NH3 slip sensor supply voltage drops below the lower limit. Usually a partial short to ground in the supply line, an undersized ground path with high resistance, or an internal supply collapse in the SCR/dosing module. Sensor output is held invalid until the supply recovers.
P24EB.t: NH3 Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit Low

c: Supply line shorted to battery voltage
Failed voltage regulator in the dosing module
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P24EC.d: The NH3 slip sensor supply voltage rises above the upper limit. Either the supply is shorted to battery voltage or an internal regulator in the dosing module has failed open. The sensor electronics may be damaged if the condition persists, so the ECM disables the input.
P24EC.t: NH3 Sensor Supply Voltage Circuit High

c: New sensor installed but not coded/learned to the ECM
Corrupted calibration memory after voltage drop
Module software outdated, reflash may resolve
P24ED.d: The NH3 slip sensor stores its individual calibration coefficients in non-volatile memory (EEPROM/flash). The ECM cannot read valid calibration values — either checksum fails, the memory is empty after replacement, or communication with the sensor electronics is broken. Without the trim values the raw ammonia reading is unreliable.

c: Internal processor or firmware fault
Brown-out from supply voltage dips
Module software outdated, reflash may resolve
P24EE.d: The microcontroller inside the smart NH3 slip sensor reports an internal performance fault — failed self-test, watchdog reset, or out-of-range plausibility checks. The sensor cannot guarantee its output value, the ECM marks the channel invalid and disables SCR closed-loop control on this branch.

c: Broken wake-up wire or unplugged connector
Failed wake-up input stage in the module
Pin pushed back out of connector body
P24EF.d: The wake-up line that brings a sleeping ECU back from low-power mode is open. Many networks use a dedicated hardware wake-up wire (door-latch trigger, terminal 15, CAN wake-up) so modules can stay asleep with the ignition off. Without it, the module either fails to wake up at start-up or stays awake and drains the battery.

c: Wake-up wire shorted to ground
Door, hood or terminal switch stuck closed
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P24F0.d: The wake-up input on the control module reads stuck low — usually a short to ground or a permanently asserted wake signal. The module either keeps waking up unnecessarily and drains the battery, or it cannot distinguish a real wake event from the stuck low level.

c: Wake-up wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P24F1.d: The wake-up input reads above the expected range — typically a short to battery voltage. The module sees a permanent wake-up request, never enters sleep mode and drains the battery while parked.

c: One sensor drifting outside tolerance
Residual heat in the charge-air cooler after a hot soak
P24F2.d: After a long key-off soak both the EGR temperature sensor and the charge-air cooler outlet temperature sensor must read approximately the same ambient temperature. The ECM compares them and detects an implausible delta. One of the sensors drifts, is wired wrong, or is exposed to a heat source the model does not know about.
P24F2.t: EGR Temperature/Charge Air Cooler Temperature Correlation

c: One temperature sensor drifting outside tolerance
Recently active reductant tank heater warming the tank above ambient
P24F3.d: After a long key-off soak the AdBlue/DEF tank temperature and the fuel tank temperature should read close to each other (both at ambient). The ECM detects an implausible spread, which usually means one of the two sensors drifts, is wired wrong, or has a heat source nearby that the plausibility model does not account for.
s: Check engine light or NOx warning on
Possible no-start countdown after ignore period

c: Aged sensor element with reduced response speed
Soot clogging the protective tube
P24F4.d: The pre-catalyst NOx sensor on bank 1 (sensor 1) reacts too slowly when NOx in the exhaust drops from a high to a low level — for example after a fuel cut or transition into low-load. Aged ceramic cells, soot deposits or condensation inside the sensor protective tube slow the diffusion of NOx to the measuring element.
s: Check engine light or NOx warning on
Possible no-start countdown after ignore period
P24F4.t: NOx Sensor Delayed Response - High to Low Bank 1 Sensor 1

c: Aged sensor element with reduced response speed
Soot clogging the protective tube
P24F5.d: The post-catalyst NOx sensor on bank 1 (sensor 2) reacts too slowly when NOx in the exhaust drops from a high to a low level. Same failure mechanism as the upstream sensor — aged element, soot or condensate — but post-catalyst the consequence is a degraded SCR conversion-efficiency monitor.
s: Check engine light or NOx warning on
Possible no-start countdown after ignore period
P24F5.t: NOx Sensor Delayed Response - High to Low Bank 1 Sensor 2

c: Mechanically stuck open valve from soot or coking
Broken return spring
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
P24F6.d: On systems that inject HC dosing fuel or AIR-assisted reductant into the aftertreatment, a purge valve clears the line after each dosing event. The ECM detects the valve stuck open — pressure or flow does not build up against a closed valve, so the dosing line cannot be charged. Common on diesel HC-doser hardware (DPF regen support).
P24F6.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Stuck Open

c: Stuck closed by deposits or seized armature
Open coil — valve never opens
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
P24F7.d: The aftertreatment HC dosing or reductant purge valve is stuck closed. The ECM commands purge but the line is not cleared, leaving residual fluid that can foul nozzles or freeze in cold weather. Subsequent dosing events also fail because backpressure does not match the model.
P24F7.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Stuck Closed

c: Open or shorted control wire
Failed driver stage in the dosing module
P24F8.d: General electrical fault in the control circuit of the aftertreatment fuel/air purge valve. The ECM cannot drive the valve coil according to plausibility checks — open, short or unexpected feedback voltage. Until cleared, dosing line purge is suspended.
P24F8.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Control Circuit

c: Aged solenoid with weakened magnetic force
Coked armature with increased friction
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P24F9.d: The valve coil is electrically intact, but the response (current rise time, return-current decay, position feedback) does not match the ECM model. Typical for solenoids losing magnetic strength after long thermal cycling, or armatures with increased friction from coking.
P24F9.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Control Circuit Range/Performance

c: Control wire shorted to ground
Failed low-side driver stuck on
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P24FA.d: The control circuit of the aftertreatment purge valve reads stuck low — usually a short to ground or a failed low-side driver. The valve is energised continuously when it should be off, or the diagnostic feedback voltage is pulled below threshold.
P24FA.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Control Circuit Low

c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Open ground or open coil
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P24FB.d: The control circuit of the aftertreatment purge valve reads stuck high — typically a short to battery voltage or an open ground/return path. The driver cannot pull the line low to actuate the valve.
P24FB.t: Exhaust Aftertreatment Fuel Air Purge Valve Control Circuit High

c: Partial short across the heater element
Driver overheating due to poor cooling on the module
P24FC.d: The PM (soot) sensor heater is driven by a current-limited stage so it can burn off accumulated soot before each measurement. The driver reports current or junction temperature above the safe limit and disables itself. Often a partial short across the heater or sensor element after coolant intrusion.
P24FC.t: Particulate Matter Sensor Heater Control Circuit Driver Current/Temperature Too High

c: Incorrect or non-OEM DPF installed
Coding mismatch after part replacement
P24FD.d: The ECM identifies the installed particulate filter A as the wrong part — backpressure signature, regeneration efficiency or coded part-number do not match the application. Common after a non-OEM aftermarket DPF or a wrong-application replacement.
s: Check engine light or DPF warning light on

c: Incorrect or non-OEM SCR catalyst installed
Coding mismatch after part replacement
P24FE.d: The ECM identifies the installed SCR catalyst as the wrong part — NOx conversion efficiency, NH3 storage capacity or coded part-number do not match the expected application. Typical after fitting a non-OEM SCR brick or after a coding error following replacement.
s: Sulfur (rotten egg) smell from exhaust under load

c: Tank heater stuck on
Heat soak from exhaust or engine bay
P24FF.d: The temperature of the AdBlue/DEF in the dosing system exceeds the safe limit — risk of thermal decomposition (NH3/biuret formation) and clogged dosing nozzles. Often caused by a stuck-on tank heater, a stalled coolant return or proximity to a hot exhaust component.
s: Check engine light or NOx warning on
Possible no-start countdown after ignore period

c: L-terminal shorted to ground
Alternator regulator failed
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2500.d: The L-terminal feedback line from the alternator (charging warning lamp circuit) reads below the lower limit. The lamp may stay on, and battery voltage may drift if regulation feedback is also affected.

c: L-terminal shorted to supply
Alternator regulator failed
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2501.d: The L-terminal feedback from the alternator reads above the upper limit — short to supply or open ground side. Charging diagnostics cannot run cleanly.

c: Alternator output fault
Voltage regulator fault
P2502.d: The ECU detects an out-of-range charging system voltage without specifying high or low. Indicates a generic charging fault that requires further sub-code investigation.

c: Weak alternator output
Faulty voltage regulator
Slipping drive belt
P2503.d: The ECU detects that battery voltage during operation stays below the regulated target. The alternator output is insufficient to maintain charge under load, eventually leading to battery depletion.

c: Faulty voltage regulator
Poor alternator ground
P2504.d: The ECU detects a battery voltage above the regulated upper limit. The voltage regulator is not limiting alternator output, risking damage to electronic modules and battery overcharge.

c: Failed main relay
Blown fuse on the ECM power feed
Corroded connector pin at the ECM
P2505.d: The ECM/PCM monitors the main switched battery feed (typically terminal 15 / ignition-switched supply via the main relay). A general fault is reported — either the input is missing entirely or it does not match the expected timing relative to ignition state. Engine may not start or stay running.

c: Aged main relay contacts with rising contact resistance
Weak battery sagging during crank
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P2506.d: The switched-battery input to the ECM/PCM is present, but the level or transient behaviour is out of plausibility — sagging during cranking, slow ramp-up after main-relay close, or noisy. Often caused by aged main relay contacts or a weak battery feed under load.

c: Main relay does not pull in
Open supply wire
Severely discharged battery
P2507.d: The ECM/PCM switched-battery input reads below threshold while the ignition is on. Either the main relay does not close, the supply wire is broken or shorted to ground, or the battery is too low. Engine usually fails to start until the input recovers.

c: Alternator regulator overvoltage
Improper external power source or jump-start
P2508.d: The ECM/PCM switched-battery input reads above the upper threshold. Most often caused by a charging system overvoltage (failed alternator regulator) or wrong jump-start procedure. Sustained high voltage risks damaging ECU electronics.

c: Poor battery cable connection
Intermittent main relay
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration
P2509.d: The ECU detects sporadic interruptions of its supply voltage. The fault is set when supply drops below a threshold for short periods, often during cranking or due to a poor connection.

c: Open or shorted wiring to the sensor
Corroded connector at the oil pan
P250A.d: General electrical fault on the engine oil level sensor circuit. The ECM cannot read a plausible level signal (analog level, ultrasonic or capacitive sender). Without a valid level reading the ECM disables oil-low warnings and dynamic service-interval calculation.

c: Aged or contaminated sender
Foaming oil under high RPM masking the level
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P250B.d: The oil level sensor is electrically intact, but the level reading is implausible — for example a constant value across drives, jumps that cannot match real oil consumption, or readings outside the design range. Often a contaminated or aged float/ultrasonic sender.
P250B.t: Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

c: Signal wire shorted to ground
Sender shorted internally
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P250C.d: The oil level sensor signal voltage reads below the lower limit, typically a short to ground or an open at the reference end of the sender. The ECM treats the input as invalid and ignores oil-low warnings until the circuit is repaired.
P250C.t: Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit Low

c: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
Open signal return
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P250D.d: The oil level sensor signal voltage reads above the upper limit, typically a short to reference voltage or an open signal return. Pegged at maximum, the ECM cannot distinguish full from invalid and disables the level monitor.
P250D.t: Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit High

c: Loose or oil-soaked connector
Cracked sender housing
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration
P250E.d: The oil level signal jumps or drops out intermittently — usually loose contacts, vibration cracks at the sender or oil sloshing on bumpy roads. The ECM filters short transients but flags the input when the noise pattern exceeds the diagnostic limits.
P250E.t: Engine Oil Level Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

c: High oil consumption between services
External oil leak
Missed top-up since last service
P250F.d: The oil level monitor reports the engine oil level below the safe minimum after sensor checks pass. Continued operation risks bearing damage and oil-pump cavitation, so the ECM sets a critical warning, may reduce torque and asks the driver to add oil immediately.

c: Main relay contacts pitted
Sense wiring corroded
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P2510.d: The voltage reported on the main power relay sense line for the engine controller does not match expectation. The ECU may shut down too early or stay awake too long, draining the battery.
P2510.t: ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit Range/Performance

c: Aged main relay contacts
Chafed sense wire shorting intermittently
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration
P2511.d: The sense (feedback) line that lets the ECM verify the main power relay has actually closed shows intermittent dropouts. The ECM expects to see battery voltage on this line whenever the relay is energised — short losses suggest aged contacts, vibration or chafed wiring.
P2511.t: ECM/PCM Power Relay Sense Circuit Intermittent

c: Open request wire or unplugged module
Failed input stage in the EDR
Pin pushed back out of connector body
P2512.d: The Event Data Recorder (EDR / black box) request line — used by the ECM or restraint module to trigger the EDR to capture pre-crash data — is open. The ECM cannot trigger an event capture, so any subsequent crash event would not be recorded reliably.

c: Request wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P2513.d: The EDR request line reads stuck low — typically a short to ground or a permanently asserted request. The ECM either sees a constant request (which it cannot service) or cannot pulse the line high to fire a real event capture.
P2513.t: Event Data Recorder Request Circuit Low

c: Request wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P2514.d: The EDR request line reads stuck high — typically a short to battery voltage. The ECM cannot pulse the line back low to release the request, so the EDR may either ignore further requests or sit in a permanent triggered state.
P2514.t: Event Data Recorder Request Circuit High

c: Open or shorted wiring to the sensor
Failed sensor element
P2515.d: General electrical fault in the second A/C refrigerant pressure sensor circuit. Sensor B usually monitors the low-side or compressor-suction pressure (in addition to high-side sensor A). The ECM cannot read a plausible value and disables variable compressor control to avoid evaporator freeze-up or overpressure.
P2515.t: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor B Circuit

c: Low refrigerant charge
Contaminated or aged sensor diaphragm
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P2516.d: A/C refrigerant pressure sensor B is electrically intact, but its reading does not match the system model — for example pressures that do not fall when the compressor is off, do not change with ambient temperature, or contradict pressure sensor A. Often a refrigerant charge issue or a contaminated sensor.
P2516.t: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor B Circuit Range/Performance

c: Signal wire shorted to ground
Missing 5 V reference at the sensor
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2517.d: A/C refrigerant pressure sensor B signal voltage reads below the lower limit. Either a short to ground in the signal wire, an open reference voltage at the sensor, or an internal short. The ECM ignores the reading and disables A/C closed-loop control until the circuit recovers.
P2517.t: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor B Circuit Low

c: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
Open signal return at the sensor
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2518.d: A/C refrigerant pressure sensor B signal voltage reads above the upper limit. Typically a short to reference voltage in the signal line, an open signal return, or an overpressure event briefly pegging the sensor. ECM disables variable compressor control to protect the system.
P2518.t: A/C Refrigerant Pressure Sensor B Circuit High

c: Open or shorted A/C request wire
HVAC module not transmitting the request
P2519.d: General electrical fault on the A/C compressor request input A. This input tells the ECM that the HVAC controller wants the A/C compressor engaged. With the input invalid, the ECM cannot enable the compressor clutch — A/C does not cool, idle-up compensation is not applied.

c: Open switch wire or unplugged switch
Failed PTO enable switch
Pin pushed back out of connector body
P251A.d: The Power Take-Off (PTO) enable switch input to the ECM is open. PTO is used on trucks and work vehicles to drive auxiliary equipment from the engine — without a valid enable signal the ECM refuses to enter PTO operating mode, idle speed control changes do not apply.

c: Switch wire shorted to ground
Switch stuck closed
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P251B.d: The PTO enable switch input reads stuck low — typically a short to ground or a permanently closed switch. The ECM either sees PTO enabled when the operator has not requested it, or cannot release the PTO mode after work.

c: Switch wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P251C.d: The PTO enable switch input reads stuck high — typically a short to battery voltage. The ECM cannot pull the input low, so the switch state is unreadable and PTO mode is locked out for safety.

c: Broken shutdown wire or unplugged work attachment
Pin pushed back out of connector body
Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor
P251D.d: The PTO engine-shutdown command line is open. This safety input lets a connected work attachment (or operator switch) request an immediate engine shutdown — for example when an interlock is opened on a stationary aerial work platform. With the line broken, the safety shutdown cannot be commanded.

c: Shutdown wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P251E.d: The PTO engine-shutdown command line reads stuck low — usually a short to ground or a permanently asserted shutdown request. The ECM may treat this as an active shutdown command and refuse to start or keep the engine running while in PTO mode.

c: Shutdown wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P251F.d: The PTO engine-shutdown command line reads stuck high — typically a short to battery voltage. The ECM cannot pulse the line low to acknowledge a shutdown request, so the operator-side safety chain is effectively disabled.

c: Request wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P2520.d: The A/C compressor request input A reads stuck low — typically a short to ground or a permanently asserted request. The ECM either sees A/C demanded all the time (cannot release idle-up, raises fuel use) or cannot distinguish a real request from the stuck low level.

c: Request wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P2521.d: The A/C request input A reads stuck high — typically a short to battery voltage. The ECM cannot pull the line low to read switch state, so the A/C compressor request is treated as invalid and the clutch stays disengaged.

c: Open or shorted A/C request wire B
HVAC module not transmitting request B
P2522.d: General electrical fault on the second A/C request input B. Many vehicles have two HVAC zones, a rear evaporator request, or a redundant request line — input B carries that signal. With the input invalid, the ECM cannot honour zone B compressor demand or rear-evap operation.

c: Request wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P2523.d: The A/C request input B reads stuck low — short to ground or permanently asserted request. Same effect as input A stuck low, applied to the second HVAC channel.

c: Request wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P2524.d: The A/C request input B reads stuck high — typically a short to battery voltage. The ECM cannot read the switch state, request B is treated as invalid.

c: Open or shorted wiring to the sensor
Failed sensor element
P2525.d: General electrical fault on the vacuum reservoir pressure sensor circuit. The reservoir stores manifold or pump-generated vacuum for systems like brake booster, EGR actuators or HVAC dampers. Without a valid reading the ECM disables vacuum-pump duty cycle control.

c: Leaking reservoir or vacuum line
Aged sensor with offset drift
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P2526.d: The vacuum reservoir pressure sensor is electrically intact, but the reading does not match the model — vacuum that does not build up after pump activation, does not bleed off when consumers draw, or stays at one value. Often a partly clogged hose, a leaking reservoir or an aged sensor.
P2526.t: Vacuum Reservoir Pressure Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

c: Signal wire shorted to ground
Missing 5 V reference at the sensor
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2527.d: Sensor signal voltage below the lower limit — usually a short to ground or open reference. The ECM disables vacuum pump control until the input recovers.
P2527.t: Vacuum Reservoir Pressure Sensor Circuit Low

c: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
Open signal return
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2528.d: Sensor signal voltage above the upper limit — usually a short to reference voltage or open signal return. ECM disables vacuum pump control to avoid overshooting.
P2528.t: Vacuum Reservoir Pressure Sensor Circuit High

c: Loose connector
Chafed harness
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration
P2529.d: The sensor signal jumps or drops out intermittently — loose connector, vibration, or chafed harness. The ECM filters short transients but flags the input when noise exceeds limits.
P2529.t: Vacuum Reservoir Pressure Sensor Circuit Intermittent

c: Open or shorted wiring to the sensor
Failed sensor electrode after long use
P252A.d: General electrical fault on the engine oil quality sensor — typically a capacitive/dielectric sensor that estimates oil aging from permittivity, viscosity proxies and conductivity. With no valid reading the dynamic service-interval algorithm falls back to the fixed-interval default.

c: Contaminated sensor electrode
Oil grade outside the sensor calibration range
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P252B.d: The oil quality sensor is electrically intact, but the readings do not match the model — for example permittivity that does not change after an oil change, or shifts inconsistent with km/h driven. Often a contaminated electrode or oil that does not fit the sensor calibration.
P252B.t: Engine Oil Quality Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

c: Signal wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P252C.d: Sensor signal voltage below the lower limit — typically a short to ground in the signal line or an internal short across the sensor electrode.
P252C.t: Engine Oil Quality Sensor Circuit Low

c: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P252D.d: Sensor signal voltage above the upper limit — typically a short to reference voltage or an open signal return.
P252D.t: Engine Oil Quality Sensor Circuit High

c: Loose oil-soaked connector
Cracked sensor housing
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration
P252E.d: The oil quality sensor signal jumps or drops out — usually a loose connector at the oil pan, an oil-soaked harness or vibration cracks at the sensor housing.
P252E.t: Engine Oil Quality Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

c: Overfilled at last service
Fuel dilution from incomplete DPF regeneration
Coolant intrusion (head gasket / cooler)
P252F.d: The oil level monitor reports the engine oil level above the safe maximum after sensor checks pass. Overfilling raises foaming, blow-by and crankcase pressure — and on diesels with regen-by-injection, fuel dilution can drive the level up by itself. The ECM warns the driver and may flag for service.

c: Faulty ignition switch contacts
Wiring or connector fault
P2530.d: The ECU detects an electrical fault on the ignition switch run position input. The signal indicating that the ignition is in the run position is missing or implausible.

c: Run input wire shorted to ground
Switch contact stuck closed
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2531.d: The ignition switch Run-position input reads stuck low — short to ground or a permanently closed contact. The ECM cannot tell when the operator releases the switch from Run, so accessory and crank logic gets confused.
P2531.t: Ignition Switch Run Position Circuit Low

c: Run input wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P2532.d: The ignition switch Run-position input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage or open switch return. The ECM cannot detect when the operator turns the switch back to off/accessory, so module sleep and accessory power timeouts do not work correctly.
P2532.t: Ignition Switch Run Position Circuit High

c: Open or shorted On/Start wire
P2533.d: General electrical fault on the ignition switch On/Start (terminal 50 / crank) input. The ECM uses this signal to know when the starter is energised — without it the ECM cannot raise fuel and timing for cranking, the engine struggles to start or stalls right after.

c: On/Start wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P2534.d: The On/Start input reads stuck low — short to ground or permanently closed contact. The ECM may see crank request when the key is at rest, blocking accessory functions or causing unexpected starter cut-off logic.
P2534.t: Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit Low

c: On/Start wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P2535.d: The On/Start input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage. The ECM cannot read the crank state, modules dependent on this signal are unable to time their wake-up correctly.
P2535.t: Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit High

c: Open or shorted ACC wire
P2536.d: General electrical fault on the ignition switch accessory (terminal 75 / ACC) input. ACC tells the ECM that radio, fans, accessory loads should be powered without the engine running. With the input invalid, the body controller may misjudge accessory power timing.

c: ACC wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P2537.d: The ACC input reads stuck low — short to ground or permanently closed contact. The ECM may see ACC active continuously and refuse to enter sleep, draining the battery.
P2537.t: Ignition Switch Accessory Position Circuit Low

c: ACC wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P2538.d: The ACC input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage. The ECM cannot detect when the operator releases the switch from ACC, accessory power timeouts do not work.
P2538.t: Ignition Switch Accessory Position Circuit High

c: Open or shorted wiring to the sensor
Failed sensor element
P2539.d: General electrical fault on the low-pressure fuel system sensor — typically the lift-pump or pre-supply pressure sensor that monitors the rail feeding the high-pressure pump. With no valid reading, the ECM cannot verify that lift pressure is sufficient for HP-pump intake.
P2539.t: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit

c: Open sense wire
Pin pushed back out of connector body
Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor
P253A.d: The PTO sense (engagement feedback) line is open. This input tells the ECM whether the PTO clutch or driveline is actually engaged after a request — it closes the loop on the PTO enable command. With it broken, the ECM cannot confirm engagement and refuses to ramp up to PTO speed setpoints.

c: Sticky or worn PTO clutch
Mis-adjusted limit switch
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P253B.d: The PTO sense circuit is electrically intact, but the engagement feedback does not match the command. The ECM requests engage and sees no engaged feedback (or vice versa) within the expected time window — drive-line slip, sticky clutch, or a mis-adjusted limit switch.

c: Sense wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P253C.d: The PTO sense input reads stuck low — short to ground or limit switch stuck closed. The ECM may see PTO continuously engaged.

c: Sense wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P253D.d: The PTO sense input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage or open switch return. The ECM cannot detect engagement.

c: Loose connector
Chattering limit switch
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration
P253E.d: The PTO sense signal jumps or drops out — usually loose connectors, a chattering limit switch, or vibration on the work attachment.

c: Service interval exceeded
High DPF regeneration load with fuel dilution
P253F.d: The oil quality monitor concludes that the engine oil has reached the end of its useful life — based on permittivity, soot content, fuel dilution and total operating hours. The ECM requests an oil change before the next regen cycle to prevent accelerated bearing wear.

c: Weak in-tank or lift pump causing real pressure deviation
Restricted fuel filter or kinked supply line
Low-pressure sensor reading offset
Outdated engine software (manufacturer update available)
P2540.d: P2540 is the plausibility check of the low-pressure fuel sensor, which measures supply pressure between the in-tank or lift pump and the high-pressure pump. The signal is electrically valid but does not match the commanded or expected pressure. VW's 2014 Touareg book sets it on the 3.6 L V6 when the measured pressure deviates from target beyond calibrated limits. Ram's bulletin 18-021-25 for the 2025 Ram 3500 with the 6.7 L Cummins lists P2540 and P2543 among the faults addressed by a PCM software update, so calibration can play a role as well. A weak supply pump or a clogged filter produces a genuine deviation. P2539 is the circuit fault, P2541/P2542 low/high, P2543 intermittent. Expect hesitation or hard starting.
s: Hesitation or power loss under load
P2540.t: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

c: Signal wire shorted to ground
5 V reference supply missing or pulled down by another sensor
Failed low-pressure fuel sensor
P2541.d: P2541 means the signal of the low-pressure fuel sensor is below its valid range - typically a short to ground on the signal line or a lost 5 V sensor supply. VW's 2014 specification books set it below 0.2 V on the Passat, CC and Touareg (VW wording: short to ground or low input), whereas a signal above 4.8 V leads to P2539. CARB requires every emissions-relevant input to be checked for circuit faults and out-of-range values. Without a valid reading the engine computer can only run the fuel supply pump on a substitute value, so pressure control becomes coarse. P2540 is the plausibility fault, P2542 the high-side fault, P2543 an intermittent signal. Symptoms range from none to hesitation under load or hard starting.
P2541.t: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit Low

c: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
Open signal return
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2542.d: The low-pressure fuel system sensor signal voltage is above the upper limit. Either a short to reference voltage in the signal line, an open signal return, or a sensor reading pegged high after an internal failure. The HP-pump pressure-control strategy falls back to default.
P2542.t: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit High

c: Loose or corroded pin at the sensor connector
Chafed signal or supply wire with intermittent contact
Outdated engine software (manufacturer update available)
P2543.d: P2543 flags a low-pressure fuel sensor signal that drops out or jumps for short moments while staying inside its electrical range most of the time - a loose pin, a chafed wire or a sensor with an internal contact problem. Ram's bulletin 18-021-25 for the 2025 Ram 3500 with the 6.7 L Cummins lists P2543-00 next to P2540-00 among the faults corrected by a PCM software update, which shows that calibration can also produce entries. Other manufacturers do not publish thresholds for this code. CARB requires input components to be checked for circuit faults and, where feasible, rationality. P2541/P2542 describe a steady low or high signal, P2540 a plausibility fault. The code often comes and goes, sometimes with brief stumbling.
P2543.t: Low Pressure Fuel System Sensor Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

c: CAN communication error
Fault in requesting module
P2544.d: The ECU detects an invalid torque-management request signal A from another control unit (e.g. transmission, ESP, ABS) on the CAN bus. Cooperative torque control cannot be performed as expected.
P2544.t: Torque Management Request Input Signal A

c: Requesting module sending invalid values
Communication bus corruption between modules
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P2545.d: The ECM receives torque-management requests from other modules (TCM during shifts, ABS/ESC during traction events, hybrid controller). Input A is electrically intact but its values do not match the system model — out-of-range steps, jumps, or persistent values that other modules cannot confirm.
P2545.t: Torque Management Request Input Signal A Range/Performance

c: Signal wire shorted to ground
CAN message stuck at minimum value
P2546.d: Torque management input A reads stuck low — analog short to ground or message stuck at minimum value. The ECM cannot trust the request and falls back to a safe default.
P2546.t: Torque Management Request Input Signal A Low

c: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
CAN message stuck at maximum value
P2547.d: Torque management input A reads stuck high — analog short to reference voltage or message stuck at maximum value. The ECM rejects the request to avoid running unintended high-torque commands.
P2547.t: Torque Management Request Input Signal A High

c: Open or shorted wire / invalid CAN message
P2548.d: General electrical fault on the second torque-management request input B. Used when more than one module needs to request torque adjustments — typically TCM on input A and ABS/ESC on input B, or chassis vs powertrain. With B invalid, only the A-side request is honoured.
P2548.t: Torque Management Request Input Signal B

c: Requesting module sending invalid values
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
Sensor mounting loose - signal damping
P2549.d: Input B is electrically intact but the values are implausible — same failure mode as the A-side performance fault, applied to the second torque-management channel.
P2549.t: Torque Management Request Input Signal B Range/Performance

c: Open wire or unplugged switch
Pin pushed back out of connector body
Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor
P254A.d: The PTO speed-selector switch 1 input is open. This switch lets the operator pick a preset PTO operating speed (idle, 800, 1200 rpm, etc.). With the input broken, the ECM cannot apply any operator-selected speed and falls back to a default speed.

c: Contaminated rotary contact
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
Sensor mounting loose - signal damping
P254B.d: The selector input is electrically intact but the value is implausible — multiple positions asserted at once, or a value that cannot map to any of the configured speed presets. Often a sticky multi-position switch or a contaminated rotary contact.

c: Switch wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P254C.d: PTO speed selector 1 input reads stuck low — short to ground or analog signal pegged at minimum. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P254C.t: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 1 Circuit Low

c: Switch wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P254D.d: PTO speed selector 1 input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage or analog signal pegged at maximum.
P254D.t: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 1 Circuit High

c: Worn rotary contact
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration
Harness routed against vibrating component
P254E.d: The PTO speed selector signal jumps or drops out — usually a worn rotary contact or vibration on the work attachment.
P254E.t: PTO Speed Selector Sensor/Switch 1 Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

c: Open or shorted hood-switch wire
Aged switch with corroded contacts
P254F.d: General electrical fault on the engine hood (bonnet) switch circuit. The hood switch tells the body controller and (on hybrids) the high-voltage system that the hood is open — used for security, alarm and HV-safety interlock. With the input invalid, alarm logic and HV interlock fall back to a safe state.

c: Signal wire shorted to ground
P2550.d: Torque management input B reads stuck low — short to ground or message at minimum. ECM rejects the request, only A-side is used.
P2550.t: Torque Management Request Input Signal B Low

c: Signal wire shorted to reference voltage
P2551.d: Torque management input B reads stuck high — short to reference voltage or message at maximum. ECM rejects the request to avoid unintended high-torque commands.
P2551.t: Torque Management Request Input Signal B High

c: Open or shorted inhibit wire
P2552.d: General electrical fault on the throttle/fuel inhibit input A. This input lets external safety functions (immobilizer, hybrid HV interlock, anti-theft) override the throttle or cut fuel delivery. With the input invalid the safety override is unreliable, so the ECM falls back to its safe default — typically inhibit asserted to err on the side of safety.

c: Requesting module sending an inconsistent value
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
Sensor mounting loose - signal damping
P2553.d: The throttle/fuel inhibit A signal is electrically intact but its value does not match the system context — for example asserted while the immobilizer reports OK, or de-asserted while a hybrid HV interlock is active. The ECM cannot trust the signal.

c: Inhibit wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P2554.d: Throttle/fuel inhibit A reads stuck low — short to ground or permanently asserted. ECM may treat it as continuous inhibit and refuse normal operation.

c: Inhibit wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P2555.d: Throttle/fuel inhibit A reads stuck high — short to battery voltage. ECM cannot read the inhibit state and falls back to the safe default.

c: Open or shorted wiring to the sensor
Corroded connector at the expansion tank
P2556.d: General electrical fault on the engine coolant level sensor/switch circuit. Many vehicles use a simple float-switch in the expansion tank, others use a continuous-level analog sensor. With the input invalid the ECM cannot warn for low coolant before overheating starts.

c: Stuck float
Trapped air around the sensor
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P2557.d: The coolant level sensor is electrically intact, but the readings are implausible — for example a level that does not move at all over many drive cycles, or jumps that cannot match real coolant loss. Often a stuck float, contaminated electrode or air-locked sensor.

Pin pushed back out of connector body
Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor
P255A.d: The second PTO speed-selector switch input is open. Switch 2 typically encodes a binary or multi-bit code together with switch 1 — together they select one of several preset PTO speeds. With switch 2 broken, only the half of the bit pattern is available, so several presets cannot be reached.

Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
Sensor mounting loose - signal damping

P255C.d: PTO speed selector 2 input reads stuck low — short to ground or analog signal pegged at minimum. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.

P255E.d: PTO speed selector 2 signal jumps or drops out — usually a worn rotary contact or vibration on the work attachment.

Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
Sensor mounting loose - signal damping
P255F.d: The A/C request input A is electrically intact, but its value does not match the system context — for example asserted while the HVAC controller reports off, toggling rapidly, or sustained while compressor pressures cannot support it. The ECM disables A/C clutch engagement until the input becomes plausible.

Missed top-up since last service
Head gasket leaking coolant into combustion
P2560.d: The coolant level monitor reports the engine coolant below the safe minimum after sensor checks pass. Continued operation risks overheating, head warping and head-gasket failure. The driver is warned and the ECM may reduce engine power until the level is restored.

c: Internal fault in the HVAC module — read its DTCs
P2561.d: The A/C / HVAC control module has requested the ECM to illuminate the malfunction indicator (MIL) because of an emissions-relevant fault on its side. The original fault is stored in the HVAC module — this code only signals that the ECM has honoured the request.
P2561.t: A/C Control Module Requested MIL Illumination

c: Open or shorted wiring to the position sensor
Failed Hall element after thermal cycling
P2562.d: General electrical fault on the turbocharger boost control position sensor A — the feedback sensor on the wastegate or VGT actuator (often a contactless Hall sensor). Without valid position feedback the ECM cannot close the loop on boost control and falls back to open-loop duty cycle.
s: Charging may not start or interrupts
P2562.t: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Circuit

c: Kinked, twisted or leaking vacuum hose to the boost actuator
Leaking actuator diaphragm or sticking vanes
Broken or missing adjustment stud, actuator travel out of tolerance
P2563.d: P2563 means the position feedback of the turbocharger boost control actuator - variable vanes or wastegate - does not match the commanded position, although the sensor circuit itself is electrically intact. GM's 2009 Duramax diesel table sets it when vane position differs from target by 15 % or more for 5 s (Type B, warning light after two trips). VW's 2014 Passat TDI book compares the control deviation with a map based on engine speed and torque, and VW bulletin 21-15-06 links P2563 on 2.0 L TDI engines to kinked vacuum hoses, a leaking vacuum diaphragm or a broken adjustment stud on the turbocharger. P2562/P2564/P2565 are circuit faults, P2566 an intermittent signal. Boost is often limited, so power drops noticeably.
s: Noticeable loss of power, limp mode
Underboost code P0299 stored at the same time
P2563.t: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance

c: Signal wire shorted to ground
Missing 5 V reference at the sensor
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2564.d: Position sensor A signal voltage below the lower limit — short to ground in the signal line or open reference voltage at the sensor.

P2565.d: Position sensor A signal voltage above the upper limit — short to reference voltage in the signal line or open signal return.

c: Loose or corroded pin at the position sensor connector
Heat-damaged or chafed sensor wiring near the turbocharger
Worn position sensor in the actuator
P2566.d: P2566 reports that the signal from the boost control position sensor flickers or drops out briefly instead of being steadily wrong. VW bulletins 21-15-04 (2015) and 21-15-06 (2020) for 2009-2014 Jetta, Golf and Jetta SportWagen with the 2.0 L TDI (CBEA, CJAA) list P2566 together with P2562-P2565 and P0299 for the complaint of lacking power; there the position sensor G581 sits in the vacuum diaphragm, and the repair path starts with vacuum hoses, diaphragm and the actuator travel. No thresholds are published. CARB requires turbocharger electronic components to be monitored as comprehensive components. P2563 is the plausibility fault, P2564/P2565 a steady low or high signal. Expect intermittent power loss and a warning light.
s: Intermittent loss of power or limp mode
Check engine light, sometimes going out again
P2566.t: Turbocharger Boost Control Position Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

c: Failed radiator identification/temperature sensor
Damaged sensor wiring or connector at the radiator
Replacement radiator without coating or without sensor fitted
P2567.d: P2567 is the general circuit fault of the sensor on a direct ozone reduction (DOR) radiator - a radiator with a catalytic coating that converts ground-level ozone in the passing air and earns low-emission vehicles an NMOG credit. CARB section (e)(14) requires the OBD system to detect a missing or deteriorated DOR function. No manufacturer publicly documents P2567 itself. VW's 2014 books (CC, Tiguan) use the sibling codes P2568-P2570 for radiator sensor G611, which reports an ID and temperature over LIN, and MINI fits a comparable sensor on the radiator of B46M PZEV engines to confirm the coated radiator. P2568 is the plausibility fault, P2569-P2571 low, high and intermittent. Often the radiator with its bonded sensor is replaced.
s: No change in driveability or engine cooling
Possible failed emissions inspection because of the stored code
P2567.t: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Temperature Sensor Circuit

c: Aftermarket radiator without ozone coating or without the identification sensor
Identification sensor not bonded after radiator replacement
Identification/temperature sensor failed its self-test
P2568.d: P2568 is the plausibility check of the sensor on a direct ozone reduction (DOR) radiator, whose coating converts ozone in the cooling air. VW's 2014 specification books for the CC and Tiguan set it on a failed ID check or a failed functional check of the temperature sensor. VW Tech Tip 19-12-01 explains that on 2009-2015 Eos, Jetta, GTI, Passat and Tiguan with the 2.0 L TSI (CCTA, CBFA) this code refers to the radiator identification sensor G611; a new radiator comes with the sensor packed separately, to be bonded on. A non-coated aftermarket radiator or an unbonded sensor therefore triggers P2568. P2569/P2570 are LIN electrical faults, P2567 the general circuit fault. CARB section (e)(14) requires DOR monitoring.
s: Check engine light, often after a radiator replacement
No change in driveability or engine cooling
P2568.t: Direct Ozone Reduction Catalyst Temperature Sensor Circuit Range/Performance

c: Signal wire shorted to ground
Sensor shorted internally
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P2569.d: Direct Ozone Reduction (DOR) catalysts are coated radiator surfaces or dedicated catalysts that decompose tropospheric ozone passing over the radiator — used for low-emissions vehicles. The temperature sensor monitoring the DOR brick reads stuck low — short to ground or sensor short.
s: Sulfur (rotten egg) smell from exhaust under load

Without a valid signal the deterioration monitor is disabled.
s: Sulfur (rotten egg) smell from exhaust under load

Coating worn off the radiator surface, contaminated by road salt and grime, or thermally aged after many heat cycles. Replacing the affected radiator/coating restores function.
s: Sulfur (rotten egg) smell from exhaust under load

P2578.d: General electrical fault on the turbocharger/supercharger shaft speed sensor A — a high-frequency Hall or eddy-current sensor on the compressor shaft. The ECM uses turbo speed for overspeed protection (typically 200,000+ rpm) and for closed-loop boost on VGT systems. With no valid speed the ECM limits boost.
s: Possible blue or black smoke from exhaust
Whistling or hissing sound from intake

Aged Hall element
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P2579.d: Turbo speed sensor A is electrically intact, but the speed reading does not match the model — for example a speed that does not climb when boost rises, drifts away from the air-mass-flow estimate, or jumps. Often blade-fouling, a contaminated sensor tip or aged element.
s: Possible blue or black smoke from exhaust
Whistling or hissing sound from intake

Failed driver in the control module
Pin pushed back out of connector body
P257A.d: The control circuit that drives the vacuum reservoir control valve (or vacuum pump motor) is open. The ECM cannot energise the actuator, so vacuum is no longer maintained on demand and consumers like brake booster, EGR or HVAC dampers may run out of vacuum.

c: Control wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation

Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P257D.d: The hood switch is electrically intact, but its state is implausible — for example reporting hood-open while vehicle speed is rising, or rapid toggles. Usually a worn switch with high contact bounce or a misaligned hood actuator.

c: Switch wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P257E.d: The hood switch input reads stuck low — short to ground or stuck-closed switch. The body controller may treat the hood as permanently open and refuse to arm the alarm or close the HV interlock.

c: Switch wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P257F.d: The hood switch input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage or open switch return. The body controller cannot detect when the hood is opened.

Open supply at the sensor
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance

Failed sensor module
P2583.d: General fault on the radar/lidar/camera distance-range sensor used by adaptive cruise control. On systems with a single sensor or three sensors with a center unit, this code refers to the central sensor — without it, ACC distance control is disabled and the system falls back to plain cruise.
P2583.t: Cruise Control Front Distance Range Sensor Single Sensor or Center

P2584.d: The fuel additive control module — typical for diesel cars with a separate Eolys/Cerine additive tank that aids DPF regeneration — has requested the ECM to illuminate the MIL because of an emissions-relevant fault on its side. The original fault is in the additive module itself.

c: Additive tank low — service refill required
P2585.d: The fuel additive control module asks for the additive-low warning lamp to be illuminated — the additive tank (Eolys/Cerine, used to lower DPF regen temperature) is approaching empty or has reached a service threshold. Continued driving without refilling will eventually disable DPF regeneration.

Aged Hall element

Failed driver in the control module
P258A.d: The control circuit driving the electric vacuum pump (used to maintain brake-booster vacuum on direct-injection or hybrid powertrains where the engine is not always running) is open. The ECM cannot run the pump on demand — booster vacuum drops, pedal feel hardens, brake assist may be reduced.

c: Aged motor brushes or dry vanes
Leaking vacuum line
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P258B.d: The vacuum pump control circuit is electrically intact, but the pump response does not match the model — pump runs longer than expected to reach setpoint, current draw rises (mechanically tight) or vacuum does not build at all. Aged motor brushes, dry vanes or a leaking line are typical causes.

Open pump motor winding

Connector with intermittent contact under vibration

c: Actuator mechanically stuck near low end
Sensor pegged low
P2598.d: Position sensor A reports a value stuck near the low end of its travel even when the actuator is commanded to move. Either the actuator is mechanically stuck closed (wastegate jammed shut, VGT vanes seized at minimum opening) or the sensor itself is pegged low. Boost is uncontrolled — overboost on diesels with VGT, underboost on wastegate-stuck systems.
s: Charging may not start or interrupts

P2599.d: Position sensor A reports a value stuck near the high end of its travel — actuator stuck open (wastegate held wide open, VGT vanes seized at maximum opening) or sensor pegged high. Boost suffers — typically underboost on VGT, overboost-protection-off on wastegate.
s: Charging may not start or interrupts

c: Actuator mechanically stuck near low end

Leaky pneumatic actuator
P259C.d: After start-up the boost-control loop on turbo A takes longer than the calibration limit to transition from open-loop to closed-loop control. Typically a slow-warming actuator (VGT vanes carbonised), a sluggish position sensor or a leaky pneumatic actuator that cannot follow setpoints quickly enough.
s: Charging may not start or interrupts

P259D.d: Same condition as the turbo A excessive-warm-up fault, applied to the second turbo. Boost control tracks commanded vs. actual manifold pressure; persistent deviation means wastegate, vanes, hose or actuator are not delivering the requested pressure.
