P259E.d: The boost-control actuator on turbo A has been operating at the low end of its travel for too long — the closed-loop controller is saturated against the lower stop trying to reach the boost setpoint. Indicates either a leak (wastegate held closed but boost still escapes) or commanded boost above what the engine can produce.
s: Charging may not start or interrupts
P259E.t: Turbocharger A Boost Control Position At Low Limit

c: Wastegate stuck closed
P259F.d: The boost-control actuator on turbo A has been operating at the high end of its travel — the controller is saturated against the upper stop trying to bleed off boost. Indicates either a wastegate stuck closed, oversized turbo for the calibration, or commanded boost limits being exceeded by ambient conditions (cold dense air).
s: Charging may not start or interrupts
P259F.t: Turbocharger A Boost Control Position At High Limit

c: Boost leak in the charge-air path
P25A0.d: Turbocharger B Boost Control Position At Low Limit: the control module has detected this fault condition. This affects turbo/supercharger boost-pressure control.
s: Charging may not start or interrupts
P25A0.t: Turbocharger B Boost Control Position At Low Limit

c: Wastegate stuck closed
P25A1.d: Turbocharger B Boost Control Position At High Limit: the control module has detected this fault condition. This affects turbo/supercharger boost-pressure control.
s: Charging may not start or interrupts
P25A1.t: Turbocharger B Boost Control Position At High Limit

c: Internal fault in the brake module — read its DTCs
P25A2.d: The primary brake system control module (ABS/ESC/iBooster) has requested the ECM to illuminate the MIL because of an emissions-relevant fault on its side — for example a regenerative braking fault on a hybrid that affects driveline torque flow. The original fault is in the brake module.
P25A2.t: Brake System Control Module A Requested MIL Illumination

c: Hood not properly latched
Failed hood latch sensor
P25A3.d: After plausibility checks the body controller has concluded that the engine hood is genuinely open while the vehicle is operating. Used to suspend HV operation on hybrids/EVs (HV interlock), block remote engine start, and trigger the alarm if armed.

c: Open or shorted switch wire
P25A4.d: General electrical fault on the fuel mode select switch — used on bi-fuel vehicles (CNG/LPG/H2/gasoline) so the driver can pick the active fuel. With the input invalid, the ECM falls back to the default fuel and disables operator-selectable switching.

c: Switch contact bounce
P25A5.d: The fuel mode select switch is electrically intact, but its state does not match operating conditions — switched to gas while gas tank is empty, or fast toggling. The ECM rejects the request to avoid stalling.

c: Switch wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P25A6.d: Fuel mode switch input reads stuck low — short to ground or stuck-closed contact. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P25A6.t: Fuel Mode Select Switch Circuit Low

c: Switch wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P25A7.d: Fuel mode switch input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P25A7.t: Fuel Mode Select Switch Circuit High

c: Worn switch contact
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration
Harness routed against vibrating component
P25A8.d: Fuel mode switch signal jumps or drops out — worn contact or vibration. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P25A8.t: Fuel Mode Select Switch Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

c: Open control wire to the solenoid
Open solenoid coil
Pin pushed back out of connector body
P25A9.d: The piston-cooling oil-jet control circuit is open. Modern engines with under-piston oil jets switch them on under high load to cool the piston crown — controlled by a solenoid valve in the oil gallery. With the circuit broken, jets cannot be commanded on or stay locked off, raising piston temperatures under load.

c: Control wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P25AA.d: The piston-cooling oil-jet control circuit reads stuck low — short to ground or low-side driver stuck on. The jets may be enabled continuously, raising oil pump load and lowering oil pressure to other consumers.
P25AA.t: Piston Cooling Oil Control Circuit Low

c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P25AB.d: Control circuit stuck high — short to battery voltage or open coil/return. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P25AB.t: Piston Cooling Oil Control Circuit High

c: Solenoid stuck closed by oil sludge
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play
P25AC.d: The control circuit is electrically intact, but the solenoid valve does not open when commanded — confirmed by oil-pressure or oil-temperature feedback that does not change after the activation pulse. Piston cooling does not engage under high load — risk of piston-crown overheating and ring-land cracks.
P25AC.t: Piston Cooling Oil Control Circuit Performance/Stuck Off

c: Solenoid stuck open
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play
P25AD.d: The piston cooling solenoid does not close when commanded off — jets remain active when not needed. Oil pressure to top-end consumers may sag, and warm-up takes longer because the cooling jets remove heat from the pistons during cold start.
P25AD.t: Piston Cooling Oil Control Circuit Stuck On

c: Low engine oil level
Sludge-clogged oil gallery
Worn oil pump
P25AE.d: With the piston-cooling jets commanded on, the dedicated oil-pressure sensor in that gallery reads below the safe threshold. Insufficient flow to the jets means real piston cooling is not happening — the ECM warns the driver and may reduce torque to protect the pistons.
P25AE.t: Piston Cooling Oil Pressure Too Low

c: Internal fault — read the module DTCs
P25AF.d: A dedicated coolant-temperature control module (used on engines with electric coolant pumps and electronic thermostats to keep the cylinder head and block at independent setpoints) has requested the ECM to illuminate the MIL because of an emissions-relevant fault on its side. Original fault is in that module.
P25AF.t: Coolant Temperature Control Module Requested MIL Illumination

c: Stuck float
Bent float arm catching the tank wall
P25B0.d: Fuel level sensor A (typically the float in the main fuel tank section) reports a value that does not change over a long driving distance — the float is mechanically stuck against the tank wall, baffle or pump module. Without level changes the EVAP monitor cannot run and remaining-range estimates are wrong.

c: Stuck float
P25B1.d: Same condition as sensor A stuck, applied to the second fuel level sensor B. Saddle tanks (often AWD vehicles) and large trucks use two sensors — one per tank chamber — averaged for total level. A stuck B leaves only A and reduces accuracy.

c: One stuck float — inspect both
P25B2.d: The ECM detects that one of the two level sensors is stuck but cannot identify which from the available signals — for example because the saddle-tank algorithm sees implausible delta only intermittently. Both sensors should be inspected.
P25B2.t: Fuel Level Sensor A or B Stuck

c: Seized wastegate linkage
Broken return spring
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
P25B3.d: Wastegate A is mechanically stuck open. Exhaust gas bypasses the turbine even at low load — turbo cannot reach target speed, boost is permanently low and the engine feels asthmatic. Common causes are seized linkage, broken return spring or carbon-locked wastegate flap.
s: Possible blue or black smoke from exhaust
Whistling or hissing sound from intake

c: Carbon-locked wastegate flap
Seized linkage
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
P25B4.d: Wastegate A is mechanically stuck closed. The turbo cannot bleed off exhaust at high load — boost overshoots the setpoint, risking overboost cut-off and damage to the turbo bearing. Carbon-locked flap, seized linkage or aged actuator are typical causes.
s: Possible blue or black smoke from exhaust
Whistling or hissing sound from intake

c: Seized wastegate linkage
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play
P25B5.d: Same as wastegate A stuck open, applied to the second wastegate (twin-turbo, sequential or two-stage). Boost control tracks commanded vs. actual manifold pressure; persistent deviation means wastegate, vanes, hose or actuator are not delivering the requested pressure.
s: Possible blue or black smoke from exhaust
Whistling or hissing sound from intake

c: Carbon-locked wastegate flap
Carbon or debris buildup preventing free movement
Component wear with age - mechanical play
P25B6.d: Same as wastegate A stuck closed, applied to the second wastegate. Boost control tracks commanded vs. actual manifold pressure; persistent deviation means wastegate, vanes, hose or actuator are not delivering the requested pressure.
s: Possible blue or black smoke from exhaust
Whistling or hissing sound from intake

c: Open or shorted wire
P25B7.d: General electrical fault on the auxiliary ignition switch On/Start input. Used on commercial vehicles or upfit applications where a second ignition switch (in a sleeper cab, work platform or crew compartment) can crank the engine.
P25B7.t: Auxiliary Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit

c: Wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P25B8.d: Auxiliary ignition switch On/Start input reads stuck low — short to ground or stuck-closed contact. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P25B8.t: Auxiliary Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit Low

c: Wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P25B9.d: Auxiliary ignition switch On/Start input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.
P25B9.t: Auxiliary Ignition Switch On/Start Position Circuit High

c: Open switch wire
Pin pushed back out of connector body
Cracked solder joint inside the module or sensor
P25BA.d: The DPF/SCR forced-regeneration request switch — used on commercial vehicles to let the operator force a parked regeneration when the automatic regen has been postponed too often — is open. The ECM cannot honour an operator request for forced regen.

c: Switch wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Harness chafing through insulation
P25BB.d: Regeneration control switch input reads stuck low — short to ground or stuck-closed contact. The ECM may see a constant regen request which it cannot service while the vehicle is moving.

c: Switch wire shorted to battery voltage
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
Supply wire pinched against B+ source
P25BC.d: Regeneration control switch input reads stuck high — short to battery voltage. Wiring faults of this kind typically come from chafing, water ingress at connector seals, or pin push-back — a wiggle test on the harness while the code is active often confirms the location.

c: Turbocharger oil seal leak feeds engine oil into the intake
Oil collected in the intercooler is sucked into the engine on load
Failed PCV / crankcase breather floods intake with oil mist
P25BD.d: The engine controller commanded a forced shutdown after detecting unmetered fuel reaching the combustion chambers. Common on diesels with leaking turbo seals or cracked intercoolers that drip oil into the intake — the engine then runs on the oil and can overspeed.

c: Broken wire or corroded connector on the disable control line
Open coil in the alt-fuel disable relay
Output driver in the alt-fuel control module faulty
P25BE.d: The controller cannot drive the alternative-fuel disable line that switches a bi-fuel vehicle (CNG, LPG, hydrogen) back to gasoline. An open detected on the control side blocks the safety shutoff for the gas system.
P25BE.t: Alternative Fuel Disable Control Circuit / Open

c: Disable control wire shorted to a B+ supply
Output driver stuck on inside the control module
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25BF.d: Voltage on the alternative-fuel disable control line is above the expected window. Often a short to battery upstream of the relay or a stuck-on driver in the control module.
P25BF.t: Alternative Fuel Disable Control Circuit High

c: Disable control wire shorted to ground
Low-side driver internally shorted
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25C0.d: Voltage on the alternative-fuel disable control line is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a failed driver pulling the line low.
P25C0.t: Alternative Fuel Disable Control Circuit Low

c: Open feedback wire between relay and control module
Feedback contact in the disable relay corroded or stuck
P25C1.d: The feedback signal that confirms the alt-fuel disable command was carried out is missing or out of range. The fuel system cannot verify that the gas circuit is shut.

c: Feedback wire shorted to a B+ supply
Pull-up resistor in the input stage failed
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25C2.d: The disable feedback signal sits above its valid window. Typical cause is a short to battery on the feedback wire or a failed pull-up in the input stage.
P25C2.t: Alternative Fuel Disable Signal Circuit High

c: Feedback wire shorted to ground
Open pull-up resistor in the controller input
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25C3.d: The disable feedback signal sits below its valid window. Usually a short to ground or an open pull-up that lets the input float low.
P25C3.t: Alternative Fuel Disable Signal Circuit Low

c: Open sensor element or broken sensor wire
Corroded connector on the booster sensor pigtail
P25C4.d: The temperature sensor monitoring the electric brake booster (iBooster, eBooster) returns no usable signal. Without temperature feedback the controller derates booster assist to protect the motor.
s: Possible blue or black smoke from exhaust
Whistling or hissing sound from intake
P25C4.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit

c: Sensor drift or contamination on the temperature element
Sensor not seated properly against the booster motor housing
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P25C5.d: The booster temperature sensor reading is implausible relative to commanded assist or coolant temperature. The signal moves too slowly, sticks, or never reaches expected values during operation.
s: Possible blue or black smoke from exhaust
Whistling or hissing sound from intake
P25C5.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit Range/Performance

c: Internal short in the sensor element
Sensor signal wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25C6.d: The booster temperature signal is below the lower diagnostic threshold. Typical causes are a shorted sensor element or a short to ground in the harness.
s: Possible blue or black smoke from exhaust
Whistling or hissing sound from intake
P25C6.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit Low

c: Open sensor element
Sensor signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25C7.d: The booster temperature signal is above the upper diagnostic threshold. Common causes are an open sensor or a short to a 5 V reference in the harness.
s: Possible blue or black smoke from exhaust
Whistling or hissing sound from intake
P25C7.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit High

c: Sensor connector not fully seated or pin tension lost
Harness chafed against booster housing or pedal bracket
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration
P25C8.d: The booster temperature signal jumps or drops out for short moments. Usually a loose connector or a chafed wire that opens during vibration or thermal expansion.
s: Possible blue or black smoke from exhaust
Whistling or hissing sound from intake
P25C8.t: Brake Booster Temperature Sensor A Circuit Intermittent/Erratic

c: Active DTC stored in the secondary brake module
Communication loss interpreted as MIL request
P25C9.d: A second brake system control module (typically the redundant secondary unit on by-wire or AV-grade brake systems) has signalled an emissions-relevant fault and requested the engine controller to switch on the MIL.
P25C9.t: Brake System Control Module B Requested MIL Illumination

c: Open coil in the park-lock solenoid
Broken control wire between ECU and solenoid
P25CA.d: The controller cannot drive the park-lock pin that secures the intake camshaft phaser on bank 1 in its base position at engine off. Without the lock, the next start can suffer poor combustion or rough idle until the phaser builds oil pressure.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25CA.t: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit / Open Bank 1

c: Control wire shorted to ground
ECU low-side driver internally shorted
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25CB.d: The intake camshaft park-lock control line on bank 1 is below the expected voltage window. Usually a short to ground or a low-side driver shorted internally.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25CB.t: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit Low Bank 1

c: Control wire shorted to a B+ supply
ECU output driver stuck on
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25CC.d: The intake camshaft park-lock control line on bank 1 is above the expected voltage window. Typical causes are a short to battery or a stuck-on driver in the controller.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25CC.t: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit High Bank 1

c: Open coil in the park-lock solenoid
Broken control wire between ECU and solenoid
P25CD.d: The controller cannot drive the park-lock pin that secures the intake camshaft phaser on bank 2 in its base position at engine off. Without the lock, the next start can suffer poor combustion or rough idle until the phaser builds oil pressure.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25CD.t: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit / Open Bank 2

c: Control wire shorted to ground
ECU low-side driver internally shorted
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25CE.d: The intake camshaft park-lock control line on bank 2 is below the expected voltage window. Usually a short to ground or a low-side driver shorted internally.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25CE.t: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit Low Bank 2

c: Control wire shorted to a B+ supply
ECU output driver stuck on
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25CF.d: The intake camshaft park-lock control line on bank 2 is above the expected voltage window. Typical causes are a short to battery or a stuck-on driver in the controller.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25CF.t: Intake Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit High Bank 2

c: Open coil in the park-lock solenoid
Broken control wire between ECU and solenoid
P25D0.d: The controller cannot drive the park-lock pin that secures the exhaust camshaft phaser on bank 1 in its base position at engine off. Without the lock, the next start can suffer poor combustion or rough idle until the phaser builds oil pressure.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25D0.t: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit / Open Bank 1

c: Control wire shorted to ground
ECU low-side driver internally shorted
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25D1.d: The exhaust camshaft park-lock control line on bank 1 is below the expected voltage window. Usually a short to ground or a low-side driver shorted internally.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25D1.t: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit Low Bank 1

c: Control wire shorted to a B+ supply
ECU output driver stuck on
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25D2.d: The exhaust camshaft park-lock control line on bank 1 is above the expected voltage window. Typical causes are a short to battery or a stuck-on driver in the controller.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25D2.t: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit High Bank 1

c: Open coil in the park-lock solenoid
Broken control wire between ECU and solenoid
P25D3.d: The controller cannot drive the park-lock pin that secures the exhaust camshaft phaser on bank 2 in its base position at engine off. Without the lock, the next start can suffer poor combustion or rough idle until the phaser builds oil pressure.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25D3.t: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit / Open Bank 2

c: Control wire shorted to ground
ECU low-side driver internally shorted
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25D4.d: The exhaust camshaft park-lock control line on bank 2 is below the expected voltage window. Usually a short to ground or a low-side driver shorted internally.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25D4.t: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit Low Bank 2

c: Control wire shorted to a B+ supply
ECU output driver stuck on
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25D5.d: The exhaust camshaft park-lock control line on bank 2 is above the expected voltage window. Typical causes are a short to battery or a stuck-on driver in the controller.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25D5.t: Exhaust Camshaft Actuator Park Lock Control Circuit High Bank 2

c: Soot or carbon deposits prevent valve from reaching the stop
Worn linkage between actuator and valve flap
Position sensor not aligned with valve shaft
P25D6.d: During self-calibration of the exhaust heat exchanger bypass valve A, the position sensor never reached the expected mechanical stop. The controller cannot zero the position reference, so commanded openings will be inaccurate.
P25D6.t: Exhaust Heat Exchanger Exhaust Bypass Valve A Position Sensor Stop Performance

c: Open sender resistor or broken float
Corroded tank pump module connector
P25D7.d: A third fuel level sensor (C) used on multi-tank trucks, dual-saddle SUVs, or auxiliary fuel systems returns no usable signal. Without it, calculated fuel level and EVAP monitor enabling will be off.

c: Float arm stuck on baffle or fuel pump module
Worn spot on the resistor track at common fill level
P25D8.d: The third fuel level sensor reading does not change as expected with consumption or refuelling. Float may be sticking, or the resistor track has localised wear.

c: Internal short in the sender resistor
Signal wire shorted to ground
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25D9.d: The third fuel level sensor signal is below the lower diagnostic threshold. Usually a shorted sender or a short to ground in the harness.
P25D9.t: Fuel Level Sensor C Circuit Low

c: Open sender resistor
Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25DA.d: The third fuel level sensor signal is above the upper diagnostic threshold. Common causes are an open sender or a short to the 5 V reference.
P25DA.t: Fuel Level Sensor C Circuit High

c: Tank module connector not fully seated
Harness chafed near tank straps
Connector with intermittent contact under vibration
P25DB.d: The third fuel level sensor signal jumps or drops out for short moments. Usually a loose connector or a chafed wire that opens during driving vibration.
P25DB.t: Fuel Level Sensor C Circuit Intermittent

c: Float arm jammed against tank wall, baffle or pump module
Resistor wiper seized by varnish from old fuel
P25DC.d: The third fuel level sensor reads a constant value across known consumption or refuelling events. Float arm or resistor wiper is mechanically stuck.

c: Park-lock pin stuck in the locked groove
Low oil pressure cannot push the lock pin out
Oil control valve blocked by debris
P25DD.d: Camshaft phaser A on bank 1 will not unlock from its base position. The phaser stays at the park-lock angle and cannot be advanced or retarded as commanded.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25DD.t: A Camshaft Position - Stuck In Locked Position Bank 1

c: Worn vanes or housing inside the phaser
Sludge or contaminated oil prevents return to base
Oil control valve leaks internally
P25DE.d: Camshaft phaser A on bank 1 cannot reach its base position at engine shutdown so the lock pin never engages. Next cold start may run rough until oil pressure builds.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25DE.t: A Camshaft Position - Unable to Achieve Locked Position Bank 1

c: Oil control valve spool sticks under varnish
Stretched timing chain shifts cam reference
Wrong oil viscosity slows phaser response
P25DF.d: Camshaft phaser A on bank 1 follows the commanded angle too slowly, oscillates, or shows steady-state error outside tolerance. Closed-loop control of cam timing is degraded.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25DF.t: A Camshaft Position Control Performance Bank 1

c: Park-lock pin stuck in the locked groove
Low oil pressure cannot push the lock pin out
Oil control valve blocked by debris
P25E0.d: Camshaft phaser A on bank 2 will not unlock from its base position. The phaser stays at the park-lock angle and cannot be advanced or retarded as commanded.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25E0.t: A Camshaft Position - Stuck In Locked Position Bank 2

c: Worn vanes or housing inside the phaser
Sludge or contaminated oil prevents return to base
Oil control valve leaks internally
P25E1.d: Camshaft phaser A on bank 2 cannot reach its base position at engine shutdown so the lock pin never engages. Next cold start may run rough until oil pressure builds.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25E1.t: A Camshaft Position - Unable to Achieve Locked Position Bank 2

c: Oil control valve spool sticks under varnish
Stretched timing chain shifts cam reference
Wrong oil viscosity slows phaser response
P25E2.d: Camshaft phaser A on bank 2 follows the commanded angle too slowly, oscillates, or shows steady-state error outside tolerance. Closed-loop control of cam timing is degraded.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25E2.t: A Camshaft Position Control Performance Bank 2

c: Park-lock pin stuck in the locked groove
Low oil pressure cannot push the lock pin out
Oil control valve blocked by debris
P25E3.d: Camshaft phaser B on bank 1 will not unlock from its base position. The phaser stays at the park-lock angle and cannot be advanced or retarded as commanded.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25E3.t: B Camshaft Position - Stuck In Locked Position Bank 1

c: Worn vanes or housing inside the phaser
Sludge or contaminated oil prevents return to base
Oil control valve leaks internally
P25E4.d: Camshaft phaser B on bank 1 cannot reach its base position at engine shutdown so the lock pin never engages. Next cold start may run rough until oil pressure builds.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25E4.t: B Camshaft Position - Unable to Achieve Locked Position Bank 1

c: Oil control valve spool sticks under varnish
Stretched timing chain shifts cam reference
Wrong oil viscosity slows phaser response
P25E5.d: Camshaft phaser B on bank 1 follows the commanded angle too slowly, oscillates, or shows steady-state error outside tolerance. Closed-loop control of cam timing is degraded.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25E5.t: B Camshaft Position Control Performance Bank 1

c: Park-lock pin stuck in the locked groove
Low oil pressure cannot push the lock pin out
Oil control valve blocked by debris
P25E6.d: Camshaft phaser B on bank 2 will not unlock from its base position. The phaser stays at the park-lock angle and cannot be advanced or retarded as commanded.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25E6.t: B Camshaft Position - Stuck In Locked Position Bank 2

c: Worn vanes or housing inside the phaser
Sludge or contaminated oil prevents return to base
Oil control valve leaks internally
P25E7.d: Camshaft phaser B on bank 2 cannot reach its base position at engine shutdown so the lock pin never engages. Next cold start may run rough until oil pressure builds.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25E7.t: B Camshaft Position - Unable to Achieve Locked Position Bank 2

c: Oil control valve spool sticks under varnish
Stretched timing chain shifts cam reference
Wrong oil viscosity slows phaser response
P25E8.d: Camshaft phaser B on bank 2 follows the commanded angle too slowly, oscillates, or shows steady-state error outside tolerance. Closed-loop control of cam timing is degraded.
s: Power loss especially in mid-rpm range
P25E8.t: B Camshaft Position Control Performance Bank 2

c: Open electromagnetic clutch coil
Worn friction surfaces leave the air gap too large to attract
Corroded armature plate stuck open
P25E9.d: The clutch that engages the mechanical supercharger to the engine drive will not close. The supercharger stays disengaged so boost from this stage is unavailable, which limits torque and may also affect cooling pump drives shared with the same belt.
s: Check engine or transmission warning light on
Possible limp mode (locked in one gear)
Slipping or shuddering during gear changes

c: Armature plate seized to the pulley face
Driver stuck on keeps clutch energised
Failed pulley bearing welds clutch surfaces
P25EA.d: The clutch that engages the mechanical supercharger to the engine drive will not open. The supercharger remains coupled at all loads, increasing parasitic loss and fuel consumption when boost is not needed.
s: Check engine or transmission warning light on
Possible limp mode (locked in one gear)
Slipping or shuddering during gear changes

c: Coil resistance increased due to thermal damage
High-resistance contact in the clutch connector
Sensor element aged beyond calibration window
P25EB.d: The supercharger clutch control current does not match the commanded value within tolerance. Either coil resistance has drifted or the driver feedback is implausible.
s: Check engine or transmission warning light on
Possible limp mode (locked in one gear)
Slipping or shuddering during gear changes

c: Control wire shorted to ground
Internal short in the clutch coil
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25EC.d: Voltage on the supercharger clutch control line is below the expected window. Usually a short to ground or a shorted clutch coil.
s: Check engine or transmission warning light on
Possible limp mode (locked in one gear)
Slipping or shuddering during gear changes

c: Control wire shorted to a B+ supply
Open clutch coil
Connector pins corroded - high contact resistance
P25ED.d: Voltage on the supercharger clutch control line is above the expected window. Typical causes are a short to battery or an open coil that lets the driver float high.
s: Check engine or transmission warning light on
Possible limp mode (locked in one gear)
Slipping or shuddering during gear changes

c: Open pump motor winding or worn brushes
Broken control wire between ECU and pump

P2602.d: P2602 reports that the control circuit of electric coolant pump A reads low - a short to ground, or a corresponding report from the driver stage. Which pump is A varies: Ford's 2020-2023 gasoline OBD summary defines it as the auxiliary pump of the high-temperature loop for cabin heating, checked continuously over 5 s above 11 V; GM's 2008 3.6 L LLT table uses an after-run pump (P2602 = circuit to ground, stored only as pending code without warning light). VW's 2014 books set it below about 3.0 V on the Passat and CC and below 2.8-3.2 V on the Touareg. P2600 is the open circuit, P2601 the performance fault, P2603 the high-side fault. Without the pump, heater output or after-run cooling of a hot engine may suffer.
s: Fault code stored; warning light depends on manufacturer (none at GM)
No after-run of the pump after a hot shutdown
P2602.t: Coolant Pump A Control Circuit Low

c: Control wire shorted to battery voltage
Seized or sluggish pump drawing excessive current
Faulty driver stage in the ECM
P2603.d: P2603 means the control circuit of electric coolant pump A reads high - typically a short to battery voltage, or an overcurrent seen by the driver stage. Ford's 2020-2023 gasoline OBD summary assigns pump A to the auxiliary high-temperature loop for cabin heating and sets P2602/P2603 when the smart driver reports a fault within 5 s. GM's 2008 3.6 L LLT table monitors its after-run pump for a circuit fault to voltage (pending code only, no warning light). VW's 2014 books use a current threshold: about 0.60-1.20 A on the Passat and CC, 5.5-10 A on the Touareg. CARB requires output components to be checked for circuit faults. P2600 is the open circuit, P2601 performance, P2602 the low-side fault. Heater output or after-run cooling may be lost.
s: Fault code stored; warning light depends on manufacturer (none at GM)
Higher coolant temperature after hot shutdown
P2603.t: Coolant Pump A Control Circuit High

P2604.d: P2604 is the functional check of intake air heater A - the grid heater in the intake that warms the charge air of a diesel engine for cold starts. The circuit responds, but current, voltage drop or heating effect do not match the command. CARB requires glow plugs and intake air heaters to be monitored for proper functional response and for correct current and voltage drop. Volvo's heavy-truck engine bulletins (2020, 2022) list P2604-7F among the codes caused by a weak pre-heat relay and fix it with a software update, a check of terminal tension at heater and relay, and a new relay plus supply cable. P0540-P0543 cover the electrical faults of heater A, P2605-P2608 heater B, P2609 the system. Expect hard cold starts and white smoke.
s: White smoke and rough running after a cold start
P2604.t: Intake Air Heater A Circuit Range/Performance

P3402.d: This code reports that cylinder 1 does not respond as expected when the engine computer switches it off or back on, although the control circuit itself tests fine. Ford lists P3402 in its Variable Displacement Engine monitor for 2020-2023 gasoline engines: it runs continuously during deactivation, entry and exit, between 400 and 4500 rpm and once oil pressure has had about two seconds to build. GM handles the mechanical check for cylinder 1 under its own code P3498 instead. Wiring faults on the same channel set P3401, P3403 or P3404. A driver typically notices a warning lamp, a shake when the engine changes modes, or a misfire on cylinder 1.

P3403.d: The engine computer drives the deactivation valve for cylinder 1 through an output stage that checks its own wiring. P3403 means that check found the control line pulled to ground. GM documents it for the L84 and L86 V8s (2019): with the driver off, an impedance below 0.5 ohm to ground counts as a fault, and 20 failures in 25 samples taken every 250 ms set a Type B code, so the lamp comes on after the second trip. Ford's VDE monitor flags the same short via its smart driver within 5 seconds. An open line is P3401, a short to battery voltage P3404, a mechanical failure P3402. The engine then stays in all-cylinder mode, mainly costing fuel.
s: Check engine lamp on after two trips
Engine no longer switches to reduced-cylinder mode

P3404.d: P3404 is the short-to-power counterpart within the cylinder 1 group. GM tests it while the low-side driver is switched on: if the output still shows less than 0.5 ohm to supply voltage, the current has no proper path through the solenoid, and 20 of 25 samples at 250 ms set a Type B fault. The test only runs with at least 11 V at the powertrain relay and about 425 rpm (L84; 400 rpm on the L86). Ford names P3404 for the single deactivating cylinder of its VDE engines. Typical culprits are a control wire touching a supply line or a solenoid with shorted windings. Compare P3403 (short to ground) and P3401 (open).

P3405.d: J2012 reserves P3405 for an open control circuit of a separate exhaust valve actuator on cylinder 1. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The common systems do not need it: in GM's Dynamic Fuel Management one solenoid per cylinder feeds oil to both intake and exhaust lifters, and Ford's VDE only lists intake codes for cylinder 1. A GM patent application uses one shared hydraulic valve and only sets the order, with the exhaust valves switched off and back on before the intake valves; a Ford patent watches the exhaust valve via exhaust pressure. A separate exhaust actuator would fall under CARB's output component rule, which asks for continuity checks. If used, an open coil or wire would set P3405, while P3401 covers the intake side and P3406-P3408 the other exhaust faults.
s: Cylinder deactivation or valve switching disabled

P3406.d: Where an engine controls the exhaust valves of cylinder 1 separately, P3406 would mean the exhaust side does not follow the command although the circuit checks pass. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Ford holds a patent that detects an exhaust valve still opening after deactivation through pressure changes in the exhaust, and a GM patent, using one shared control valve, has the exhaust valves deactivate and also reactivate before the intake valves, so a lagging exhaust side is a real failure mode. Production systems from GM and Ford instead check the whole cylinder (GM P3498, Ford P3402). Electrical faults on this channel are P3405, P3407 and P3408; if the cylinder keeps pumping exhaust, the driver may feel roughness.

P3407.d: P3407 stands for a short to ground in the control circuit of a dedicated exhaust valve actuator on cylinder 1. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, so there are no published thresholds. As an analogy, GM's intake-side code P3403 counts an impedance under 0.5 ohm to ground, seen with the driver off, as a fault. CARB requires such output circuits to be checked for shorts. Engines with one shared solenoid per cylinder, like GM's AFM and DFM V8s, report this fault under the intake-side codes instead. An open exhaust circuit would be P3405, a short to power P3408. The car usually keeps running normally on all cylinders, with a warning lamp.

P3408.d: If an engine has its own actuator for the exhaust valves of cylinder 1, P3408 marks a control circuit that reads high, usually a short to battery voltage. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. For comparison, GM checks the intake-side P3404 with the driver switched on and flags under 0.5 ohm to supply. A GM patent application switches intake and exhaust valves together through one shared hydraulic valve, exhaust side first, and describes no separate exhaust channel either. With one solenoid per cylinder, as on GM's DFM, the code is not needed. Siblings: P3405 open, P3406 function, P3407 short to ground; P3404 is the intake-side equivalent.

On the 3.6 L V6 (LGX, LGZ) cylinder 2 is one of the two active fuel management cylinders, and an engineering bulletin links P3409 to oil leaking from the rocker arm oil control valve in the camshaft cover. On the L84 V8 with Dynamic Fuel Management every cylinder has a solenoid; GM flags an open circuit when it sees more than 200 kohm with the driver off, 20 of 25 samples at 250 ms, Type B. P3412.d: On GM's L84 V8 each cylinder, including cylinder 2, has a valve lifter oil solenoid bolted into the block valley. NHTSA's description of the system notes these solenoids are driven with peak-and-hold current for fast response. P3412 is set when the control line for cylinder 2 is shorted to supply voltage: GM checks it with the driver on and treats under 0.5 ohm to power as failed, 20 of 25 samples at 250 ms, Type B. In that state the computer cannot pull the solenoid properly and drops cylinder 2 from deactivation. Related codes are P3409 for an open circuit, P3411 for a short to ground and P3410 when the circuit is fine but the cylinder does not respond.

c: Wiring shorted to ground

c: Oil leaking at the cylinder 5 control valve into its connector (GM 3.6 L V6)
Broken wire or spread terminal in the solenoid circuit
Open coil in the cylinder 5 solenoid
Engine control module output fault
P3433.d: P3433 reports an open control circuit to the deactivation valve of cylinder 5, and GM has used it across three generations. The 2007 V6 with Displacement on Demand, which shut off cylinders 1, 3 and 5, already flagged a short or open after 30 failures in 100 samples at 250 ms above 800 rpm. On the 3.6 L V6 (LGX, LGZ) cylinder 5 is an active fuel management cylinder, and GM tied P3433 to oil leaking from the rocker arm control valve in the camshaft cover. The 2019 L84 V8 tests every cylinder with a 200 kohm limit. Each time it is a Type B code. P3434 to P3436 are the function and short codes for the same cylinder.
s: Oil seepage at the valve cover control valve (V6)

c: Oil leaking past the cylinder 5 control valve seal
Switching rocker or lifter of cylinder 5 not latching
Solenoid tip broken off in the bore
Low or aged engine oil
P3434.d: With P3434 the computer has found that cylinder 5 does not switch off or back on correctly, while the control circuit tests fine. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's L84 runs the equivalent test under P349C: manifold pressure stays too high while cylinder 5 is commanded off, meaning its valves keep working. For 3.6 L V6 engines, GM bulletin 21-NA-036 describes the field picture: misfires on cylinder 5 (P0305), sometimes only after a reduced-cylinder phase, from oil leaking past the control valve or rockers that do not latch, and asks to check for a solenoid tip broken off in the bore. Wiring faults for this cylinder are P3433, P3435 and P3436.

c: Oil in the cylinder 5 valve connector creating a leakage path (GM 3.6 L V6)
Control wire shorted to ground
Shorted cylinder 5 solenoid
Engine control module driver fault
P3435.d: P3435 flags a short to ground on the control line of the cylinder 5 deactivation valve. GM documents it codewise twice: in the 2019 tables for the L84 V8, with under 0.5 ohm to ground in the driver-off state, 20 of 25 samples at 250 ms and Type B, and in an engineering bulletin for 3.6 L V6 engines (LGX, LGZ) where P3435 appears along with P3433 and P3409 when oil leaks from the rocker arm control valve. Oil that wicks into the connector can create exactly such a leakage path. P3433 is the open circuit, P3436 the short to power, P3434 a mechanical failure. In daily driving the engine simply stays on all cylinders.
s: Oil wetness at the valve cover around the control valve (V6)
P3435.t: Cylinder 5 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit Low

c: Control wire touching a voltage supply
Shorted coil in the cylinder 5 solenoid
Engine control module output stage defect
P3436.d: P3436 is the short-to-power code for the cylinder 5 deactivation valve. Publicly it is documented by GM for the L84 V8 (2019), where Dynamic Fuel Management uses a dedicated valve lifter oil solenoid for each of the eight cylinders. The engine computer checks the line while its low-side driver is on; an impedance below 0.5 ohm toward supply voltage counts as a fault, confirmed by 20 of 25 samples at 250 ms, with at least 11 V and 425 rpm. As a Type B code it lights the lamp after two consecutive trips. Because the solenoid then cannot be switched in a controlled way, cylinder 5 is excluded from deactivation. Siblings: P3433 open, P3435 short to ground, P3434 function.
s: Check engine lamp after two trips
P3436.t: Cylinder 5 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit High

c: Broken wire or connector to the cylinder 5 exhaust actuator
Open actuator coil
Engine control module driver fault
P3437.d: P3437 is reserved for an open circuit in a separate exhaust valve actuator on cylinder 5. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM, the main user of cylinder 5 deactivation codes (2007 V6, 3.6 L V6, L84 V8), only publishes the intake-side group P3433 to P3436, because its systems switch both valves of a cylinder together; NHTSA's description of Dynamic Fuel Management states that each solenoid feeds intake and exhaust lifters. CARB still expects any emission-relevant actuator to be checked for continuity, which is what this code would report. P3438 to P3440 are the other exhaust codes for cylinder 5, P3433 the intake-side open.

c: Exhaust lifter or rocker of cylinder 5 slow to switch
Insufficient oil pressure for switching
Exhaust actuator valve sticking
P3438.d: P3438 describes an exhaust side of cylinder 5 that is commanded to deactivate or reactivate but does not follow, with an intact circuit. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Two patents show why the exhaust side matters: in a GM patent application one shared valve switches the exhaust valves off, and back on, before the intake valves, so an exhaust lifter that lags breaks that order, and Ford detects an exhaust valve still opening after deactivation from exhaust pressure. If the exhaust valve keeps opening while the cylinder is off, the engine can run rough. GM's DFM engines report a cylinder whose valves stay active as P349C. The electrical codes for this channel are P3437, P3439 and P3440.
s: Roughness or noise while cylinders are switched off

c: Control wire of the exhaust actuator grounded
Internally shorted exhaust actuator
Faulty engine control module output
P3439.d: P3439 would report a short to ground in the control circuit of a dedicated exhaust valve actuator on cylinder 5. No manufacturer documents this code publicly, and no threshold is published for it. The closest documented reference is the intake-side P3435, which GM's L84 sets at under 0.5 ohm to ground with the driver off, after 20 of 25 samples. CARB's output component rules call for exactly this kind of short-circuit check on any actuator that can affect emissions. Engines that switch both valves of cylinder 5 with one solenoid report a short only through P3435. Exhaust-side siblings are P3437 (open), P3438 (function) and P3440 (short to power).
s: Engine runs on all cylinders only
P3439.t: Cylinder 5 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit Low

c: Exhaust actuator control wire shorted to voltage
Shorted actuator coil
Engine control module output stage fault
P3440.d: P3440 closes the cylinder 5 block and stands for a high signal, usually a short to supply voltage, in the circuit of a separate exhaust valve actuator. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The code only makes sense on an engine with a separate exhaust actuator; a Ford patent, for example, checks via exhaust pressure whether an exhaust valve still opens after deactivation. Current production systems that deactivate cylinder 5 drive both valves from one solenoid, and GM reports a short to power there as P3436, checked with the driver on and a 0.5 ohm limit. If a dedicated exhaust channel did short high, the computer would stop using deactivation and light the lamp. Compare P3437, P3438 and P3439.
P3440.t: Cylinder 5 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit High

c: Solenoid harness broken or chafed through (on the 5.7 L Hemi by the manifold heat shield)
Open coil in the cylinder 6 deactivation solenoid
Loose or corroded connector at the cylinder 6 solenoid
Control module software that needs an update (Chrysler TSB 18-002-25)
P3441.d: Cylinder 6 belongs to both classic V8 deactivation groups, so P3441 is a code that real engines set. On GM V8s with Active Fuel Management, which park cylinders 1, 7, 6 and 4, the 2019 tables list it for the L86 truck engine and the LT4 Corvette: with the low-side driver off, more than 200 kohm between output and ground counts as an open, and 20 failures in 25 samples (every 250 ms, from 400 rpm) store a Type B code. The L84 with Dynamic Fuel Management runs the same check from 425 rpm. Chrysler names P3441 for the 5.7 L Hemi with MDS; a STAR case blames a heat shield rubbing through the solenoid harness. Shorts on this circuit are P3443 and P3444.
s: Engine no longer drops to four-cylinder mode
Possibly circuit codes for cylinders 1, 4 and 7 as well if the shared harness is damaged

c: Oil level too low, wrong grade or worn oil, so pressure builds too slowly
Deactivating lifter of cylinder 6 not locking or unlocking
Cylinder 6 solenoid valve sticking or its oil screen clogged
Code stored after a voltage dip during cranking, cured by an ECM update (GM analogue 20-NA-204)
P3442.d: P3442 would flag cylinder 6 failing to switch off or back on while its control circuit is electrically sound. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. Both large users of cylinder 6 deactivation picked their own numbers instead: GM's L84 reports a cylinder 6 that keeps breathing as P349D, judged from filtered manifold pressure in 22 of 25 opportunities (Type B), and Chrysler's 5.7 L Hemi uses P1416, Cylinder 6 Reactivation Control Performance. GM also warns that P349D can set after a voltage dip during cranking, which an ECM update cures. Real mechanical faults usually trace back to the oil supply or a lifter that does not latch. Electrical faults on the same channel are P3441, P3443 and P3444.
s: Jerk or vibration when the engine changes between eight and four cylinders
Fuel consumption rises because deactivation is locked out

c: Insulation of the cylinder 6 control wire worn through to ground
Cylinder 6 solenoid shorted internally to its housing
Moisture or oil bridging the pins of the solenoid connector
Output stage in the engine control module damaged
P3443.d: Here the engine computer has found the cylinder 6 solenoid's switched lead pulled to ground. GM spells out the test for its 2019 V8s (L84, L86 and the LT4 Corvette): while the low-side driver is off, an impedance under 0.5 ohm toward ground is a fault, and 20 hits among 25 checks while the powertrain relay supplies at least 11 V store a Type B code. GM adds that some controllers record the open-circuit code P3441 at the same moment, so the pair does not prove two separate faults. On the L84 each solenoid also has a high-side feed, and a short to ground there carries GM's own code P3114. P3444 is the short to voltage on this channel. Cylinder deactivation stays off until the fault is repaired.
s: Check engine lamp on from the second faulty trip
P3441 stored at the same time on some GM controllers
P3443.t: Cylinder 6 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit Low

c: Cylinder 6 control wire in contact with a supply wire in the harness
Shorted turns in the cylinder 6 solenoid coil
Faulty output stage in the engine control module
P3444.d: P3444 is set when the output that switches the cylinder 6 deactivation solenoid to ground still sees supply voltage while it is turned on, meaning the line has a short to power instead of a path through the coil. GM tests this on the 2019 L84, L86 and LT4 V8s with a limit of 0.5 ohm to controller power, 20 errors out of 25 samples at 250 ms intervals and Type B lamp logic. On the L84, whose solenoids also have a switched high-side feed, a short to voltage on that feed has the separate GM code P3115. Because the ECM can no longer energize the valve, cylinder 6 simply keeps firing and the engine gives up four-cylinder operation. Compare P3441 (open) and P3443 (short to ground).
s: Engine runs on all eight cylinders permanently
Slightly higher fuel consumption at light load
P3444.t: Cylinder 6 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit High

c: Broken wire or loose connector at the cylinder 6 exhaust actuator
Actuator coil interrupted
Output stage in the control module faulty
P3445.d: P3445 is defined for a break in the wiring of a stand-alone actuator that would control the exhaust valves of cylinder 6. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. The engines that deactivate cylinder 6 today, GM's AFM and DFM V8s and Chrysler's Hemi with MDS, publish only intake-side codes for this cylinder (P3441, and at GM also P3443 and P3444). NHTSA's description of GM's DFM hardware explains why: a single solenoid per cylinder sends oil to the intake and the exhaust lifters alike, which then unlock one after the other. An engine with its own exhaust-side actuators would have to check their wiring for continuity under CARB's rules for output components, and that is the fault this code names. P3446 to P3448 complete the exhaust group.

c: Exhaust lifter of cylinder 6 switching late or not at all
Oil pressure too low for reliable switching
Exhaust control valve sticking
P3446.d: P3446 stands for an exhaust valve on cylinder 6 that does not follow a deactivation or reactivation command although its circuit is intact. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM watches a closely related failure under a code of its own: on the 2019 L84, P318E (Cylinder 6 Trapped High Pressure Exhaust Charge) looks for an exhaust valve that fails to open and let the burned gas out, recognised by crankshaft jerk in 66 of 100 samples, Type B, with immediate protective action. A Ford patent covers the opposite case, an exhaust valve that keeps opening after shut-off, detected from exhaust pressure. The electrical codes for this exhaust channel are P3445, P3447 and P3448.
s: Knock-like noise or vibration when the cylinder is switched back on

c: Exhaust actuator wire of cylinder 6 chafed against the engine
Internal short to ground in the exhaust actuator
Damaged driver in the engine control module
P3447.d: P3447 is about a ground fault on the lead of a stand-alone exhaust actuator for cylinder 6. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM, the one maker publishing the full set of cylinder 6 circuit codes, switches both valves of the cylinder with one solenoid and reports a ground short as the intake-side P3443: impedance below 0.5 ohm toward ground while the driver is off, 20 of 25 samples, Type B. A comparable test would apply here, because CARB requires circuit monitoring for every emission-relevant output. NHTSA notes that GM inhibits deactivation as soon as a solenoid driver circuit fault is present, so the practical result is an engine running on all cylinders. P3445 (open) and P3448 (short to power) are the neighbouring exhaust codes.
P3447.t: Cylinder 6 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit Low

c: Exhaust actuator wire touching a supply line
Shorted turns in the exhaust actuator coil of cylinder 6
Engine control module output stage faulty
P3448.d: If cylinder 6 had its own exhaust valve actuator, P3448 would report its control line shorted to battery voltage. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. A GM patent application on cylinder deactivation switches both sides through one shared hydraulic valve and only lets the exhaust valves go first, off and back on, so it shows no separate exhaust control either; GM's production V8s likewise put both lifters on one solenoid and publish only P3444 for a short to power on cylinder 6. That test, below 0.5 ohm to power with the driver switched on and 20 of 25 samples, is the reference for how such a fault would be judged. With the actuator unusable, deactivation is blocked. P3445 to P3447 are the sibling exhaust codes.
P3448.t: Cylinder 6 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit High

c: MDS harness at the rear of the driver-side head worn through by the manifold heat shield (5.7 L Hemi)
Cylinder 7 solenoid coil open
Solenoid connector loose or corroded
PCM calibration needing an update (Chrysler TSB 18-002-25)
P3449.d: P3449 tells you the engine computer lost continuity in the circuit to the cylinder 7 deactivation solenoid. Chrysler documents it twice for the 5.7 L Hemi with MDS: a 2025 bulletin for the 2023 RAM 1500 eTorque lists it next to a cylinder 7 misfire (P0307) and fixes it with new PCM software, and a STAR case names P3449 first when the driver-side manifold heat shield has worn through the MDS harness at the rear of the cylinder head. GM uses the code on AFM V8s (L86, LT4 Corvette) and on the DFM L84, flagging more than 200 kohm in the off state, 20 of 25 samples, Type B. P3451 and P3452 report shorts, P3450 a mechanical fault on cylinder 7.
s: Rough idle or misfire on cylinder 7 (P0307) on the 5.7 L Hemi

c: Locking pins in a cylinder 7 lifter sticking from wear or dirt
Insufficient or aged oil delaying the switch
Oil screen or passage to the cylinder 7 solenoid blocked
Leaking O-ring on the solenoid lets pressure escape
P3450.d: P3450 is meant for a cylinder 7 whose valves do not switch as commanded while the solenoid circuit itself checks out. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. In practice the lifters do the switching: NHTSA's account of GM's system shows oil pressure pushing spring-loaded locking pins inward so the lifter body moves without lifting the valve, and DFM only engages with coolant between 40 and 126 °C, more than 20 s of running and above 13 km/h. When that mechanism fails on cylinder 7, GM's L84 sets P349E from manifold pressure, and Chrysler's Hemi sets P1417, Cylinder 7 Reactivation Control Performance. P3449, P3451 and P3452 are the electrical codes for the same cylinder.
s: Ticking noise from the valve train

c: Cylinder 7 control wire pinched or chafed to ground
Cylinder 7 solenoid shorted internally
Oil or water inside the solenoid connector
Defective driver in the engine control module
P3451.d: P3451 means the switched ground line of the cylinder 7 deactivation solenoid has contact with ground somewhere along its way. GM documents the check for the L84 and L86 trucks and the LT4 Corvette (2019): with the driver off, less than 0.5 ohm to ground, 20 hits in 25 samples taken every 250 ms, Type B, meaning the warning lamp waits for a second faulty trip. According to GM, certain controllers log the open-circuit code P3449 along with it, so both codes together need not mean two faults. On the L84 the high-side feed of the same solenoid reports a ground short under its own code P3117. P3452 is the short to power on this channel, P3450 the mechanical fault.
s: Check engine lamp on after two trips
P3449 may be stored as well
No four-cylinder mode, higher fuel use
P3451.t: Cylinder 7 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit Low

c: Cylinder 7 control wire shorted to a voltage feed
Low-resistance coil in the cylinder 7 solenoid
Engine control module driver defective
P3452.d: Unlike the open and ground-short checks, GM can only detect P3452 while the cylinder 7 solenoid driver is switched on, because a short to supply voltage shows up as an output that will not pull low when it should. The 2019 tables for the L84, L86 and LT4 set the limit at 0.5 ohm to controller power and need 20 errors out of 25 samples, Type B. The check therefore depends on the ECM actually commanding deactivation; on GM's DFM engines that only happens with coolant above 40 °C, more than 20 s after start and above 13 km/h, according to NHTSA. Typical causes are a harness pressed against a feed wire or a solenoid with shorted windings. P3449 and P3451 are the other circuit codes for cylinder 7.
s: Check engine lamp on, often only after longer warm drives
P3452.t: Cylinder 7 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit High

c: Interrupted wire to the cylinder 7 exhaust actuator
Burnt-out actuator coil
Corroded actuator connector
P3453.d: P3453 is the code SAE assigns to an open circuit in a dedicated exhaust valve actuator for cylinder 7. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's description of Dynamic Fuel Management, published by NHTSA, shows how exhaust control works without such an actuator: the same oil signal unlocks the intake lifter at once, while the exhaust lifter waits until the valve spring load drops on the base circle of the cam. Separate wiring exists only in designs with an extra exhaust actuator, and CARB would require its continuity to be monitored. Actual cylinder 7 circuit faults on GM and Chrysler V8s show up as P3449 instead. P3454 to P3456 are the other exhaust codes; P3455 is the short to ground.

c: Exhaust lifter of cylinder 7 stuck in the unlocked state
Oil pressure or oil quality inadequate for switching
Exhaust control valve slow or sticking
P3454.d: P3454 covers an exhaust valve on cylinder 7 that does not switch as commanded, with no electrical fault on its control circuit. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM's own cylinder 7 check P318F on the 2019 L84 shows why the exhaust side matters: if the exhaust valve fails to open and release the burned gas, the trapped charge is compressed again, cylinder pressure climbs and the intake mechanism can be damaged on reactivation, so the ECM reacts at once (crankshaft jerk test, 66 of 100 samples, Type B). A Ford patent tackles the reverse problem, an exhaust valve still opening after deactivation, spotted through exhaust pressure. P3453, P3455 and P3456 are the electrical codes.
s: Hard knock or jolt when cylinder 7 is reactivated

c: Solenoid or wiring shorted to ground
ECM low-side driver failed
Connector corrosion or pin damage
P3455.d: The engine control module has detected a low voltage condition in the control circuit of the cylinder 7 exhaust valve deactivation solenoid. A short to ground or low-side driver fault prevents proper actuation of the exhaust valve during cylinder deactivation events on cylinder 7.
P3455.t: Cylinder 7 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit Low

c: Actuator wire of cylinder 7 shorted to battery voltage
Exhaust actuator coil with shorted turns
Current driver in the control module failed
P3456.d: P3456 would flag a cylinder 7 exhaust valve actuator whose control line is shorted to supply voltage. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. According to NHTSA's summary of the DFM system, GM drives its deactivation solenoids with peak-and-hold current drivers for fast, repeatable switching, and one solenoid serves both valves of the cylinder, so a short to power is caught under the intake-side code P3452 instead (below 0.5 ohm to power with the driver on, 20 of 25 samples, Type B). CARB requires such a check for any emission-relevant output, which is why the exhaust code exists at all. A short to ground on the same channel is P3455, an open circuit P3453, a mechanical fault P3454.
s: Engine does not enter reduced-cylinder mode
P3456.t: Cylinder 7 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit High

c: Wire to the cylinder 8 solenoid broken or chafed in the lifter valley harness
Open winding in the cylinder 8 solenoid
Poor contact at the solenoid connector
Engine control module output stage faulty
P3457.d: Cylinder 8 is not among the cylinders that classic Active Fuel Management or Chrysler's MDS shut off (both use 1, 4, 6 and 7), so P3457 is documented only for newer designs. GM's 2019 tables list it for the L84 with Dynamic Fuel Management, which can deactivate every cylinder: more than 200 kohm with the low-side driver off, 20 of 25 samples every 250 ms from 425 rpm, Type B. GM's AFM/DFM information bulletin adds that the LTA and LT2 engines deactivate cylinders 2, 3, 5 and 8. GM also notes that some controllers store P3459 together with an open. P3458 is the function code for cylinder 8, P3459 and P3460 the short-circuit codes.
s: P3459 may be stored alongside on some GM controllers

c: Cylinder 8 deactivation lifter not unlocking or relocking
Oil pressure too low or oil aerated
Cylinder 8 solenoid valve sluggish or its screen blocked
False entry after low voltage while cranking, fixed by ECM update (GM analogue 20-NA-204)
P3458.d: P3458 describes a cylinder 8 that does not deactivate or reactivate as commanded although its control circuit is electrically fine. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM, the only maker with published cylinder 8 deactivation codes, files this failure under P349F on the L84: during a commanded skip, filtered manifold pressure stays above a threshold, which means the intake and exhaust valves kept working; the test runs with air charge above 120 mg and MAP/BARO between 0.30 and 0.95, and 22 failures in 25 opportunities give a Type B code. Bulletin 20-NA-204 adds that on 2021 full-size SUVs with L84 and L87 a voltage dip during cranking can set P349F without any hardware fault. Electrical faults are P3457, P3459 and P3460.
s: Check engine lamp on, sometimes going out again
Shake or roughness in light-load cruising

c: Cylinder 8 control wire grounded through damaged insulation
Internal short in the cylinder 8 solenoid
Contamination in the solenoid connector
Output driver in the engine control module damaged
P3459.d: When the ground-side control line of the cylinder 8 deactivation solenoid touches ground, the ECM stores P3459. GM publishes this test for the 2019 L84 V8 with Dynamic Fuel Management: driver off, impedance below 0.5 ohm to ground, a minimum of 11 V on the relay feed and 425 rpm, 20 errors in 25 samples, Type B. Some GM controllers log P3457 at the same time. Because a DFM engine may skip any cylinder, a fault on cylinder 8 shuts down a system that otherwise uses this cylinder routinely; GM's LTA and LT2 also include cylinder 8 in their fixed deactivation set. A ground short on the solenoid's high-side feed has its own GM code, P311A. P3460 is the short to power.
s: Check engine lamp on after the second trip
Engine runs on all eight cylinders at all times
P3459.t: Cylinder 8 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit Low

c: Cylinder 8 control wire in contact with a voltage source
Shorted turns in the cylinder 8 solenoid
Faulty driver in the engine control module
P3460.d: P3460 reports a short to supply voltage on the control circuit of the cylinder 8 deactivation solenoid, found while the output is switched on. GM lists it for the 2019 L84: under 0.5 ohm between output and controller power, 20 of 25 samples spaced 250 ms apart, Type B, with the same 11 V and 425 rpm enable limits as the other cylinder 8 circuit checks. GM's table contains a slip here: the strategy column for P3460 speaks of the cylinder 7 solenoid, while code and component name cylinder 8. Typical causes are harness damage against a feed wire or a solenoid with shorted turns; the visible result is that the engine stops using cylinder 8 deactivation. Siblings: P3457 (open) and P3459 (short to ground).
s: Cylinder deactivation inactive, slightly higher fuel use
P3460.t: Cylinder 8 Deactivation/Intake Valve Control Circuit High

c: Wire or plug to the cylinder 8 exhaust actuator broken
Exhaust actuator winding open
Control module output defective
P3461.d: In the J2012 scheme, P3461 marks lost continuity to an exhaust-side actuator of its own on cylinder 8. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. In the published sources, cylinder 8 is deactivated only by GM's newer V8s (DFM on the L84 and L87, a fixed 2-3-5-8 pattern on the LTA and LT2), and per NHTSA those engines feed both lifters of a cylinder from one solenoid, leaving no separate exhaust wiring to test. A GM patent application likewise uses one shared hydraulic valve and only staggers the exhaust valves ahead of the intake valves; only a separate exhaust actuator would fall under CARB's continuity check for output components. P3462 to P3464 are the other cylinder 8 exhaust codes, P3457 the intake-side open.

c: Exhaust lifter of cylinder 8 failing to relock in time
Oil supply to the lifter gallery insufficient
Exhaust-side control valve sticking
P3462.d: With P3462 the ECM would be saying that the exhaust valve of cylinder 8 ignores deactivation commands even though nothing is wrong electrically. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. GM covers the exhaust side of cylinder 8 on the 2019 L84 with its own code P3190, Cylinder 8 Trapped High Pressure Exhaust Charge: if crankshaft jerk, normalized by engine speed, exceeds a load-dependent threshold while the cylinder is deactivated, the exhaust valve is judged not to have opened, and 66 failures in 100 samples set a Type B code. Ford patented the complementary check for an exhaust valve that keeps opening after deactivation, based on exhaust pressure. Symptoms range from vibration in reduced-cylinder mode to a misfire on cylinder 8 (P0308).

c: Cylinder 8 exhaust actuator wire shorted to the engine block
Exhaust actuator shorted to ground internally
Driver stage in the engine control module faulty
P3463.d: P3463 would mean that the control line of a dedicated cylinder 8 exhaust actuator is shorted to ground. No manufacturer documents this code publicly. On the only engines with documented cylinder 8 deactivation, GM's L84 and its relatives, one solenoid handles both valves, and GM reports a ground short on it as P3459, testing for less than 0.5 ohm to ground with the driver off. NHTSA's summary of the system lists solenoid driver circuit faults among the reasons the ECM inhibits deactivation, which is also what a driver would notice here: the engine keeps all eight cylinders running and uses a little more fuel. P3461 covers an open, P3462 the function and P3464 a short to power in this exhaust group.
s: Engine stays on all eight cylinders
P3463.t: Cylinder 8 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit Low

c: Solenoid or wiring shorted to power
Solenoid coil open
ECM driver failed
P3464.d: The engine control module has detected a high voltage condition in the control circuit of the cylinder 8 exhaust valve deactivation solenoid. A short to voltage or open low-side path causes the driver to read above the expected range, disabling cylinder deactivation requests for cylinder 8.
P3464.t: Cylinder 8 Exhaust Valve Control Circuit High

c: Broken or chafed wire to the cylinder 9 actuator
Open coil in the cylinder 9 solenoid
Loose or corroded connector at the solenoid pack
Output stage in the engine control module failed
P3465.d: P3465 flags an open circuit to the actuator meant to shut down cylinder 9 or hold its intake valve closed. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; J2012 reserves the codes for cylinders 9 to 12 for engines with more than eight cylinders. Among such engines, Mercedes' M137 V12 (S 600 and CL 600, 1998 to 2002) had a shut-off system built around a solenoid pack and oil pressure tubes, whereas Audi's R8 V10 idles a whole bank by stopping injection and ignition. For orientation, GM treats the comparable circuit on its V8s as open above 200 kohm with the driver off, 20 failures in 25 samples. P3467 and P3468 cover shorts on the same line, P3466 a mechanical fault, P3469 the exhaust side of cylinder 9.
s: Slightly higher fuel consumption at part load

c: Oil level, pressure or quality too poor to switch cylinder 9
Leak at the oil tubes or solenoid pack feeding cylinder 9
Switching lifter of cylinder 9 sticking

No manufacturer documents this code publicly; J2012 reserves the codes for cylinders 9 to 12 for engines with more than eight cylinders. In valve-based systems the switching happens hydraulically; NHTSA's account of GM's design describes oil pressure moving locking pins inside the lifter. The Mercedes M137 V12, whose shut-off system relied on a solenoid pack and oil pressure tubes, is known for trouble with exactly those parts, exactly the kind of fault this code targets. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; J2012 reserves the codes for cylinders 9 to 12 for engines with more than eight cylinders. No manufacturer documents this code publicly; J2012 reserves the codes for cylinders 9 to 12 for engines with more than eight cylinders. A distinct exhaust actuator only exists where intake and exhaust valves are switched independently; a GM patent at least shows that the exhaust valves can follow their own timing, being deactivated before the intake valves and reactivated before them too. GM's own production system uses one solenoid per cylinder for both valves, and the publicly described ten- and twelve-cylinder systems (Audi R8 V10, Bentley W12) keep the valves moving altogether. So an open circuit here can only concern an engine that carries such hardware. P3471 and P3472 report shorts, P3470 a functional fault, P3465 the intake side.

The risk behind it is described in a Ford patent: an exhaust valve that keeps opening after shut-off spoils the gas cushion in the cylinder and can be detected from changes in exhaust pressure. The opposite case, a valve that stays shut on reactivation, traps hot gas under pressure. Neither the Lamborghini Aventador V12 nor the Huracán V10 publishes how their bank shut-off works, and Audi's V10 simply cuts injection and ignition, so this check has no known user. If such a circuit is present, test it the same way as the intake circuit: resistance to ground with the connector unplugged, then the coil. When an exhaust valve keeps working after shut-off, the trapped gas is pumped out and the cylinder cools, which a Ford patent proposes to catch through exhaust pressure. Cooling is also why Bentley alternates the idle bank of its W12 to protect cylinders and converter; Bentley, like Audi on the R8 V10, shuts down banks rather than individual valves. U0029.d: U0029 reports degraded communication although no hard wiring fault is identified: frames get lost, error counters rise or messages arrive late on vehicle communication bus A. SAE J2012 gives each vehicle bus a block of codes: the bus itself, performance, then open, low and high for the (+) and the (-) line and a short between them; which physical network carries which letter is set by the manufacturer. Modules on the affected bus may stop exchanging data, so lost-communication codes and warning lights in several systems usually appear together.

U0091.d: U0091 reports the (-) line shorted to the (+) line on vehicle communication bus G. SAE J2012 gives each vehicle bus a block of codes: the bus itself, performance, then open, low and high for the (+) and the (-) line and a short between them; which physical network carries which letter is set by the manufacturer. On CAN networks (+) normally stands for CAN-High and (-) for CAN-Low. Modules on the affected bus may stop exchanging data, so lost-communication codes and warning lights in several systems usually appear together.

In GM's network logic every node broadcasts a state-of-health message with ignition on; if it stays away while the supply is between 9 and 16 V, the listeners store a code naming the silent unit, not themselves. U0148.d: U0148 reports that the third gateway, Gateway C, has gone silent. A gateway links separate bus segments (CAN, LIN, Ethernet) and forwards messages between them, so when it drops out, every module behind it disappears too. GM's procedure for U0100-U02FF explains the mechanism: listeners expect a periodic state-of-health message and log the missing sender once it fails to arrive at 9-16 V. No manufacturer documents U0148 publicly; GM's U-code list contains only U0146 for its serial data gateway. Unlike U0146 and U0147 for gateways A and B, or U0149 and U0150 for D and E, this code names the C unit, whose role differs by maker. Often several other U-codes appear at once; MIL usually off.

Many U-codes stored across the vehicle

U0149.d: U0149 names Gateway D as the module whose messages no longer arrive. Vehicles with several gateways split the network into domains, and each gateway routes traffic between its own bus segments; losing D therefore cuts off the domain it serves. Following GM's generic U0100-U02FF logic, a receiving module stores the code when the expected periodic message with the sender's availability is missing while voltage is normal. No manufacturer documents U0149 publicly, and GM only lists U0146 for a single gateway. U0146 to U0148 cover gateways A to C, U0150 the fifth one. A history-only entry after a battery disconnect or flat battery is often harmless; an active one usually comes with many other U-codes. No MIL as a rule.

U0179.d: U0179 closes the J2012 block for remote restraint sensors and names sensor J, the tenth position (the letter I is used as well, see U0178). The airbag control unit checks that each connected satellite keeps sending; if sensor J falls silent, the unit stores U0179, switches on the airbag warning lamp and may disable the deployment paths that rely on it. No manufacturer documents U0179 publicly, and Chrysler's published Jeep list stops at the sixth satellite (U0176), so this code is rare. Bosch describes peripheral sensors in front, side and rear positions, which explains why up to ten slots exist. U0170 to U0178 cover sensors A to I, U0151 the airbag unit itself. No MIL; repairs only by trained staff.

U0181.d: U0181 says the module that controls automatic headlamp levelling has dropped off the bus. That module reads ride-height sensors on the axles and drives the actuator motors in the headlamps to keep the beam at the right angle under load. GM uses the code: the Saab 9-5 (2010-2011) U-code list names it Lost Communication With Headlamp Leveling Control Module, and a GM bulletin for the 2017-2021 GMC Acadia and Cadillac XT5 lists U0181 among the U-codes caused by a chafed dash harness or water in the BCM. Per GM it sets when the module's supervised periodic message is missing at 9-16 V. U0180 is the automatic lighting module, U0182 and U0183 the front and rear lighting modules. No MIL; beam height may stay fixed.

U0182.d: U0182 is logged when the front lighting control module stops talking on the bus. This module drives front lamp functions such as swivelling or adaptive beam patterns. GM lists it as Lost Communication With Lighting Control Module - Front in the Saab 9-5 (2010-2011) U-code list. Chrysler uses it for the adaptive front lighting module: a 2014 Jeep Grand Cherokee field report filed with NHTSA shows U0182-00 Lost Communication With Adaptive Front Lighting Control Module next to other network codes. GM's logic: the code sets when the module's supervised periodic message stops arriving at 9-16 V. U0181 is the headlamp levelling module, U0183 the rear lighting module. No MIL; cornering or adaptive light may fall back to a basic beam.
s: Lighting warning lamp or message in the cluster

U0188.d: U0188 means the second networked disc player or changer, module B, no longer answers. Disc changers hold several CDs or DVDs and were often mounted apart from the radio, in the dash, a console or the boot, and linked to the infotainment bus. Receiving units set a lost-communication code once the expected periodic message of a node is missing, as GM's U0100-U02FF procedure explains for all such codes. No manufacturer documents U0188 publicly; GM's U-code list has no disc player entries at all. U0187 names player A, U0189 and U0190 players C and D. Many newer cars have no disc drive, so a stray entry can also come from wrong coding. Only playback from that unit is lost; no MIL.
s: Disc source B missing or not selectable
Discs not ejected or not played
Code stored in the radio or head unit
U0188.t: Lost Communication With Digital Disc Player/Changer Module B
